# Vilivity (full text)

> The wellness standard for Black people: food, movement, rest, recovery, mind, skin and hair. Each entry opens with a plain answer, then do, avoid and when to see someone, then the evidence. Every claim has a source and a tier (A tested in people like you, B tested elsewhere or observed in Black populations, C lab only, D untested) with a strength (strong, moderate, thin). Entries are not yet clinically reviewed. This is information, not medical advice.

## Acne on dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/acne-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Acne in dark skin often leaves dark marks that last longer than the spots, so treating acne early matters most. Retinoid creams and benzoyl peroxide are the usual first treatments, and benzoyl peroxide does not bleach skin. Hair oil, cocoa butter and shea butter on spot-prone skin can clog pores.

Do:
- Treat acne early: the earlier it is treated, the less likely dark spots and scarring. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Mild acne: try a retinoid, salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Wash twice a day with a gentle cleanser and remove make-up at the end of the day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]
- Choose skincare and make-up labelled non-comedogenic (will not clog pores). [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]
- Ask a pharmacist about treatments, then a doctor if you have tried and it is not better. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]

Avoid:
- Picking or squeezing spots: it can cause scars. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]
- Scrubbing skin: it irritates and can make acne worse. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]
- Hair oil, cocoa butter or shea butter on acne-prone skin: they can clog pores and cause spots. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Skipping benzoyl peroxide for fear it bleaches: the BAD calls that a debunked myth. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]

See someone when:
- Spots are deep, painful, many, or leaving scars or dark marks (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Skin is hot, swollen and sore, which may be infection: redness can be harder to see on brown and black skin (doctor).
- Acne is affecting your mood or confidence (doctor).

## African black soap
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/black-soap-and-african-black-soap/
Module: Skin
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Nobody has tested African black soap on acne, eczema or dark marks in people. A dermatologist says it cleans about as well as other soaps, and some people find it drying. Treat it as a cleanser, not a treatment. Whether it helps your skin is untested.

Do:
- Patch-test a small area first, especially if your skin is dry or sensitive. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "African black soap" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/african-black-soap]
- Start two or three times a week, and moisturise afterwards. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "African black soap" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/african-black-soap]
- Check what is in your bar: the review describes the traditional recipe, not every product sold under the name. [tested: Ogunbiyi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33571401/]

Avoid:
- Using it as a treatment for acne, eczema or dark marks: no trial found. [tested: PubMed 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=African+black+soap]
- Using it with chemical exfoliants, or if you have eczema, or dandruff. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "African black soap" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/african-black-soap]
- Carrying on if skin turns red or stings: switch brand or stop. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "African black soap" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/african-black-soap]
- Believing a lightening or scar-fading claim on the label. [tested: Ogunbiyi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33571401/]

See someone when:
- Skin that was fine becomes sore, red or flaky after using it (doctor or dermatologist).
- Eczema, acne or a rash is not improving after a few weeks (doctor or dermatologist).
- Dark marks are spreading or you are tempted to lighten skin (see skin lightening entry; dermatologist).

## Baby skin care (newborns and infants)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/baby-skin-care/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Newborn skin needs very little: plain water baths for the first month, no cleansers or lotions, and leave vernix on. Jaundice and rashes can be harder to see on brown and black skin, so check the whites of the eyes. A large review, mostly in babies at high risk of eczema, found routine moisturiser probably made no difference to eczema.

Do:
- Bathe in plain water only for at least the first month; no cleansers, lotions or medicated wipes. [clinical guidance: Derbyshire Family Health Service (NHS), "Skin care" (your baby's first year), https://derbyshirefamilyhealthservice.nhs.uk/our-services/0-5-years/your-babys-first-year/skin-care]
- Leave vernix, the white coating at birth, on the skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Getting to know your newborn", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/after-the-birth/getting-to-know-your-newborn/]
- Check the whites of the eyes for jaundice: yellowing may be less obvious on brown or black skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Getting to know your newborn", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/after-the-birth/getting-to-know-your-newborn/]
- If your baby has jaundice in the first 24 hours, get them checked by a health professional straight away. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Getting to know your newborn", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/after-the-birth/getting-to-know-your-newborn/]
- Sunscreen only on babies 6 months or older; protect younger babies with shade and clothing. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]

Avoid:
- Cleansers, lotions and medicated wipes in the first month. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Getting to know your newborn", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/after-the-birth/getting-to-know-your-newborn/]
- Routine moisturiser to prevent eczema: probably makes no difference, and the trials were mostly in babies at high risk. [tested: Kelleher 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36373988/]
- Treating dry, cracked skin in an overdue baby with products: it is usually the vernix absorbed before birth. [clinical guidance: Derbyshire Family Health Service (NHS), "Skin care" (your baby's first year), https://derbyshirefamilyhealthservice.nhs.uk/our-services/0-5-years/your-babys-first-year/skin-care]

See someone when:
- Jaundice in the first 24 hours, or yellowing that is spreading, or a baby who is sleepy or feeding poorly (doctor, midwife or NHS 111 in the UK).
- Skin is blistered, crusty, leaking or hot (urgent doctor or NHS 111 in the UK).
- Eczema or a rash that is not settling (doctor or health visitor in the UK).

## Collagen supplements for skin and joints
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/collagen-supplements/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Collagen supplements may add a little skin moisture in trials, but the best-quality trials and the ones not paid for by the industry found no clear skin effect. Our search found no trial in Black participants or on dark skin. Check labels for fish if you are allergic, and treat promised skin changes as unproven.

Do:
- Check the source on the label before you take it: marine collagen may not suit you if you have a fish allergy. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Collagen Peptides: Benefits and Side Effects", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/what-do-collagen-peptides-do]
- Judge it by the best-quality trials: those not paid for by the industry found no skin effect. [tested: Myung 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40324552/]

Avoid:
- Paying for it to change wrinkles, hydration or elasticity: the careful meta-analysis found no clinical evidence for that. [tested: Myung 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40324552/]
- Assuming a supplement is checked: Cleveland Clinic notes supplements are not well regulated, and stomach upset can happen. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Collagen Peptides: Benefits and Side Effects", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/what-do-collagen-peptides-do]

See someone when:
- Itching, swelling or breathing trouble after taking it (urgent care).
- Dark patches, new marks or skin changes you are trying to treat (dermatologist; see skin ageing and dark marks).
- Stomach upset that continues (pharmacist or doctor).

## Dark circles under the eyes
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/dark-circles-under-the-eyes/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark circles under the eyes can come from pigment, thin skin showing blood vessels, or lost volume, and the cause decides the treatment. A systematic review found many treatments help some people, from creams and peels to fillers, but the studies are weak and not specific to Black skin. Daily sunscreen is a sensible start.

Do:
- Ask a dermatologist to work out which kind you have: pigment, structure, blood vessels or a mix. [tested: Michelle 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32740208/]
- Apply sunscreen daily, SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- For pigment-type circles, creams and peels are the treatments the review found useful. [tested: Michelle 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32740208/]

Avoid:
- Expecting one cream to fix every kind: fillers or fat grafting suit volume loss, surgery suits loose skin, creams suit pigment. [tested: Michelle 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32740208/]
- Taking any claim on trust: the review calls the evidence scarce and weak and says to read recommendations selectively. [tested: Michelle 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32740208/]

See someone when:
- Swelling, pain or vision changes around the eyes (doctor urgently).
- Circles that appeared suddenly, are one-sided, or follow a new medicine (doctor).
- You are considering fillers, lasers or surgery (dermatologist or an accredited specialist).

## Dark marks after acne (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/dark-marks-after-acne/
Module: Skin
Tier: A thin (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark marks after spots are common in dark skin and slow to fade. One trial in Black adults found a prescription retinoid cream lightened them, though many users were irritated. Treating spots early and wearing sunscreen are the main advice. Bleaching products can do real harm.

Do:
- Treat the spots early so fewer marks form. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Ask a doctor or dermatologist about a prescription retinoid cream. [tested: Bulengo-Ransby 1993, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8479462/]
- Wear sunscreen daily: broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, tinted with iron oxide if you can. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Be patient: a mark a few shades darker usually fades in 6 to 12 months. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Choose products labelled fragrance-free or for sensitive skin. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]

Avoid:
- Bleaching creams of unknown content, or liquid bleach. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Imported skin products that may hide steroids or mercury. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Picking or scrubbing marks: irritation can worsen pigmentation. [tested: Davis 2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20725554/]

See someone when:
- Acne is leaving marks, cysts or scars (doctor or dermatologist: early treatment is the advice).
- A dark mark is growing, new in an unusual place, or does not fade over many months (dermatologist).
- You are considering a peel or laser (dermatologist who treats dark skin: irritation can worsen marks).

## Dark or swollen lips
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/dark-or-swollen-lips/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark lips are often a harmless variation in pigment. Smoking and an allergy to a lip product can also darken lips, and a single new dark spot needs a clinician to look at it. Sudden lip swelling can be an allergic reaction, so call emergency services (999 in the UK) if your throat tightens or breathing is hard.

Do:
- Tell your doctor if you smoke or use tobacco: it was linked to pigmentation of the lips in a small Indian study. [tested: Sarswathi 2003, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14705454/]
- Stop a lip product you think is causing itching, scaling or darkening, and ask a doctor or dermatologist: allergy to lip product ingredients can darken lips. [tested: Figueiredo 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39396149/]
- See a dermatologist before any laser or peel on the lips: a Thai study found benefit in 20 people, with no untreated group. [tested: Ng 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36037096/]

Avoid:
- Ignoring a single new or changing dark patch on a lip: a benign type exists, but it can look like melanoma and needs a clinician. [tested: Ho 1993, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8425968/]
- Waiting at home if your lips, mouth or throat suddenly swell: call 999. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Angioedema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/angioedema/]

See someone when:
- One new, growing or changing dark spot on a lip (doctor, then dermatologist, within weeks).
- Dark, itchy or scaly lips after starting a lip product, toothpaste or medicine (doctor or dermatologist).
- Your lips, mouth, throat or tongue swell suddenly, or breathing or swallowing is hard (999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).
- Lips that swell again and again with no clear cause (doctor, who may refer for allergy testing).

## Dark velvety patches on the neck and folds (acanthosis nigricans)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/acanthosis-nigricans/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark, thick, velvety patches in the neck, armpits or groin are called acanthosis nigricans. They are often a sign of insulin resistance, and the UK's NHS says to have them checked by a doctor. Scrubbing and lightening creams do not treat the cause. They fade over time once the cause is treated.

Do:
- See a doctor for new dark patches: it could be a sign of an underlying condition. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acanthosis nigricans", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/]
- Ask about the cause, which is most often obesity, and about hormone or insulin treatment. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acanthosis nigricans", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/]
- If a medicine is the cause, ask about changing it. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acanthosis nigricans", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/]
- Ask for a dermatologist if you want help with the appearance after the cause is addressed. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acanthosis nigricans", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/]

Avoid:
- Treating it as a skin-only problem: the UK's NHS says there is no specific treatment for the patches themselves. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acanthosis nigricans", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/]
- Ignoring it: in 89 African Americans with the patches, 19 had diabetes and insulin levels rose with severity of neck involvement. [tested: Stuart 1997, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9264219/]

See someone when:
- New dark, velvety patches on the neck, armpits or groin (doctor).
- You have any skin change you are unsure about (doctor).

## Eczema on dark skin (atopic eczema, including babies)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/eczema-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Eczema on dark skin often looks grey, purple, brown or darker, not red, with very dry, thickened or bumpy skin. Moisturising at least twice a day, washing with emollient instead of soap, and a pharmacist or doctor for steroid creams are the standard care. A trial of a prescription cream included many Black participants.

Do:
- Moisturise (emollient) at least 2 times a day and carry on even when it improves. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Wash with an emollient instead of soap. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Keep cool and keep nails short, with anti-scratch mittens for babies. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Use a fragrance-free cream or ointment, hypoallergenic, made for sensitive skin. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Eczema types: Atopic dermatitis overview", https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/eczema/types/atopic-dermatitis]
- See a pharmacist for mild eczema and a doctor if treatments are not helping. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]

Avoid:
- Aqueous cream: it can irritate skin and make eczema worse. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Soap, washing detergent and fabrics that set it off. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Scratching: gently rub the area instead. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- Changing the diet (including a breastfeeding mother) unless a doctor says to. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]

See someone when:
- Eczema is blistered, crusty, leaking, painful, warm or suddenly worse, or you feel unwell (urgent doctor or NHS 111 in the UK: it may be infected).
- Treatments are not helping, or a baby has eczema and you are unsure (doctor).
- Skin stays darker, lighter or thickened after flares (doctor or dermatologist).

## Finding a dermatologist who knows dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/finding-a-dermatologist-for-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark skin is under-represented in textbooks, and in one test dermatologists and AI both did worse on dark-skin photos, so it is fair to ask a clinician about their experience. In the UK a GP referral is the route; the BAD hub shows how common conditions look on black and brown skin.

Do:
- Ask your doctor for a referral if treatment is not helping; the UK's NHS may refer you to a dermatologist. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Read the BAD hub on how common conditions look on black and brown skin before the appointment. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Ask what share of their patients have skin of colour and where they trained for it. [common advice, untested: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026, https://www.blackhealth.org/articles/how-to-find-a-black-dermatologist/]
- Photograph the area in bright natural light on a neutral background and take close-ups. [common advice, untested: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026, https://www.blackhealth.org/articles/how-to-find-a-black-dermatologist/]

Avoid:
- Assuming a specialist will recognise your condition from a textbook picture: the dark-skin share of images in medical textbooks is small. [tested: Louie 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501717/]
- Treating a US directory as a UK guide: the Black Health article is about US clinics and insurance. [common advice, untested: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026, https://www.blackhealth.org/articles/how-to-find-a-black-dermatologist/]

See someone when:
- A skin problem is not improving with treatment (doctor).
- A mole or mark is changing (doctor, soon).
- You were told "it is nothing" and the area is still changing (ask for a second opinion).

## How skin conditions look on dark skin (redness, rashes, rosacea, sunburn)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/conditions-look-different-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Redness on dark skin can look pink, purple, brown, grey or just a subtle darkening, so it is easy to miss. Eczema, rosacea and sunburn all happen on dark skin and are often under-diagnosed. Compare the affected area with your unaffected skin, and tell your doctor what changed.

Do:
- Look for colour change, comparing the affected area with unaffected skin. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Remember that sunburn can happen on dark skin even if it is uncommon, and may not look red. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]
- Look for infection signs such as hot, swollen skin: redness can be harder to see on brown and black skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/]
- Look at the UK's NHS eczema gallery, which shows dark brown skin as well as light, so you know the range of appearance. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Atopic eczema", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atopic-eczema/]
- For shingles, look for blotches on one side of the body that become itchy blisters: the UK's NHS says the redness can be harder to see on brown and black skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Shingles", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/shingles/]

Avoid:
- Assuming no redness means no inflammation: in Black patients with rosacea, many had skin-coloured papules rather than classic redness. [tested: Dlova 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28639713/]
- Relying on textbook photos to judge your own skin: the dark-skin share of images in four core medical textbooks was 4.5%. [tested: Louie 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501717/]
- Assuming you cannot burn: the BAD says it can happen. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/support-resources/skin-of-colour/]

See someone when:
- Redness-free but warm, swollen, painful or spreading skin (doctor or NHS 111 in the UK).
- A rash that has not settled in two weeks or keeps coming back (doctor).
- A facial rash with bumps and no obvious cause (doctor, then dermatologist: rosacea can be missed).

## Keloids and piercings
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/keloids-and-piercings/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Keloids run in families and are much more common in people of African ancestry. Nobody has tested whether avoiding piercings prevents them, but the UK's NHS advises prone people to avoid piercings and tattoos. If one forms, early treatment is the advice.

Do:
- If you are prone to keloids, avoid piercings and tattoos. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- Treat acne early to reduce scarring. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- See a doctor early about a raised scar: treatment started early may stop it growing. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- Think before elective surgery: any skin injury can trigger one. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- Ask what the UK's NHS lists as options: steroid injections or cream, silicone dressings or gels, cryotherapy or laser. None removes a keloid; they improve how it looks. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]

Avoid:
- Expecting any treatment to remove a keloid: the UK's NHS says treatments only improve appearance. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- Surgery to cut out a keloid on its own: the UK's NHS says it is likely to grow back bigger. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Keloid scars", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/keloid-scars/]
- Metal-backed earrings on a piercing that has already formed a lump: one series linked the metal backs to the site. [tested: Hochman 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25715880/]

See someone when:
- A scar is raised, growing beyond the original wound, itchy or painful (dermatologist or doctor, early).
- An earlobe lump follows a piercing and keeps growing (dermatologist).
- A keloid returns after removal (dermatologist).

## Laser hair removal on dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/laser-hair-removal-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Laser hair removal can work in medium to dark skin, but the laser also targets skin pigment, so burns and dark or pale marks are more likely. A review of trials found Nd:YAG lasers gave fewer dark marks than light-based IPL devices. Choose an experienced clinician and ask which laser they use.

Do:
- Ask which device will be used: a review found Nd:YAG laser gave fewer dark marks than IPL in skin types III-VI. [tested: Dorgham 2020, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31587390/]
- Choose a clinician who treats dark skin regularly, with conservative settings and sequential, lower-energy treatments. [tested: Dreifus 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/]
- Practise strict sun protection before and after treatment. [tested: Dreifus 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/]
- If thick, dark hair on your face, neck or chest is the problem, see a doctor before only removing it: the UK's NHS says hormones are the usual cause and lists shaving or waxing, eflornithine cream for the face, the pill and weight loss; laser and electrolysis last longer but are usually not permanent or on the NHS. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hirsutism" (excessive hair growth), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hirsutism/]

Avoid:
- Assuming any laser is safe for dark skin: melanin competes for the laser energy, so burns, blisters, scars and dark or pale marks are more likely. [tested: Dreifus 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/]
- Assuming one device is best: alexandrite laser reduced hair counts more than IPL, but the trials are small and mixed. [tested: Dorgham 2020, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31587390/]

See someone when:
- Blisters, burns, or dark or pale patches after treatment (dermatologist).
- Thick, dark hair on the face, body or chest, especially with irregular periods (doctor: the UK's NHS says a blood test may check hormones); urgent if it starts suddenly with a deeper voice or growing muscles.
- Razor bumps or ingrown hairs are the reason you want laser (see the shaving entry; dermatologist).

## Melasma
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/melasma/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Melasma is brown or greyish patches on the face, linked to sun, pregnancy and hormonal medicines. There is no cure, but sun protection plus a prescribed cream usually helps, and it can return. The best-studied cream is hydroquinone, in trials that were not specifically in Black people, so see a dermatologist before lightening products.

Do:
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat and broad-spectrum sun cream, SPF 30 or above with a high UVA rating. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]
- Choose sun cream with iron oxides for added protection against visible light. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]
- Avoid sunbeds. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]
- Ask your prescriber about triggers such as the contraceptive pill and hormone therapy before changing anything. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]
- Ask about skin camouflage if you want to cover patches while treating. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]

Avoid:
- Expecting a cure: there is none, and it may come back in another pregnancy. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]
- Hydroquinone for more than a few weeks at a time without advice: it can irritate, over-lighten or occasionally darken skin. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient information leaflet "Melasma", https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/melasma/]

See someone when:
- Dark patches appear on your face and you are not sure what they are (doctor or dermatologist, to rule out other causes).
- A treatment irritates, darkens or lightens skin (stop and see a dermatologist).
- Patches appeared with a new pill or hormone treatment (prescriber).

## Moisturising and 'ashy' skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/moisturising-and-ashy-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: A thin (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Ashiness is dry skin showing as a grey-white look on dark skin. In a small trial of women with darker skin types, a moisturising body wash or mild bar used regularly reduced dryness and ashiness, with no untreated comparison group. Whether Black skin is naturally drier is contested.

Do:
- Moisturise straight after bathing, once you have patted the skin dry. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Emollients", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/emollients/]
- Smooth moisturiser on; do not rub it in hard. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Emollients", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/emollients/]
- Use a mild or moisturising cleanser regularly. [tested: Feng 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21464886/]
- Choose fragrance-free or sensitive-skin products if your skin is easily irritated. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, skin care for skin of colour, https://www.aad.org/public/skin-hair-nails/skin-care/skin-of-color]
- Take moisturiser from a tub with a clean spoon, or use a pump. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Emollients", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/emollients/]

Avoid:
- Any product that stings or burns: stop using it. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, skin care for skin of colour, https://www.aad.org/public/skin-hair-nails/skin-care/skin-of-color]
- Believing ashiness is dirt or illness: in the trial it behaved as dryness. [tested: Feng 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21464886/]
- Ordinary soap on very dry skin: the UK's NHS suggests an emollient soap substitute for washing. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Emollients", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/emollients/]
- Naked flames or smoking near thick emollient on skin or clothes: it is a fire risk. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Emollients", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/emollients/]

See someone when:
- Dry patches are cracked, red, weeping or itch badly or keep returning (doctor or dermatologist).
- Dryness spreads, thickens or leaves darker patches (dermatologist).
- A rash covers large areas or a child has persistent itchy, dry skin (doctor).

## Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/shaving-and-razor-bumps/
Module: Skin
Tier: A thin (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Razor bumps happen when tightly curled hair grows back into the skin after shaving. In one trial of Black men, shaving two or three times a week gave fewer ingrown hairs than daily shaving, but bump counts and doctor-rated severity did not differ. Small trials found hair-removal creams gave fewer bumps but more irritation.

Do:
- Shave with the grain, on soft skin: after a shower, or with a warm, damp washcloth held on first. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Razor bumps: how to prevent them", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/hair/razor-bump-prevention]
- Avoid stretching the skin, use a razor with fewer blades, or switch to clippers. [common advice, untested: US Army (army.mil), R. Sanders PA, "Simple shaving tips to promote healthier skin", 8 Jul 2019, https://www.army.mil/article/224058/simple_shaving_tips_to_promote_healthier_skin]
- Shave every two or three days rather than daily if ingrown hairs are your main problem. [tested: Daniel 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23652888/]
- Use a moisturising shaving cream and a soothing aftershave. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Razor bumps: how to prevent them", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/hair/razor-bump-prevention]
- Grow the hair out if bumps keep coming back: the UK's NHS says not shaving is the best prevention, on any shaved site (face, neck, legs, armpits, chest, back, pubic area); if you do shave, go with the direction of growth and leave at least 1mm of stubble. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Ingrown hairs", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ingrown-hairs/]

Avoid:
- Tweezing hairs out: the review lists it with shaving as a trigger. [tested: Perry 2002, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11807473/]
- A dull razor: replace a disposable after 5 to 7 shaves. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Razor bumps: how to prevent them", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/hair/razor-bump-prevention]
- Expecting advanced shaving products to cut bumps: bump counts were the same, though users felt better and itched less. [tested: Daniel 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23652888/]
- Hair-removal creams on irritated skin: they caused more irritation than a razor. [tested: Kindred 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21916277/]

See someone when:
- Bumps become pus-filled, painful, or leave dark marks or scars (doctor or dermatologist).
- You are considering laser or a prescription cream (dermatologist: both are clinic or prescription treatments).
- You need to shave for work or service and it keeps flaring (occupational health or doctor).
- Small blisters that burst to leave sores, with tingling, burning or itching around the genitals, thighs or bottom (sexual health clinic, soon: the UK's NHS says genital herpes sores may be less red on brown and black skin, so test rather than guess).

## Shea butter
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/shea-butter/
Module: Skin
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Shea butter has been used on skin and hair in West Africa for generations, but no controlled trial has tested plain shea butter on skin. The studies that exist used shea-containing creams or compounds taken from shea, which are not the same thing. Whether it beats other moisturisers is untested.

Do:
- Patch-test a small area first. [common advice, untested: Healthline, "What is shea butter", https://www.healthline.com/health/beauty-skin-care/what-is-shea-butter]
- If you have a latex allergy, use refined shea only: raw shea contains latex. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Shea butter benefits" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/shea-butter-benefits]
- Keep it cool, dry and out of sunlight, and scoop with a clean, dry spoon. [common advice, untested: Baraka Shea Butter (a seller), "How to store shea butter", https://www.barakasheabutter.com/blogs/baraka-blogs/how-to-store-shea-butter]
- Use it as a moisturiser, not a treatment for eczema, wounds or scars. [tested: Micali 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29368843/]

Avoid:
- Claims that it cures eczema, stretch marks or scars: none is tested. [tested: Micali 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29368843/]
- Using it on acne-prone skin or with dandruff, say dermatologists: it may clog pores, and the dandruff yeast can grow in it. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Shea butter benefits" (dermatologist quoted), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/shea-butter-benefits]
- Butter that smells sour, sharp or chemical: it has gone off. [common advice, untested: Baraka Shea Butter (a seller), "How to store shea butter", https://www.barakasheabutter.com/blogs/baraka-blogs/how-to-store-shea-butter]

See someone when:
- Eczema or dry patches are cracked, weeping, or not settling after a few weeks of moisturising (doctor or dermatologist).
- A wound has not healed in four weeks (doctor or nurse).
- You get a rash or swelling after using it.

## Skin ageing in dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/skin-ageing-in-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Reviews say darker skin tends to show lines and sun damage later, helped by more melanin and a thicker, more compact dermis. It is, though, more prone to uneven colour and dark spots. These reviews cover several groups, not only Black people. Daily sunscreen and not smoking are the best-supported habits.

Do:
- Apply sunscreen daily before going outdoors: SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum, water-resistant. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Do not smoke: it speeds up skin ageing. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Do not use tanning beds. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-in-your-20s]
- Cleanse gently and avoid scrubbing. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]

Avoid:
- Scrubbing and over-exfoliating. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-in-your-20s]
- Assuming you are immune: darker skin is more vulnerable to uneven colour and dark spots. [tested: Vashi 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26962390/]
- Smoking. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]

See someone when:
- A new dark spot that is growing, changing or itchy (doctor: it could be a mole, see the skin cancer entry).
- Dark spots that bother you (doctor or dermatologist, before lightening products).
- Skin irritation from an anti-ageing product (stop; pharmacist or doctor).

## Skin cancer and moles on dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/skin-cancer-and-moles-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Skin cancer is much rarer in Black people, but it can happen, and when melanoma does, outcomes are worse. It is often on palms, soles or under nails rather than sun-exposed skin. Check your whole skin, including those places, and have any new, changing or non-healing mark looked at early.

Do:
- Check your whole body, including palms, soles, toenails, fingernails and between the toes. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to check your skin for skin cancer", https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/find/check-skin]
- Look at moles that change size, shape or colour, or are uneven, mixed in colour or large. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of melanoma skin cancer", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms/]
- Know that rarer melanomas can affect the soles of the feet, palms, eyes or genitals. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of melanoma skin cancer", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms/]
- Apply sunscreen daily before going outdoors: broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, water-resistant (general AAD advice; see the sunscreen entry for dark skin). [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Record what you find on a body mole map so you can spot changes. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to check your skin for skin cancer", https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/find/check-skin]

Avoid:
- Assuming dark skin means no risk: melanoma is far rarer but registry data show it is found at a later stage and survival is lower. [tested: Cormier 2006, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17000949/]
- Ignoring a dark streak under a nail or a new mark on a palm or sole: acral melanoma makes up about a third of melanomas in Black patients. [tested: Bradford 2009, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19380664/]
- Waiting on a sore that will not heal: in dark-skinned groups squamous cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, often on non-sun-exposed sites. [tested: Gloster 2006, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17052479/]

See someone when:
- A new mole, or a mole that changes size, shape or colour (doctor, then dermatologist).
- A dark streak in a nail, or a new patch on a palm or sole (doctor or dermatologist, soon).
- A sore, scaly or lumpy area that does not heal (doctor or dermatologist).
- Any new skin change you are unsure about, including around the genitals (doctor or sexual health clinic).

## Skin lightening and bleaching creams
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/skin-lightening-creams/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Many skin lightening creams contain mercury, strong steroids or high-strength hydroquinone, and reported cases show serious skin and kidney harm. Lightening the whole body is not supported as safe. If dark patches or marks are the worry, there are treatments that target them and are tested in dark skin.

Do:
- Read the label for mercury, mercurous chloride, calomel, mercuric or mercurio. [clinical guidance: US FDA consumer update, "Mercury poisoning linked to skin products", https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/mercury-poisoning-linked-skin-products]
- If you find mercury on a label, stop using it, wash your hands and skin, and call a doctor or poison centre. [clinical guidance: US FDA consumer update, "Mercury poisoning linked to skin products", https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/mercury-poisoning-linked-skin-products]
- See a doctor or dermatologist for dark patches, if home care is not working. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Wear sunscreen daily on any skin you are treating. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]

Avoid:
- Creams with no label, no ingredient list, or only a foreign-language one. [clinical guidance: US FDA consumer update, "Mercury poisoning linked to skin products", https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/mercury-poisoning-linked-skin-products]
- Imported products that may hold undisclosed steroids or mercury. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Liquid bleach on the skin, ever. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- Letting a cream touch children: mercury exposure can reach family members. [clinical guidance: US FDA consumer update, "Mercury poisoning linked to skin products", https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/mercury-poisoning-linked-skin-products]

See someone when:
- Skin has become thin, streaky, bruises easily, or has new stretch-like marks (dermatologist or doctor).
- Blue-black or grey marks appear on the face, especially over cheeks and temples (dermatologist).
- You feel unwell after using a cream that may contain mercury, for example swelling, a metallic taste, sore gums or nausea, or you notice changes in your urine (doctor, the same day if severe).
- You want to stop and the skin darkens or flares when you do (dermatologist).

## Skincare routine basics (and Korean multi-step routines)
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/skincare-routine-basics/
Module: Skin
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A short routine is what dermatologist guidance recommends: gentle cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen. Scrubbing irritates and over-exfoliating is a common reason people see a dermatologist. I found no human study showing a long multi-step routine, Korean or otherwise, improves dark skin. Stop any product that burns or stings.

Do:
- Cleanse gently with warm water and your fingertips, not tools. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Use a fragrance-free moisturiser, with ceramides if your skin looks ashy. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dry skin remedies for darker skin tones", https://www.aad.org/public/darker-skin/secrets/dry-skin/dry-skin-remedies-darker-skin]
- Apply sunscreen daily: SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum, water-resistant. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Choose products for your skin type: oily, dry, normal, combination or sensitive. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- If a product irritates your skin, stop using it right away. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-in-your-20s]

Avoid:
- Scrubbing: it irritates and can worsen any skin condition, including acne. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]
- Overusing exfoliating products you see on social media: dermatologists frequently treat the damage. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-in-your-20s]
- Hot water and long baths on dry skin. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dry skin remedies for darker skin tones", https://www.aad.org/public/darker-skin/secrets/dry-skin/dry-skin-remedies-darker-skin]
- Smoking: the AAD's skin-care tips say don't smoke. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/care/skin-care-tips-dermatologists-use]

See someone when:
- Skin is burning, stinging, peeling or breaking out after a product (stop it; pharmacist or doctor if it does not settle).
- Dark patches, spots or irritation that a basic routine does not fix (doctor or dermatologist).
- A skin change you are unsure about (doctor).

## Stretch marks and fading scars
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/stretch-marks-and-scar-fading/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No cream, butter or oil has been shown to stop stretch marks, and a trial of cocoa butter in pregnant women found it made no difference. They usually fade over time. Retinoid creams or hyaluronic acid may help new ones, and laser carries a higher risk of dark marks and burns in dark skin.

Do:
- Expect stretch marks to fade over time, though not always completely. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Stretch marks", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stretch-marks/]
- Ask a pharmacist or doctor about retinoid cream or hyaluronic acid, if you are not pregnant. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Stretch marks", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stretch-marks/]
- If you want laser or other devices, see a dermatologist who treats dark skin often and ask for cautious settings and strict sun protection. [tested: Dreifus 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/]
- Raised, growing scars are a different problem; see the keloid entry. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Stretch marks", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stretch-marks/]

Avoid:
- Paying for cocoa butter to prevent stretch marks in pregnancy: no difference from placebo lotion. [tested: Osman 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18715434/]
- Retinoid creams in pregnancy: they may harm the baby. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Stretch marks", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stretch-marks/]
- Laser or energy devices from anyone without dark-skin experience: pigment competes with the target and raises the risk of dark or pale marks, blisters and scars. [tested: Dreifus 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/]

See someone when:
- Stretch marks appear with no pregnancy, puberty or weight change (doctor: rarely a hormone condition).
- A scar is raised, growing or itchy (doctor or dermatologist, early).
- Dark or pale patches, blisters or scars follow a laser treatment (dermatologist).

## Sunscreen on dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/sunscreen-on-dark-skin/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Dark skin burns less easily and melanoma is rarer, but when it happens it is found later and survival is worse. In a small test on normal skin, visible light left darker, longer-lasting pigment than long-wave UVA. A broad-spectrum sunscreen is reasonable; whether sunscreen prevents melanoma in Black skin is untested.

Do:
- Wear a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher daily; a tint with iron oxide blends in and guards against visible light. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]
- The UK's NHS advises at least SPF 30 and 4-star UVA, applied generously and reapplied every two hours in strong sun. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sunscreen and sun safety", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/sunscreen-and-sun-safety/]
- Check palms, soles, nails and under the nails now and then for new or changing marks. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Melanoma skin cancer: symptoms", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms/]
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat and avoid the midday sun when you can. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "How to fade dark spots", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots]

Avoid:
- Assuming a new dark mark on a palm, sole or under a nail is a bruise: if it has not gone in a few weeks, see a doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Melanoma skin cancer: symptoms", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms/]
- Assuming dark skin cannot get skin cancer: the UK's NHS says people of all skin tones can. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sunscreen and sun safety", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/sunscreen-and-sun-safety/]
- Treating the SPF test rule as proof that sunscreen does not work on you. [tested: US 2026, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-201/subpart-C/section-201.327]

See someone when:
- A dark streak under or around a nail, or a new or changing dark spot on a palm, sole, finger or toe (dermatologist, promptly).
- A mole or mark that is growing, changing colour, bleeding or not healing (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Any wound on the foot that does not heal (doctor): acral melanoma is commonly found late.

## Sweat, body odour and deodorant
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/body-odour-and-sweat/
Module: Skin
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Sweating and odour are normal. I found nothing showing dark skin needs different handling. Antiperspirants, which reduce sweat, are the main tool; deodorants only mask smell. Loose, breathable clothing helps. If sweating is heavy, lasting, at night or running in your family, see a doctor.

Do:
- Ask a pharmacist for a stronger antiperspirant rather than a deodorant. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Wear loose-fitting clothes, and wear socks that absorb moisture changed twice a day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Wear leather shoes, and vary them day to day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Use armpit shields to protect clothing if needed. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]

Avoid:
- Tight clothes and synthetic fabrics such as nylon. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Alcohol and spicy food if they set it off. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]
- Enclosed boots or sports shoes that make feet sweat more. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/excessive-sweating-hyperhidrosis/]

See someone when:
- Sweating has lasted at least 6 months, happens weekly, or stops you getting on with your day (doctor).
- Sweating happens at night, or there is a family history (doctor).
- You take medicine for another condition and the sweating started after (doctor).

## Vitiligo
URL: https://vilivity.com/skin/vitiligo/
Module: Skin
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Vitiligo is loss of skin colour in patches, an autoimmune condition, not an infection. Patches are usually permanent, though treatment can bring back colour in some people: a prescription cream did in trials, with responses seen across skin types (not compared type by type). Pale patches burn more easily, so use sunscreen. Camouflage cream can cover them.

Do:
- See a doctor for diagnosis: they may use a Wood's lamp, a UV lamp that makes patches easier to see. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]
- Use a high SPF sunscreen on pale patches: they are more vulnerable to sunburn. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]
- Try skin camouflage cream if you want to cover small patches. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]
- Ask about treatment if the patches are severe or making you unhappy. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]

Avoid:
- Expecting patches to return to normal by themselves: they are usually permanent. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]
- Leaving pale patches unprotected in strong sun. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]
- Treating pale patches yourself as a fungal infection before a doctor confirms: vitiligo can be mistaken for conditions such as pityriasis versicolor, a fungal pigment loss. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitiligo", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitiligo/]

See someone when:
- Pale or white patches appear on your skin (doctor, to confirm it is vitiligo and not another condition).
- The patches are spreading or affecting your confidence or mood (doctor, then dermatologist).
- A treatment makes skin sore or irritated (the prescriber).

## Babies' and children's hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/children-and-babies-hair/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Children's hair is best handled the way adults' is: gently, with hair wet and conditioned for detangling. Tight braids and updos are linked to traction alopecia in Black girls; larger braids, fewer extensions and looser styles are advised. Cradle cap is harmless. My search found nothing aimed at adoptive parents, but the same guidance applies.

Do:
- Detangle only when hair is wet and conditioned. [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]
- Choose larger braids or locs, fewer extensions, and loosen tight styles. [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]
- Remove extensions at least monthly and allow 4 to 6 weeks of recovery between long styles. [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]
- For cradle cap, massage in emollient or coconut oil, brush gently, then wash with baby shampoo. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Cradle cap", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cradle-cap/]
- Use a satin pillowcase. [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]

Avoid:
- Tight braids and cornrows: in one caregiver survey cornrows were associated with traction alopecia among girls from non-dermatology clinics only, not the dermatology clinic group. [tested: Rucker 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20728245/]
- Olive oil, peanut oil, soap, adult shampoos or fragranced products on cradle cap. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Cradle cap", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cradle-cap/]
- Picking cradle cap crusts: it can raise the risk of infection. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Cradle cap", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cradle-cap/]

See someone when:
- Thinning, bald patches or a sore scalp from a hairstyle (doctor or paediatrician).
- Cradle cap that does not improve after a few weeks, or covers the whole body (doctor).
- Crusts that bleed or leak fluid, or swollen areas (doctor).

## Braids, cornrows and twists for men and boys
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/mens-and-boys-braids-cornrows-and-twists/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested braid styles in men or boys. A South African school survey found traction alopecia mostly in girls with relaxed hair, and neck bumps (acne keloidalis nuchae) in boys with frequent haircuts. Dermatologists' advice is the same for everyone: loose braids, hairline left free, rest between styles.

Do:
- Keep braids and cornrows loose; scalp pain after installation means they are too tight. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Take braids out within about 6 weeks and leave the delicate hairline out of the braids. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Braid in alternate directions rather than always pulling the same way. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Moisturise hair and scalp regularly between wash days, braided or not. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Hiding a thinning hairline with the same tight style that caused it: a dermatologist says this is common and delays help. [common advice, untested: BlackDoctor (a dermatologist is speaking; her name is not in the captions), YouTube, "A Dermatologist Explains: How to Reverse Traction Alopecia", https://youtu.be/0HEL_WF-HaQ]
- Heavy extensions or beads, which add weight and tension. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Assuming very close, frequent cuts at the nape are free of risk: in a school survey neck bumps went with frequent haircuts (association only). [tested: Khumalo 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17553035/]

See someone when:
- A hairline or crown that is thinning or receding (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Firm bumps, pus or scarring at the back of the neck (doctor or dermatologist).
- A child with scalp pain, bumps or patchy hair loss after braids (doctor).

## Braids, twists and extensions: tension, how long, itch
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/braids-twists-and-extensions/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Braids that hurt are too tight; pain after installation means pull on the scalp. Dermatologists advise taking braids out within about six weeks and extensions within eight, giving your scalp a break, and keeping the hairline loose. Itch can come from build-up or an allergy to synthetic hair or glue. "Protective" has never been tested.

Do:
- Ask for braids to be installed loosely by a trained professional; scalp pain means too tight. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Take braids out within 6 weeks and extensions within 8. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Consider leaving out the delicate hairline edges, and avoid heavy beads or very long extensions. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Cleanse the scalp between installs: diluted shampoo, condition mainly the lengths, blot dry and let it dry fully. [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]
- Alternate the direction of parts so the stress does not sit in one place. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Tight braids or weaves on relaxed hair. [tested: Khumalo 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/]
- Braiding soon after a relaxer. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Leaving a style in because it still looks neat while your scalp stings. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]
- Scratching or ignoring an itch that comes with a rash: synthetic hair and adhesives can cause contact dermatitis. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

See someone when:
- Pain, bumps, pus, crusting or a rash that does not settle when the style comes out (doctor).
- Hair thinning at the edges or temples (doctor, then dermatologist).
- A shiny scalp with no visible hair openings (dermatologist soon: scarring).
- Itch with flaking that has not settled after four weeks of an anti-dandruff shampoo (doctor).

## CCCA: scarring hair loss at the crown
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/
Module: Hair
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: CCCA is a scarring hair loss that starts as a thin patch at the crown and spreads outwards. It mostly affects women of African descent and men can have it. Scarred follicles do not regrow, so treatment aims to stop it spreading. The earlier a dermatologist sees it, the more hair is kept.

Do:
- See a dermatologist early; the BAD says early assessment and treatment matter most. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Ask about a scalp biopsy if the diagnosis is unclear. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Reduce heat styling, tight styles and hardening gels or sprays; relax professionally no more than every 6 to 8 weeks. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Protect bald areas from the sun. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Do not ignore pain, tenderness or pimples caused by a hairstyle; remove or adjust the style. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]

Avoid:
- Quick-fix online products for crown thinning. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Relying on over-the-counter minoxidil alone: a Black Health article attributes to the AAD that it cannot stop CCCA. [common advice, untested: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "Hair loss in Black women: CCCA", updated July 2026 (a US advocacy site; the page carries a sponsored telehealth promotion; it attributes its minoxidil statement to the AAD, whose page was not opened), https://www.blackhealth.org/articles/hair-loss-black-women-ccca/]
- Leaving a pulling style in while the scalp stings. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]

See someone when:
- A thin patch at the crown that is slowly growing, or breakage at the crown (dermatologist, soon).
- A shiny scalp with no visible hair openings (dermatologist soon).
- Burning, itch, tingling or soreness at the crown (doctor or dermatologist).
- Hair thinning in a man at the crown with itch (dermatologist; men get CCCA too).

## Chebe powder: length retention, growth claims and safety
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/chebe-powder-and-hair-length/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Chebe is a traditional herbal hair powder, mixed with oil or butter and coated on the lengths. My search found no study of it on hair or in people. A doctor quoted by PureWow says it does not grow hair. Any benefit is untested, so patch test first and avoid heavy coating on thin strands.

Do:
- Patch test first, since its side effects are unknown. [common advice, untested: PureWow, "Chebe powder for hair" (quotes Dr Sunitha Posina, an internist, and two hair professionals), https://purewow.com/beauty/chebe-powder-for-hair]
- Use it as a conditioning treatment on the lengths: a stylist suggests a weekly treatment left on for at least an hour. [common advice, untested: PureWow, "Chebe powder for hair" (quotes Dr Sunitha Posina, an internist, and two hair professionals), https://purewow.com/beauty/chebe-powder-for-hair]

Avoid:
- Heavy application on thin or fine strands: a stylist warns it is heavy and can cause breakage. [common advice, untested: PureWow, "Chebe powder for hair" (quotes Dr Sunitha Posina, an internist, and two hair professionals), https://purewow.com/beauty/chebe-powder-for-hair]
- Expecting hair growth: Dr Sunitha Posina says there is no evidence it grows hair. [common advice, untested: PureWow, "Chebe powder for hair" (quotes Dr Sunitha Posina, an internist, and two hair professionals), https://purewow.com/beauty/chebe-powder-for-hair]

See someone when:
- Itching, a rash or burning on your scalp after using it (doctor or dermatologist).
- Thinning at the hairline or temples, whatever you use (doctor or dermatologist; ask about traction).
- Hair breaking despite careful care (doctor or a hair and scalp specialist).

## Chemical relaxers and hair straighteners
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/chemical-relaxers/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Studies disagree on whether relaxers raise cancer risk, and none can prove cause. In the large Black women's cohort, heavy use showed no clear rise in uterine cancer overall but a higher risk after the menopause; breast cancer results were largely null. Relaxed hair under tight styles carried the highest risk of hair loss.

Do:
- Have a professional apply it. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Touch up new growth only, every two to three months at most. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Space treatments out: frequent use carried the highest risk in the Sister Study. [tested: Chang 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36245087/]
- See a doctor about heavy or long periods. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]

Avoid:
- Putting tight braids or weaves on relaxed hair. [tested: Khumalo 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/]
- Applying relaxer to hair that has already been relaxed. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Leaving scalp burns: more burns tracked with more fibroids in one cohort. [tested: Wise 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22234483/]

See someone when:
- Any bleeding after the menopause (doctor, promptly).
- Heavy or prolonged periods, pelvic pressure or pain (doctor or women's health doctor).
- Scalp burns that blister, ooze or do not heal (doctor or dermatologist).
- Hair thinning, particularly at the crown or edges (dermatologist).

## Choosing a stylist, braider or loctician
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/choosing-a-stylist-braider-or-loctician/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study shows that a stylist's training or specialism gives better hair or scalp outcomes. In one small US survey, most Black cosmetologists had never heard of two scarring hair-loss conditions. Book a consultation or a simple wash first, watch how they handle your hair, and tell them when a style hurts.

Do:
- Book a consultation or a simple wash and condition first, to see how they handle your hair before a long service. [common advice, untested: Going Natural, "How to select a natural hairstylist" (a natural-hair blog), https://going-natural.com/how-to-select-a-natural-hairstylist/]
- Ask about their experience with your hair type, the products they use and the price before you book. [common advice, untested: Going Natural, "How to select a natural hairstylist" (a natural-hair blog), https://going-natural.com/how-to-select-a-natural-hairstylist/]
- Have braids put in by a trained, qualified professional, and relaxers by a trained, experienced one. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Say so if it hurts: scalp pain after installation means braids are probably too tight. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- For locs, ask a loctician how often to retwist: one booking site says about every 4 weeks for starter locs and every 8 to 12 weeks or more for mature locs, and that retwisting too often can cause thinning and breakage. [common advice, untested: StyleSeat (a booking platform), "How often should you retwist locs" (loctician tips credited to Tara Cline; no qualifications listed), https://www.styleseat.com/blog/how-often-should-you-retwist-locs/]

Avoid:
- Expecting your stylist to spot scalp disease: in one survey most cosmetologists had not heard of lichen planopilaris or CCCA. [tested: Onamusi 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40654542/]

See someone when:
- Hair loss, bald patches, or a scalp that is sore, itchy or scaly: a doctor, for a dermatology referral, not a stylist.
- A stylist or braider tells you to see a doctor about your scalp (doctor or dermatologist).
- A hairline that keeps moving back (doctor or dermatologist).

## Colouring and bleaching afro-textured hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/colouring-and-bleaching-textured-hair/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
