Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Bleaching and dyeing damage the hair surface whatever the curl, in lab tests on hair samples; no study has tested a colour or bleach routine in people with coiled hair. Dermatologists advise 2 weeks after a relaxer, and the UK's NHS a strand test at least 48 hours before dyeing, because dye can cause allergy.

Do:
- Do a strand test at least 48 hours before dyeing, and buy a home patch-test kit if you think you may be allergic. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hair dye reactions", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hair-dye-reactions/]
- Leave 2 weeks between a relaxer and dyeing or heat straightening. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Watch for stinging, burning, itch, swelling or blisters for up to 72 hours; a rash can look darker or be harder to see on brown and black skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hair dye reactions", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hair-dye-reactions/]
- If you react, wash hair and scalp straight away with mild shampoo and stop using the dye. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hair dye reactions", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hair-dye-reactions/]

Avoid:
- Assuming bleach is kinder to coily hair: in a lab, bleaching and dyeing damaged the surface in every curl type. [tested: Bloch 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31237371/]
- Stacking bleach, straightening and heat on the same hair: lab work found combined treatments changed the fibre more than single ones. [tested: Dos 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31111104/]
- Dyeing soon after a relaxer: the BAD leaflet says this causes cumulative damage. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

See someone when:
- Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing after dye: call 999 (UK).
- A rash, blisters or soreness that gets worse after colouring (doctor).
- Hair breaking or thinning after colouring or bleaching (doctor or dermatologist).

## Dry, itchy, flaky scalp and dandruff
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/scalp-itch-dandruff-and-seborrhoeic-dermatitis/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Flaking and itch are often dandruff or seborrhoeic dermatitis, which is a skin reaction, not simple dryness. An anti-dandruff shampoo, such as ketoconazole, coal tar or salicylic acid, is the UK's NHS first step; ketoconazole beat placebo in trials of mixed people (low-quality evidence). Lice can affect any hair; find a live louse before treating.

Do:
- Use an anti-dandruff shampoo with ketoconazole, coal tar or salicylic acid for up to 4 weeks. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Dandruff", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dandruff/]
- Massage a medicated shampoo in, leave it 5 to 10 minutes, then rinse. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Seborrhoeic dermatitis", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/seborrhoeic-dermatitis/]
- Once clear, use the antifungal shampoo once or twice a week to keep it away. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Seborrhoeic dermatitis", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/seborrhoeic-dermatitis/]
- Choose an antifungal shampoo: ketoconazole beat placebo in a review of trials. [tested: Okokon 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25933684/]
- To check for lice, use a detection comb on wet, conditioned hair; allow 20 to 30 minutes for long, frizzy or curly hair. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]

Avoid:
- Letting product build up, or washing so seldom that the scalp is irritated. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Treating itch as lice without finding a live louse: it is the only sure way to confirm them. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]
- Assuming extensions, infrequent oiling or grooming cause it: associations only in a small survey. [tested: Rucker 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20728245/]
- Using plant oils such as tea tree or lavender for lice: the UK's NHS does not recommend them. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]

See someone when:
- Symptoms continue after at least 4 weeks of anti-dandruff shampoo, or the scalp is red, swollen or very itchy (doctor).
- Flaky, itchy patches on the face or body (doctor).
- Patches of hair loss with scale, or a scaly area that is tender (doctor: could be a scalp fungal infection).
- A rash from a new glue, dye or extension (doctor).

## Finding a stylist, trichologist or dermatologist who knows afro hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/finding-a-hair-and-scalp-specialist/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A stylist or loctician is the right person for styling and a trichologist or dermatologist for hair loss. In the UK a GP can refer you to a dermatologist; trichologists are not medically qualified, so check that they are registered and have experience with afro-textured hair. Ask directly what share of their patients have hair like yours.

Do:
- Ask a doctor for a referral to a dermatologist if hair loss or scalp symptoms persist. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hair loss", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hair-loss/]
- See a board-certified dermatologist if you notice texture change or even slight thinning. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Use the Institute of Trichologists register and ask about experience with afro-textured hair; its page does not mention afro hair or say members are medically qualified. [common advice, untested: Institute of Trichologists (professional association; its register is accredited by the Professional Standards Authority; the page does not say members are medically qualified and does not mention afro hair), http://instituteoftrichologists.co.uk/]
- Have braids, relaxers and locs done by a trained professional. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Ask a loctician or braider to loosen anything that hurts: pain equals damage. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

Avoid:
- Waiting on thinning at the crown or hairline because a stylist says it is just breakage. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Assuming a clinician will recognise your hair condition: CCCA is underrecognised and often misdiagnosed. [tested: Persson 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42910370/]

See someone when:
- Hair is thinning at the crown, hairline or part (dermatologist).
- A shiny, smooth scalp with no hair openings (dermatologist soon).
- Sudden or widespread shedding (doctor).

## Going natural: transitioning from a relaxer and the big chop
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/transitioning-to-natural-hair-and-the-big-chop/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: There is no study of the big chop or of how to grow out a relaxer, so none of this is tested. Dermatology guidance on relaxers is clear: never relax hair that is already relaxed, and avoid tight styles. The advice about the weak join between the two textures and trimming comes from hair media, not research.

Do:
- Stop putting relaxer on hair that has already been relaxed; touch up new growth only, and only every few months, if you keep relaxing. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Check braids, cornrows and weaves are not too tight: the AAD says pain equals damage. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Use a heat protectant and the lowest heat setting that gives the style, and press no more than about once a week. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Detangle with a wide-tooth comb from the ends up to the roots, in sections. [common advice, untested: MadameNoire, "4 Expert Tips To Help You Grow Out Your Relaxer" (Shannon Dawson, 12 Jun 2026; a media outlet, not a clinic), https://madamenoire.com/1674641/relaxer-hair-grow-out-tips/]
- Choose between a big chop (all relaxed hair off at once) and trimming small amounts every six to eight weeks; both are described as workable and neither has been compared. [common advice, untested: MadameNoire, "4 Expert Tips To Help You Grow Out Your Relaxer" (Shannon Dawson, 12 Jun 2026; a media outlet, not a clinic), https://madamenoire.com/1674641/relaxer-hair-grow-out-tips/]

Avoid:
- Relaxing already relaxed hair. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Direct heat on the join between relaxed and natural hair: the article says it weakens that line and can lead to snapping. [common advice, untested: MadameNoire, "4 Expert Tips To Help You Grow Out Your Relaxer" (Shannon Dawson, 12 Jun 2026; a media outlet, not a clinic), https://madamenoire.com/1674641/relaxer-hair-grow-out-tips/]
- Tight styles that pull at the join or the edges. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

See someone when:
- Hair breaking, thinning or bare patches that do not settle with gentle care (dermatologist: the AAD says earlier diagnosis means better treatment).
- Hair loss around the hairline or where a style pulls tightest (dermatologist; see the traction alopecia entry).
- Scalp burns from a relaxer that blister, ooze or do not heal (doctor or dermatologist).

## Hair breakage, growth and keeping length
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-breakage-and-length-retention/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Tightly coiled hair does grow, but it breaks more easily when combed or handled, so the length you keep depends on breakage. Company studies measure slower growth in African hair, but nobody has tested how to keep length. Gentle detangling is the best-supported step. No product is shown to repair a strand.

Do:
- Detangle gently with as few passes as you can. [tested: Molamodi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33605448/]
- Use a soft wide-spaced brush or wide-toothed comb. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Protect hair at night with a satin cap, scarf or pillowcase. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Give relaxers, heat and braids time apart rather than stacking them. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Regular trims and a break between long tight styles (4 to 6 weeks). [clinical guidance: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair", https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/teaching-kids-to-love-their-hair-comprehensive-strategies-for-curly-and-coily-hair-care]

Avoid:
- Rough or repeated combing: more strokes meant more cuticle damage. [tested: Molamodi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33605448/]
- Tight styles on relaxed hair. [tested: Khumalo 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/]
- Heat at a higher setting than the style needs. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

See someone when:
- Hair breaks or thins in a patch, or the scalp looks shiny or scarred (dermatologist).
- Shedding that is sudden or all over (doctor).
- Scalp pain, bumps or itch with the breakage (doctor or dermatologist).

## Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-growth-oils-and-supplements/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Castor oil alone and black seed oil have not been tested for hair growth in people in my search. Rosemary oil matched 2% minoxidil in one trial of 100 people with pattern baldness, none chosen for afro hair. Biotin helps only if you are deficient, and it can distort blood tests. Growth supplements are mostly brand-run trials in other groups.

Do:
- If you try rosemary oil, know the one trial was in pattern baldness and had no untreated group. [tested: Panahi 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25842469/]
- Tell your doctor and the lab if you take biotin before a blood test. [tested: Bhimireddy 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42933321/]
- If you are shedding, ask a doctor about iron, thyroid and other causes before buying a supplement. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Hair loss", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hair-loss/]
- Look after a balanced diet with iron and protein; supplements may help if your diet is restricted. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]

Avoid:
- Taking biotin for hair if you are healthy: no evidence it works. [tested: Patel 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28879195/]
- Oiling a sore, scaly or burning scalp instead of having it looked at. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Believing a quick-fix hair product without checking the evidence. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]

See someone when:
- Thinning or shedding that is sudden, patchy or does not improve (doctor).
- A shiny scalp with no visible hair openings, or burning and tenderness (dermatologist).
- Any blood test result that looks odd while taking biotin (doctor: biotin can distort results).

## Hair porosity and moisture
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-porosity-and-moisture/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: The glass-of-water float test, and routines chosen by "low, normal or high porosity", have never been tested in people. Porosity is real in the lab, but nobody has shown that choosing products by it helps. The lab does show tightly coiled hair breaks easily under rough grooming, so gentle handling is the safest advice.

Do:
- Handle hair gently, especially when detangling. [tested: Evans 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42971788/]
- Describe your hair by shape (coil, curl, wave) when talking to a stylist or doctor. [tested: Callender 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41928381/]
- Wash once a week or every other week, and condition every wash, focusing on the ends. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Use a heat protectant on wet hair before heat styling. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Many hair guides say to use lighter products if hair seems to repel water, and leave-in conditioner if it soaks water up fast. [common advice, untested: MDhair (Y. Harth MD), "Hair porosity according to dermatologists", a brand site that sells hair products, https://mdhair.co/article/hair-porosity-according-to-dermatologists]

Avoid:
- Treating the float test as a diagnosis: no validation found. [tested: PubMed 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=float+test+hair+porosity]
- Believing a porosity type tells you which product will work. [tested: PubMed 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=float+test+hair+porosity]
- Rough, forceful combing: grooming force drove breakage in the lab. [tested: Evans 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42971788/]

See someone when:
- Hair is breaking or falling out in patches or you can see scalp scarring (dermatologist).
- Sudden or widespread shedding (doctor: this is not a porosity problem).
- Scalp itch, scale or sores with the dryness (doctor or dermatologist).

## Hair shedding after pregnancy, illness or stress
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-shedding-and-thinning-after-pregnancy-or-stress/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A sudden all-over shed, usually three months after a trigger such as childbirth, illness, stress or crash dieting, is called telogen effluvium. It usually gets better on its own within months. But thinning at the crown, part or hairline can be a different condition, and some women have both. Ask a doctor to check iron and thyroid if it persists.

Do:
- See a doctor if shedding does not improve, to rule out other causes. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]
- Accept that telogen effluvium usually recovers without treatment, over many months. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]
- Ask about blood tests for thyroid and iron. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]
- Avoid harsh brushing, heat tools, harsh chemicals and tight hairstyles while it recovers. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]
- Camouflage fibres or volumising shampoos can help for severe thinning. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]

Avoid:
- Assuming all post-baby shedding is temporary: look at the crown, part and edges. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Telogen effluvium" (updated Oct 2025), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/telogen-effluvium/]
- Assuming it is only stress: in 200 women with postpartum loss most also had another hair loss disorder. [tested: Galal 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38779373/]
- Buying quick-fix supplements for a scarring or patchy loss before a diagnosis. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]

See someone when:
- Shedding that has gone on for more than 6 months (doctor).
- Thinning at the crown, part or hairline, or a shiny scalp (dermatologist).
- Burning, itching or pain with the hair loss (doctor or dermatologist).
- Hair loss with fatigue, heavy periods, weight change or other symptoms (doctor: iron, thyroid).

## Hair transplants in afro-textured hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-transplants-in-afro-textured-hair/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Transplants can be done on tightly curled hair, but the evidence is a small case series and a review, with no outcome data in Black men. Curl makes extraction harder, so the surgeon's tools and experience matter. Scarring hair loss such as CCCA must be ruled out first.

Do:
- Ask which extraction tool will be used for tightly curled hair: in a case series of 18, conventional punches often cut the follicles and a curved non-rotary punch did better. [tested: Umar 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27757365/]
- Have the scalp checked for a scarring hair-loss condition (CCCA, lichen planopilaris, frontal fibrosing alopecia) before any surgery. [common advice, untested: Dr. Kopelman and The Hair Doctors (a hair-transplant clinic's channel), YouTube, "Best Hair Loss Treatments for Black Hair", https://youtu.be/KfG05x2ijLw]
- Ask about the donor area: how much hair is there to take and how many sessions the plan needs (one surgeon says donor density can limit the target). [common advice, untested: Dr. Kopelman and The Hair Doctors (a hair-transplant clinic's channel), YouTube, "Best Hair Loss Treatments for Black Hair", https://youtu.be/KfG05x2ijLw]

Avoid:
- Operating while a scarring disease is active: the two-patient CCCA report used patients whose biopsy showed no inflammation. [tested: Callender 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25207763/]
- Assuming extraction is scarless: one surgeon says each extraction leaves a small scar, visible on a close shave. [common advice, untested: Dr. Kopelman and The Hair Doctors (a hair-transplant clinic's channel), YouTube, "Best Hair Loss Treatments for Black Hair", https://youtu.be/KfG05x2ijLw]

See someone when:
- Thinning or a receding hairline, or bald patches: a doctor, then a dermatologist, before a surgeon.
- An itchy, sore or scaly scalp with hair loss (dermatologist).
- Hair loss that is spreading from the crown (dermatologist).

## Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-texture-types-and-typing/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: The 4a, 4b and 4c letters sort curl by eye and were not checked against measured hair. They do not predict which product or routine will work. Describe your hair instead by how tight the curl is, how wide the strand is and how dense it is. Why texture changes after pregnancy or with age is untested.

Do:
- Describe your hair by curl tightness, strand width and how much hair you have, not only a letter. [tested: Callender 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41928381/]
- Describe your hair by shape (coil, curl, wave) when talking to a stylist or doctor. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Treat the letter as a label for how hair looks, not a guide to which product works. [tested: Gaines 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37212612/]
- Choose looser styles (loose plaits or twists), leave the hairline out of tight braids and take breaks between styles. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Judge a style by tightness and fit, not its name: a dermatologist says braids, twists and locs are not inherently bad, and some people are more prone to traction hair loss than others. [common advice, untested: BlackDoctor (a dermatologist is speaking; her name is not in the captions), YouTube, "A Dermatologist Explains: How to Reverse Traction Alopecia", https://youtu.be/0HEL_WF-HaQ]

Avoid:
- Choosing products by letter: no study validates the letters against measured hair. [tested: Callender 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41928381/]
- Assuming two people with the same letter have the same strand width or density. [tested: Daniels 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36374002/]
- Expecting one style to suit every curl pattern: reviews sort styles by tension and risk, and I found no study matching styles to hair type. [tested: Haskin 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27114262/]

See someone when:
- A change in texture with thinning, shedding or scalp symptoms (doctor).
- Hair texture or thickness changing suddenly in a child (doctor).
- Thinning at the crown, hairline or part (dermatologist).

## Head lice in afro-textured hair and locs
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/head-lice-in-afro-hair-and-locs/
Module: Hair
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Anyone with hair can get head lice. Old school surveys found fewer cases in children with African hair, but they conflict and none looked at locs. Treatment in locs and braids is untested. The UK's NHS advises wet combing or a medicated lotion and does not mention locs; a nit comb may not pass through tight coils.

Do:
- Treat only when you find a live louse, by wet combing with conditioner and a fine-toothed comb, or a medicated lotion if combing does not work. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]
- Treat everyone in close contact on the same day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]
- With long, frizzy or curly hair, allow 20 to 30 minutes to comb through, after plenty of conditioner. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]
- In tightly coiled hair, ask a pharmacist about applying the lotion and skipping the nit comb. [common advice, untested: Shea, Journal of the American Pharmacists Association 2023 (a pharmacy commentary, not a trial), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36241488/]

Avoid:
- Assuming afro hair or oils make lice impossible: one US school study found 15% of African American pupils infested. [tested: Estrada 2000, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11885087/]
- Plant oils (tea tree, eucalyptus, lavender), repellents or electric combs: the UK's NHS does not recommend them. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]
- Using lotions to prevent lice rather than treat them. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Head lice and nits", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-lice-and-nits/]

See someone when:
- Lice still present after the full treatment course (pharmacist, then doctor).
- A scalp that is sore, crusted or weeping after scratching (doctor).
- You cannot treat lice through locs or braids: ask a pharmacist before cutting anything.

## Heat, silk press, keratin treatments and colour
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/heat-styling-silk-press-and-smoothing-treatments/
Module: Hair
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Heat damage on afro hair has not been measured in people. Dermatologists advise a heat protectant, the lowest setting that works and no more than one press a week. One small survey links frequent heat to hairline loss. Keratin smoothing products can release formaldehyde; bleaching and dyeing damage the hair surface whatever your curl.

Do:
- Use a heat protectant on wet hair and the lowest setting that gets the style. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Press or heat-straighten no more than once a week, with a ceramic iron or comb with a dial. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Leave about two weeks between relaxing and dyeing or heat straightening. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Limit heat on natural hair left out around extensions. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Know that bleaching and dyeing caused cuticle wear and protein loss in lab samples whatever the curliness. [tested: Bloch 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31237371/]

Avoid:
- Heat-styling many times a month: higher odds of hairline recession in 197 Ghanaian women. [tested: Ayugane 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42953661/]
- Stacking relaxing, heat and braiding within a short time. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Keratin smoothing in a poorly ventilated space: simulated salon air held formaldehyde. [tested: Pierce 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22035353/]

See someone when:
- Hair breaking, thinning or scalp burns after a treatment (dermatologist or doctor).
- Hairline or crown thinning (dermatologist).
- Eye, nose or breathing irritation during or after a smoothing treatment (doctor).

## LOC and LCO: layering liquid, oil and cream
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/moisture-layering-loc-and-lco-methods/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Nobody has tested layering liquid, oil and cream on people, so there is no proof that LOC or LCO beats one product or that either order is better. Dermatologists say to moisturise regularly between washes. Lab work shows African hair holds lipids differently, but that does not test a routine.

Do:
- Moisturise regularly between wash days with a lotion, cream or oil, because tightly coiled hair is prone to dryness. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- If you layer, start with water or a water-based leave-in and put oil on top: a trichologist says oils seal and do not hydrate (advice given for locs). [common advice, untested: Naka Trichology, YouTube, "7 Loc Care Rules Every Trichologist Knows (That Nobody Talks About)" (a trichologist who wears locs), https://youtu.be/0cNKyqmUY9s]
- Use fewer products: hair that feels dry whatever you apply may be coated with build-up (advice given for locs). [common advice, untested: Naka Trichology, YouTube, "7 Loc Care Rules Every Trichologist Knows (That Nobody Talks About)" (a trichologist who wears locs), https://youtu.be/0cNKyqmUY9s]

Avoid:
- Treating LOC or LCO as proven: my PubMed search found no study of either. [tested: This 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%28%22LOC+method%22+OR+%22liquid+oil+cream%22+OR+%22layering%22+OR+%22sealing%22%29+AND+hair+AND+%28moisture+OR+hydration+OR+breakage%29]
- Adding more oil to hair that already feels coated or stiff (advice given for locs). [common advice, untested: Naka Trichology, YouTube, "7 Loc Care Rules Every Trichologist Knows (That Nobody Talks About)" (a trichologist who wears locs), https://youtu.be/0cNKyqmUY9s]

See someone when:
- Hair that breaks in patches or thins even though you moisturise regularly (doctor or dermatologist).
- An itchy, flaking or sore scalp that does not settle (doctor).
- A hairline that is moving back (doctor or dermatologist).

## Locs: starting, washing and keeping them healthy
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/locs-starting-washing-and-maintenance/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested how often to wash or retwist locs. The British Association of Dermatologists warns that very long locs and tight twisting at the roots strain the scalp and raise the risk of traction alopecia, and that locs must dry fully to avoid mould. Loc-care sites suggest washing every week to month, depending on how much you sweat.

Do:
- Do not twist locs tightly at the roots. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Find a cleansing routine that works and dry locs thoroughly to prevent mould and mildew. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- If you are very active or sweaty, wash weekly or more often; low activity can stretch to every two to four weeks. [common advice, untested: Locsanity, "How often should you wash your locs?" (a loc-care brand that sells products), https://locsanity.com/blogs/news/how-often-should-you-wash-your-locs]
- Wait about four to six weeks before first washing starter locs, and two weeks after a fresh retwist. [common advice, untested: Locsanity, "How often should you wash your locs?" (a loc-care brand that sells products), https://locsanity.com/blogs/news/how-often-should-you-wash-your-locs]
- Take weight off the scalp: very long locs raise the risk, and locs are often worn for years. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Sleeping with damp locs covered or tied up: they can develop mildew. [common advice, untested: Locsanity, "How often should you wash your locs?" (a loc-care brand that sells products), https://locsanity.com/blogs/news/how-often-should-you-wash-your-locs]
- Twisting so tightly that the scalp aches or stings. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Ignoring tenderness, bumps or thinning at the roots or hairline. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]

See someone when:
- Hair is thinning or receding at the roots or hairline (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Pain, bumps, pus or itch at the roots that does not settle (doctor).
- Flaky, itchy scalp that has not cleared with an anti-dandruff shampoo after four weeks (doctor).
- A smell that does not clear after washing and full drying (doctor; could be a fungal or bacterial scalp problem).

## Men's afro hair: waves, fades, durags and the nape
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/mens-hair-waves-fades-and-durags/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested a waves routine or durags for scalp or hair health. Barber guides say brush, moisturise and wear a satin durag; that is untested. The part with a medical record is the nape: bumps from very close cuts or shaving there can be acne keloidalis nuchae, a scarring condition in men of African descent.

Do:
- Start with a healthy scalp: treat dryness or dandruff before a brushing routine. [common advice, untested: Wise Barber, "How to get 360 waves" (a barber guide site), https://wisebarber.com/how-to-get-360-waves]
- Wear a silk or satin durag at night, with the seam outside and not tied too tight. [common advice, untested: Wise Barber, "How to get 360 waves" (a barber guide site), https://wisebarber.com/how-to-get-360-waves]
- Use a soft brush if the scalp is sensitive. [common advice, untested: Wise Barber, "How to get 360 waves" (a barber guide site), https://wisebarber.com/how-to-get-360-waves]
- Wash 4c hair every 1 to 3 weeks and use conditioner, as for any coiled hair. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- See a doctor for bumps at the back of the neck: acne keloidalis nuchae is a scarring condition. [tested: Ogunbiyi 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28008278/]

Avoid:
- Brushing hard or three times a day on a tender scalp: hard bristles can be harsh. [common advice, untested: Wise Barber, "How to get 360 waves" (a barber guide site), https://wisebarber.com/how-to-get-360-waves]
- Tying a durag or head wrap so tight it pulls. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]
- Ignoring bumps, pus or keloid-like scars at the nape; very close cuts there are suspected, not proven, triggers. [tested: Ogunbiyi 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28008278/]

See someone when:
- Bumps, pus or scars at the back of the head or neck (doctor, then dermatologist: acne keloidalis nuchae).
- Itchy, flaky scalp that has not settled after 4 weeks of an anti-dandruff shampoo (doctor).
- Hairline thinning, crown thinning or tenderness (dermatologist).

## Protecting your edges and hairline
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/edges-and-hairline/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Edges thin mainly from pulling: tight styles, glue on the hairline and frequent heat are linked to hairline loss. Caught early and with the pulling stopped, hair can regrow within months; long-standing loss can be permanent. Edge products have not been tested. If your edges are thinning, see a doctor early.

Do:
- Keep styles loose at the hairline, or leave the edges out of braids. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Put adhesive just in front of the hairline, not on it. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- If edges are thinning, stop the pulling style: regrowth may start about 3 months later. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]
- Protect thinning areas from the sun with sunscreen or a hat. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]
- Limit heat on hair at the hairline. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Heat-styling many times a month: more than two sessions a month carried higher odds of hairline recession. [tested: Ayugane 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42953661/]
- Tight styles on relaxed hair. [tested: Khumalo 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/]
- Sleeping in rollers most nights. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

See someone when:
- Edges or temples thinning or receding (doctor, then dermatologist).
- A smooth, shiny hairline with no visible hair openings (dermatologist soon: scarring).
- Pain, bumps or itch at the hairline that does not settle (doctor).

## Receding hairline and hair transplants in Black men
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/mens-hair-loss-and-hair-transplants/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Receding hairlines have several causes: inherited pattern baldness, pulling from tight styles, or scarring conditions such as CCCA, which men can get. Minoxidil and finasteride are the standard treatments but I found no trial in Black men. Transplants can be done on curly hair but need a specialist and are private in the UK.

Do:
- See a doctor if your hairline is receding; diagnosis is by pattern, history and family history. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Male pattern hair loss", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/male-pattern-hair-loss/]
- Use minoxidil 5% if you choose treatment; it takes 6 to 12 months and works only while you use it. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Male pattern hair loss", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/male-pattern-hair-loss/]
- Know finasteride can take up to 14 months and about 2% report libido or erection problems. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Male pattern hair loss", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/male-pattern-hair-loss/]
- If you have a tight style, wig or head wrap, loosen it: tight hairstyles are the commonest cause of traction alopecia. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]
- Ask for a specialist experienced in curly hair if you consider a transplant. [tested: Rogers 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24680003/]

Avoid:
- Ignoring itch, tenderness or a shiny scalp: it may be a scarring condition. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/central-centrifugal-cicatricial-alopecia/]
- Assuming a genetic baldness test from European studies applies to you: it predicted baldness poorly in African men. [tested: Janivara 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40134218/]
- Expecting regrowth after stopping treatment: hair loss resumes. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Male pattern hair loss", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/male-pattern-hair-loss/]

See someone when:
- Hairline or crown thinning (doctor).
- Itch, burning, tenderness or a shiny scalp with the loss (dermatologist; CCCA is reported in men).
- Bumps or pus at the hairline or nape (doctor).

## Relaxer, texturiser, perm and keratin: what is the difference
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/relaxer-texturiser-perm-and-keratin-differences/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A relaxer straightens, a texturiser loosens curl by being left on for less time, and a perm adds curl. Stylists say relaxer and texturiser use the same kind of chemical. No study compares their safety. Keratin smoothing products are applied with blow-drying and flat-ironing, and some release formaldehyde.

Do:
- Ask for a service by what you want: straighten, loosen the curl or add curl, and ask how long it will stay on. [common advice, untested: Brandy Lucas (a stylist), YouTube, "TEXTURIZERS VS RELAXERS WHICH IS BEST?", https://youtu.be/BVwwXKDP3HU]
- Have a relaxer done by a trained, experienced professional, on new growth only, at least 6 weeks apart. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Protect the scalp, hairline and ears with a protectant such as petroleum jelly, and never leave a relaxer on longer than instructed. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Assuming a texturiser is much safer: stylists describe it as a milder or shorter relaxer, not a different chemical, and its safety is untested. [common advice, untested: Brandy Lucas (a stylist), YouTube, "TEXTURIZERS VS RELAXERS WHICH IS BEST?", https://youtu.be/BVwwXKDP3HU]
- Relaxing hair that has already been relaxed. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Dyeing or heat-straightening within 2 weeks of a relaxer. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Using the words as if they meant the same: a perm makes hair curly (a Jheri curl is a perm), a relaxer straightens. [common advice, untested: Tress Talk with Gerdie (a salon owner), YouTube, "RELAXER, PERM or TEXTURIZER??? - Tress Talk with Gerdie sets the record straight!", https://youtu.be/il3eVVZYC_Y]

See someone when:
- Burns, blisters or sores on the scalp after a chemical service (doctor, or urgent care if severe).
- Hair coming out in clumps or a hairline that is moving back after chemical services (doctor or dermatologist).

## Scalp oiling and greasing
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/scalp-oiling-and-greasing/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Nobody has tested scalp oiling or greasing for hair growth or scalp health in a trial. In the lab, coconut oil protected hair strands from protein loss, which is about the strand, not the scalp. Whether the routine does what tradition says is untested.

Do:
- Oil the strand if you like the feel: coconut oil has the lab evidence, not the scalp. [tested: Rele 2003, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12715094/]
- A hot oil treatment about twice a month is dermatologist advice for added moisture. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]
- Wash once a week or every other week to limit product build-up. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

Avoid:
- Using oil to treat flaking, scale or sores instead of getting them looked at. [tested: Rucker 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20728245/]
- Believing oils make hair grow: no trial found. [tested: PubMed 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=hair+oiling+scalp+randomized]
- Letting product build up: dermatologists say it can dry hair out. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

See someone when:
- The scalp is itchy, flaking, sore or has scabs that persist (doctor or dermatologist).
- Patches of hair loss with a smooth or shiny scalp (dermatologist).
- Scaly patches or broken hairs, especially in a child (doctor: tinea capitis is a fungal scalp infection, one of the conditions the survey asked about).

## Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/traction-alopecia-and-protective-styles/
Module: Hair
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Tight braids, weaves and ponytails can cause traction alopecia, hair loss from pulling, and the risk is highest when tension is added to relaxed hair. Caught early it can recover; left, it can become permanent. "Protective" describes the intention: tension is what matters.

Do:
- Ask your stylist to keep styles loose, especially at the hairline. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Do not keep braids in longer than 6 to 8 weeks. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Rotate styles and give your hair breaks from tight ones. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Take a style out straight away if your scalp stings, aches or crusts. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Under a head covering, pull hair back loosely; silk or satin is gentler. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]

Avoid:
- Tight styles on chemically relaxed hair: the highest-risk combination in the South African study. [tested: Khumalo 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/]
- Glued-in weaves: sewn-in is the dermatologists' advice. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Ignoring thinning at the edges or temples: see a dermatologist as soon as you notice it. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]
- Sleeping in rollers most nights. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, hairstyles that cause hair loss / traction alopecia, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/causes/hairstyles]

See someone when:
- Hair at the edges or temples is thinning or receding (doctor, then dermatologist).
- The scalp is shiny, scarred or has no hair follicles visible (dermatologist soon: scarring can be permanent).
- There is pain, pus-filled bumps or itch that does not settle (doctor).
- Hair is thinning at the crown and spreading outwards (dermatologist; this can be a different, scarring condition).

## Twist-outs, braid-outs and wash-and-gos: technique
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/twist-outs-braid-outs-and-wash-and-gos/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested how to set a twist-out, braid-out or wash-and-go, or how long one lasts. Creators and stylists give tips and they disagree, for example on starting on wet or stretched hair. The one dermatology point is to keep twists and braids loose at the scalp.

Do:
- Work product through small, even sections of damp hair so each twist is coated, then twist from the root. [common advice, untested: nicolelise, YouTube, "THE PERFECT TWISTOUT TUTORIAL on Natural Hair| EASY & DETAILED | 2023" (a creator), https://youtu.be/iPyHoTVnVks]
- For a wash-and-go: start on freshly washed hair, apply gel in small sections and air-dry a little before stretching. [common advice, untested: Anaël Hector, YouTube, "HOW TO: The BEST Wash and Go for 4C NATURAL HAIR for Beginners" (a creator), https://youtu.be/37s5QqtPTg8]
- Keep twists and braids loose at the scalp; scalp pain means they are too tight. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Oversaturating hair with product: this creator says it leaves flakes and build-up when dry. [common advice, untested: Anaël Hector, YouTube, "HOW TO: The BEST Wash and Go for 4C NATURAL HAIR for Beginners" (a creator), https://youtu.be/37s5QqtPTg8]
- Expecting a wash-and-go to last for days on tightly coiled hair: one channel says it dries out unless redone every day or two (a view not tested, and others disagree). [common advice, untested: hairrules, YouTube, "Ask Dickey! E19: Wash N Go vs. Twist Outs & Protective Styles" (a hair-education channel; the speaker's qualifications were not checked), https://youtu.be/lcqF0ET4ndY]

See someone when:
- An itchy, sore or flaking scalp that does not settle after you take a style out (doctor).
- A hairline or crown that is thinning (doctor or dermatologist).
- Pain, bumps or pus at the roots after twisting or braiding (doctor).

## Wash day and routine for 4c hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/wash-day-routine-for-4c-hair/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Nobody has tested a wash-day routine for tightly coiled hair. UK and US dermatologists give different intervals, from every week or two to every one to three weeks, so choose what keeps your scalp comfortable. They agree on conditioner every wash and gentle detangling. Which shampoo or leave-in is best is untested.

Do:
- Wash about every one to three weeks, or sooner if there is build-up or oiliness. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Use a rinse-out conditioner every wash, focusing on the ends, then a leave-in. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Comb with a soft wide-spaced brush or wide-toothed comb. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- At night, loosely plait or twist and use a satin or silk cap, scarf or pillowcase. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Use a heat protectant on wet hair before any heat. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

Avoid:
- Rough, repeated combing: damage rose with every extra stroke in a small lab study. [tested: Molamodi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33605448/]
- Letting product build up, or washing so rarely that the scalp is irritated. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Going from relaxing to heat or dye within about two weeks. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

See someone when:
- Scalp itch or flaking that has not settled after four weeks of an anti-dandruff shampoo (doctor).
- Hair that breaks, thins or has bare patches despite gentle care (dermatologist).
- A sore, red or bumpy scalp (doctor).

## Wigs, weaves and lace glue
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/wigs-weaves-and-hair-glue/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested whether wigs protect your own hair. Dermatologists advise keeping your own hair clean and moisturised underneath, sewing in loosely, wearing a satin wig cap, and putting glue just in front of the hairline, not on it. Adhesives and synthetic hair can cause an itchy allergic rash, and removal can pull out edges.

Do:
- Keep your own hair cleansed and moisturised under the wig. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Sew-ins should not be tight; do not braid underneath too tightly. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Apply adhesive just in front of the hairline, not on it. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Wear a satin wig cap rather than cotton or nylon. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Do not leave extensions in for more than 8 weeks. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]

Avoid:
- Glue or gel on the hairline itself: removal can pull edges out. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023), https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/caring-for-afro-textured-hair/]
- Ignoring an itchy, eczema-like rash at the glue line: synthetic hair and adhesives can cause contact allergy. [tested: Collins 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39936215/]
- Leaving a tight sew-in or wig in while the scalp aches. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/traction-alopecia/]

See someone when:
- A dry, itchy, red rash at the glue line or under the wig (doctor).
- Edges thinning or receding (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Pain, bumps or pus at the hairline (doctor).

## Winter care and shrinkage for coily hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/hair/hair-in-winter-and-shrinkage/
Module: Hair
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No study has tested winter care or shrinkage in coily hair. General dermatology advice for winter applies: keep hair moisturised, air dry when you can, limit heat, and space out chemical services. Shrinkage is simply how tightly coiled hair behaves; I found nothing saying it is a problem or a sign of health.

Do:
- Keep hair moisturised in dry winter air: conditioner suited to your hair, a leave-in and, if you like, a hot oil treatment. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Air dry when you can and wait until hair is less damp before combing, because wet hair is more fragile. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Limit heat and chemicals, and space colour, perms or straightening out to eight to 10 weeks or longer in dry winter months. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Skip rubber-based bands and avoid tight buns or braids, which cause breakage. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Condition at every wash, concentrating on the ends, and use a hot oil treatment about twice a month. [clinical guidance: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

Avoid:
- Rubber bands and very tight updos under hats. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Frequent iron or dryer heat on dry winter hair. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "How to Keep Your Hair Healthy This Winter" (Jan 2021; quotes dermatologist Wilma Bergfeld and the AAD; not specific to coily hair), https://health.clevelandclinic.org/your-best-strategies-for-beautiful-hair-in-the-winter]
- Treating shrinkage as damage or as proof of health: no source opened says either. [common advice, untested: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: Tips for everyday care", https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/hair-scalp-care/hair/care-african-american]

See someone when:
- Breaking, thinning or a sore, flaky or itchy scalp that does not settle (doctor or dermatologist; see the scalp and breakage entries).
- A change in texture or appearance of your hair, even slight thinning (dermatologist: the AAD says earlier diagnosis means better treatment).

## Anxiety, depression and what helps
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/anxiety-depression-and-what-helps/
Module: Mind
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Anxiety and depression are common and treatable, and the NHS says to seek help early. In the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies, including for social anxiety and panic, without seeing a GP. Whether therapies work differently in Black adults is untested in my search, so choose a service you can attend.

Do:
- Refer yourself to NHS (UK) talking therapies for anxiety and depression, including social anxiety and panic; you must be registered with a doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- See a doctor if you think you may be depressed; the UK's NHS says not to wait. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]
- Ask about guided self-help, group or video options if in-person therapy is hard to attend. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Ask for a service or therapist you feel comfortable with; see the Black therapist finder entry for directories. [common advice, untested: BAATN (Black, African and Asian Therapy Network), homepage, https://www.baatn.org.uk/]
- Talk to someone you trust about what is happening. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]

Avoid:
- Waiting a long time before asking: the UK's NHS notes many people do. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]

See someone when:
- Anxiety or low mood lasts weeks, or stops you working, studying or leaving the house (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Panic attacks, constant worry or avoiding people and places (doctor or self-referral).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

In other countries:
- In Canada, call or text 9-8-8 for the Suicide Crisis Helpline, 24 hours a day; call 9-1-1 if your safety is at risk. (https://988.ca/)
- In the US, call or text 988 for emotional support from the 988 Lifeline. (https://988lifeline.org/)

## Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/ashwagandha/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Ashwagandha eased stress and helped sleep a little in short trials, but our search found no trial in Black participants. NCCIH says avoid it in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and with thyroid or autoimmune conditions, and rare liver injury is reported. Ask a pharmacist first, and stop if your skin or eyes turn yellow.

Do:
- Ask a pharmacist or your doctor before starting if you take any medicine, especially for thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure, sleep or seizures: NCCIH says ashwagandha might interact with them. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Ashwagandha: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha]
- Stop it and get medical advice if your skin or eyes turn yellow, or you get itching, nausea or marked tiredness: this was the pattern in the liver injury cases. [tested: Bjornsson 2020, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31991029/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Ashwagandha in pregnancy, and while breastfeeding. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Ashwagandha: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha]
- Ashwagandha if you have a thyroid or autoimmune condition, or before surgery, unless your doctor agrees. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Ashwagandha: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha]
- Taking it for more than about three months on the assumption that it is safe: NCCIH says there is not enough information on long-term safety. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Ashwagandha: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha]

See someone when:
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching or marked tiredness while taking it (doctor or urgent care).
- You have a thyroid condition or take thyroid tablets and use ashwagandha (doctor or pharmacist).
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding and have been taking it (midwife or doctor).
- You are booked for surgery (tell the surgical team you take it).

## Autism and ADHD: being missed, delayed or misdiagnosed
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/autism-and-adhd-in-black-children-and-adults/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A US review of 20 studies found delayed diagnosis and misdiagnosis of autism were the main errors, driven by limited knowledge, insurance, provider bias and assessment tools that may not suit Black and Hispanic families. Recent US prevalence in Black children is no lower than in White children. My search found no equivalent review for ADHD.

Do:
- Ask your GP for an autism assessment referral if you think you or your child may be autistic; if refused, ask to see another GP, and in England you may be able to use Right to Choose. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Autism: getting diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/autism/getting-diagnosed/]
- For a child, speak to the school or a health visitor (UK) too, as they may need to make the referral. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Autism: getting diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/autism/getting-diagnosed/]
- For ADHD in a child, speak to the teacher or SENCO and a doctor about requesting an assessment; symptoms usually start before 12. [clinical guidance: NHS, "ADHD: diagnosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder-adhd/diagnosis/]
- Write down specific examples (what happens, when, how often) to take to the appointment; the assessment asks about development and early life. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Autism: getting diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/autism/getting-diagnosed/]

Avoid:
- Accepting that it is only behaviour or discipline without an assessment: the review found provider bias in history-taking caused delays and misdiagnoses. [tested: Srivarathan 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40854799/]
- Assuming a diagnosis is unlikely because of ethnicity: US prevalence in Black children matched or exceeded White children for the 2010 and 2012 birth cohorts. [tested: Gallin 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38941049/]

See someone when:
- Your child has delayed speech, difficulty with interaction, or very repetitive behaviours (doctor, health visitor in the UK or school).
- Inattention, restlessness or impulsiveness is affecting school, work or relationships (doctor; for a child, school SENCO then doctor).
- You were told it is only behaviour and you still have concerns (ask for a second opinion from another doctor).

## Being believed by doctors, and pain
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/being-believed-by-doctors-and-pain/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Research backs your experience. In US studies Black patients were less likely than white patients to be given painkillers, and many white trainee doctors held false beliefs about biological differences that went with lower pain ratings. It is not you. Prepare, describe what the pain stops you doing, and ask for a plan.

Do:
- Note one or two things you most want the appointment to focus on before you go. [common advice, untested: Pain Concern (a UK pain charity), "Breaking Barriers #4: GP consultations", https://painconcern.org.uk/gp-consultations/]
- Say what the pain stops you doing and how it affects your life; the doctor is expected to ask about this and to record your pain level. [clinical guidance: NHS, "How to get NHS help for your pain", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/pain/how-to-get-nhs-help-for-your-pain/]
- If pain lasts more than 12 weeks and you are struggling, ask the doctor for a referral to a specialist pain clinic. [clinical guidance: NHS, "How to get NHS help for your pain", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/pain/how-to-get-nhs-help-for-your-pain/]
- If you are not satisfied, contact the surgery directly: details of the complaints process and management team are usually on its website. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Appointments and bookings at your GP surgery", https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/gps/gp-appointments-and-bookings/]
- You can change doctor's surgery for free if the relationship is not working. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Register with a GP surgery", https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/gps/how-to-register-with-a-gp-surgery/]

Avoid:
- Concluding that you are exaggerating: Black patients were less likely to get pain relief in two reviews of US studies. [tested: Lee 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31186154/]
- Leaving without a plan: the UK's NHS says painkillers are generally not the main way to manage long-term pain, so ask what the plan is. [clinical guidance: NHS, "How to get NHS help for your pain", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/pain/how-to-get-nhs-help-for-your-pain/]

See someone when:
- Severe, sudden or worsening pain, chest pain, or pain with weakness, confusion or fever (999, or your local emergency number or A&E in the UK; this trigger is generic and not sourced here).
- Pain lasting more than 12 weeks (doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Black men, depression and getting support
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/mens-mental-health-and-depression/
Module: Mind
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A survey of African American men found that everyday racism and masculine norms both went with more barriers to seeking help, partly through feeling less in control and more depressed. Depression is a health condition and treatable. You can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies, and the CALM helpline is there for men.

Do:
- See a doctor if you think you may be depressed; the UK's NHS says not to delay. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]
- Refer yourself to NHS (UK) talking therapies if you are 18 or over and registered with a doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Call CALM on 0800 58 58 58, open 5pm to midnight every day, or Samaritans (UK) on 116 123. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]
- Text SHOUT to 85258 if you do not want to talk by phone (24 hours). [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]
- Tell one person you trust what is going on. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]

Avoid:
- Waiting for it to pass if it has lasted weeks or months; the UK's NHS describes depression as lasting weeks or months, unlike a short low patch. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]
- Carrying racism's strain alone: in the survey it fed lower control and more depressive symptoms. [tested: Powell 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27337619/]

See someone when:
- Persistent sadness, loss of interest, poor sleep or appetite for weeks (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Drinking or using drugs to cope (doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Breathwork and slow breathing
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/breathwork/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: yes
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Slow breathing practice lowers stress and blood pressure a little in trials of adults generally. In the few small studies of African American adults the results were mixed, and one found breathing alone did nothing straight away. It is an extra, not a replacement for treatment.

Do:
- Sit or lie comfortably, breathe gently into your belly: in through the nose, out through the mouth, counting to five. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Breathing exercises for stress", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/self-help/guides-tools-and-activities/breathing-exercises-for-stress/]
- Keep going for at least five minutes, ideally as a daily habit. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Breathing exercises for stress", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/self-help/guides-tools-and-activities/breathing-exercises-for-stress/]
- Notice whether it helps you: effects in trials were small. [tested: Fincham 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36624160/]

Avoid:
- Treating it as a cure for high blood pressure or anxiety. [tested: Fincham 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36624160/]
- Expecting breathing alone to lower blood pressure straight away: in one tiny crossover trial it did not. [tested: Park 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24829497/]

See someone when:
- Your blood pressure stays high despite practice (doctor).
- Anxiety or low mood is stopping you functioning (doctor or talking therapy service).
- Breathing practice makes you dizzy, faint or gives chest pain (stop, and see a doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Childhood trauma and where to start
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/childhood-trauma-and-where-to-start/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Hard things in childhood, such as abuse, neglect or violence at home, raise the chance of anxiety, depression and PTSD later. What happened was not your fault. Trauma-focused therapies help, and you can start with a GP or, in England, a self-referral to NHS talking therapies. You do not have to tell the whole story at once.

Do:
- Tell a GP or someone you trust. In England, if you are 18 or over (16 in some areas), you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral; they can help with PTSD. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/ptsd-post-traumatic-stress-disorder/]
