- Ask for trauma-focused therapy, such as trauma-focused CBT or EMDR (eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing); the UK's NHS lists both among treatments, sometimes with an antidepressant. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/ptsd-post-traumatic-stress-disorder/]
- For a child or teenager, ask for a trauma-focused therapy for young people: across 51 trials, therapy cut the chance of a PTSD diagnosis in the month after treatment (odds ratio 0.51). [tested: Gillies 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27726123/]
- Look for a therapist who understands your background. In the UK, BAATN lists Black, African, Asian and Caribbean heritage therapists; elsewhere ask local directories. [common advice, untested: BAATN (Black, African and Asian Therapy Network), homepage, https://www.baatn.org.uk/]
- Use a helpline in your own country for abuse or trauma; Find a Helpline lists lines by country and by topic, including trauma and abuse. [common advice, untested: Find a Helpline, helplines by country and topic, https://findahelpline.com/]

Avoid:
- Assuming this is just who you are: in 56 studies, the more adverse childhood experiences, the higher the risk of a mental disorder (pooled odds ratio 3.18), in steps. [tested: Annor 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42066531/]
- Waiting until you are in crisis: the UK's NHS says see a doctor if you think you have symptoms of PTSD. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/ptsd-post-traumatic-stress-disorder/]
- Thinking only abuse counts: the UK's NHS lists neglect, domestic violence and witnessing violence or abuse as causes of complex PTSD. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/ptsd-post-traumatic-stress-disorder/]

See someone when:
- Flashbacks, nightmares, feeling numb or cut off, intense shame or guilt, or difficulty controlling emotions that last more than a few weeks (doctor, or a self-referral to talking therapies where that exists).
- A child who has been hurt or frightened and is not themselves: sleep, school, anger or fear changes (doctor, school or child mental health service).
- Someone is hurting you or a child now: your local emergency number and local child protection or domestic violence service.
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: call your local emergency number or a crisis line. Numbers differ by country. UK: NHS 111 (mental health option, England) or Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours; also Ireland). US: call or text 988. Canada: call or text 988. Australia: Lifeline 13 11 14. South Africa: SADAG 0800 567 567. Jamaica: 888-639-5433. Nigeria: SURPIN 0800 078 7746. Other countries: findahelpline.com.

## Colourism, skin tone and mental health
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/colourism-and-mental-health/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In US surveys of Black adults, experiencing colourism within the community went with higher odds of a psychiatric disorder, and among older adults the link between discrimination and distress was stronger in darker-skinned people. These are associations, not proof of cause. No trial has tested a way to cope with it, so use ordinary mental health support.

Do:
- Talk to someone you trust, and if it is weighing on you, self-refer to NHS (UK) talking therapies for low mood, worry or anxiety. [clinical guidance: NHS, "NHS talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- If you want a therapist who understands racism and identity, see the finding a Black therapist entry; matching made almost no difference to outcomes on average, so fit comes first. [tested: Cabral 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21875181/]
- Notice that this is a recognised social stress: the surveys treat colourism as a source of distress, so it is reasonable to raise it with a doctor or therapist as part of why you feel low or anxious. [tested: Oh 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33961079/]

Avoid:
- Assuming it is only in your head: the surveys link perceived colourism to measurable psychiatric outcomes, though they cannot show it causes them. [tested: Oh 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33961079/]

See someone when:
- Low mood, anxiety or worry that is stopping you working, studying or looking after yourself (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Drinking, drug use or eating that is getting out of your control (doctor; NHS in the UK says these need a doctor referral for talking therapy).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or Samaritans free on 116 123.

## Finding a Black therapist or one who understands being Black
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/finding-a-black-therapist/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Directories in the UK and US list Black or culturally aware therapists. Research finds people moderately strongly prefer a therapist of their own background, but matching made almost no difference to how well treatment worked on average. The gaps were widest in studies of African American clients. A good fit matters more than the label alone.

Do:
- In the UK, search BAATN, a network of Black, African and Asian therapists with a searchable directory. [common advice, untested: BAATN (Black, African and Asian Therapy Network), homepage, https://www.baatn.org.uk/]
- In the UK, look at Black Minds Matter UK, which points to a Black therapist finder and has its own therapy service (free places are limited at present). [common advice, untested: Black Minds Matter UK, homepage, https://www.blackmindsmatteruk.com/]
- In the US, search Inclusive Therapists, a directory that says applicants submit proof of identity and qualifications and which can be filtered by cultural knowledge, fees and language. [common advice, untested: Inclusive Therapists, homepage, https://www.inclusivetherapists.com/]
- In the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies for anxiety and depression without seeing a GP first; ask whether you can state a preference. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Ask any therapist how they work with racism and identity; do not wait for a perfect match, as matching changed outcomes very little on average. [tested: Cabral 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21875181/]

Avoid:
- Treating a directory listing as a recommendation: these are lists, not endorsements, and fit is judged in the first session. [common advice, untested: Inclusive Therapists, homepage, https://www.inclusivetherapists.com/]
- Booking a private therapist who is not registered with a Professional Standards Authority accredited body. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Putting therapy off until you find a match: the average outcome benefit of matching was close to zero. [tested: Cabral 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21875181/]

See someone when:
- Low mood, anxiety or trauma is stopping you working, studying or looking after yourself (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- A therapist dismisses your experience of racism or you feel worse after several sessions (change therapist; tell your doctor if you were referred).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Getting a child mental health support
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/childrens-mental-health-support/
Module: Mind
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In English child mental health services, children from Black and other minority backgrounds were more often referred through school or social care than through a doctor. The UK's NHS has guides for parents and information on services for young people. Childline offers free help to anyone under 19.

Do:
- Use the UK's NHS advice for parents guides on anxiety, depression, talking to your child about feelings and teenagers. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Advice for parents", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/children-and-young-adults/advice-for-parents/]
- Read the UK's NHS information on Children and young people's mental health services (CYPMHS), which the NHS lists as further support. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for teenagers, young adults and students", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/children-and-young-adults/help-for-teenagers-young-adults-and-students/]
- Tell your child that Childline on 0800 1111 is free for under 19s and does not show on a phone bill. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]

Avoid:
- Assuming the school route is the only way in: minority-background children were more often referred through school and social services than through a doctor. [tested: Edbrooke-Childs 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26345326/]

See someone when:
- Your child's low mood, anxiety, anger or withdrawal lasts for weeks or affects school or friendships (doctor).
- Your child talks about harming themselves or not wanting to live (urgent: crisis lines below).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Meditation
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/meditation/
Module: Mind
Tier: A moderate (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: yes
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Meditation is among the better-tested practices here. A trial in Black adults with heart disease found fewer deaths, heart attacks and strokes with Transcendental Meditation. A large review found benefit for anxiety, depression and pain, but no better than other treatments. It adds to medical care and does not replace it.

Do:
- Pick a regular time, then notice your breath, body or sounds; bring your attention back when it wanders. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mindfulness", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/self-help/tips-and-support/mindfulness/]
- Give it several weeks: the trials ran from weeks to years. [tested: Goyal 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24395196/]
- Try mindfulness in daily tasks too, such as a walk. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mindfulness", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/self-help/tips-and-support/mindfulness/]
- Keep it as an addition to guideline treatment, which is how the heart-health statement frames it. [tested: Levine 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28963100/]

Avoid:
- Stopping treatment because you meditate. [tested: Levine 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28963100/]
- Assuming all types have the same evidence: the heart trial was Transcendental Meditation. [tested: Schneider 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23149426/]
- Pushing on if it makes you feel worse: the UK's NHS says some people find it does. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mindfulness", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/self-help/tips-and-support/mindfulness/]

See someone when:
- You have chest pain, breathlessness or fainting (urgent care).
- Low mood, anxiety or trauma makes meditation distressing or hard to sit with (doctor or therapist).
- Your blood pressure stays high despite practice (doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/melatonin-for-sleep/
Module: Mind
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Melatonin may help you fall asleep a little faster for some people, but reviews disagree, and it did not clearly help adults with long-term insomnia. In Black patients it has been tested only for night blood pressure, with no effect. Rules differ by country: prescription-only in the UK, a supplement in the US. Labels often miss the real dose.

Do:
- Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you have epilepsy or take blood thinners: NCCIH says they need medical supervision with melatonin. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Melatonin: What You Need To Know", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know]
- In the UK, get it through a prescription: the NHS says melatonin is only available with a prescription there. In the US it is sold as a dietary supplement, and several other countries treat it as a prescription drug, so check your own country. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Melatonin: a medicine used for sleep problems", https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/melatonin/]
- Keep it out of reach of children: poison centre calls about melatonin in under-20s in the US rose from 8,337 in 2012 to 52,563 in 2021. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Melatonin: What You Need To Know", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know]

Avoid:
- Driving, cycling or using machinery after taking it: the UK's NHS says it can make you sleepy. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Melatonin: a medicine used for sleep problems", https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/melatonin/]
- Alcohol with melatonin: the UK's NHS says it can stop it working properly and raise side effects. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Melatonin: a medicine used for sleep problems", https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/melatonin/]
- Trusting the dose on the label: in one lab check the content ranged from 83 per cent below to 478 per cent above the label. [tested: Erland 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27855744/]

See someone when:
- Trouble sleeping most nights for more than a few weeks (doctor; consider sleep apnoea).
- Heavy daytime sleepiness, loud snoring or pauses in breathing (doctor; see sleep and sleep apnoea).
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding and thinking of using melatonin (midwife or doctor).
- A child has swallowed melatonin that was not prescribed to them (poison centre or urgent care).

In other countries:
- In the US, melatonin is sold as a dietary supplement, which the FDA regulates less strictly than a prescription or over-the-counter drug. (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know)

## Psychosis, sectioning and misdiagnosis in the UK
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/mental-health-act-psychosis-and-misdiagnosis/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In England, Black people are detained under the Mental Health Act more often than any other group, and a large review found Black Caribbean and Black African patients were far more likely to be compulsorily admitted. Why is not settled. If you are detained, you can appeal, ask for an advocate and complain.

Do:
- If detained, ask which section you are held under, and ask to see an independent mental health advocate. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mental Health Act", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/social-care-and-your-rights/mental-health-and-the-law/mental-health-act/]
- Appeal to the Mental Health Tribunal or the hospital managers; you may be eligible for legal aid for a solicitor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mental Health Act", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/social-care-and-your-rights/mental-health-and-the-law/mental-health-act/]
- Complain to the CQC if you are unhappy with how the Act was used. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mental Health Act", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/social-care-and-your-rights/mental-health-and-the-law/mental-health-act/]
- Get help earlier: call NHS 111 (UK) and choose the mental health option, or see a doctor, before a crisis; the review lists mistrust of doctors as one possible contributor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Where to get urgent help for mental health", https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/mental-health-services/where-to-get-urgent-help-for-mental-health/]
- A nearest relative can ask the local approved mental health professional service for an assessment if you are not getting help. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mental Health Act", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/social-care-and-your-rights/mental-health-and-the-law/mental-health-act/]

Avoid:
- Assuming detention cannot be challenged: appeal and advocacy rights exist. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Mental Health Act", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/social-care-and-your-rights/mental-health-and-the-law/mental-health-act/]
- Treating the rate gap as proof of a single cause: the review says explanations need testing group by group. [tested: Barnett 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30846354/]

See someone when:
- You or someone close hears voices, believes things others do not, or cannot look after themselves (doctor, or NHS 111 in the UK mental health option urgently).
- You have been detained and want to challenge it (independent mental health advocate, solicitor, Mental Health Tribunal).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Racism, racial stress and mental health
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/racism-and-mental-health/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Many studies find that people who report experiencing racism have worse mental health, including more depression, anxiety and stress. This shows a link, not proof of cause, but it means the strain is real and not a personal failing. Talking therapies, including for trauma, are available.

Do:
- Tell someone you trust how it is affecting you; talking about feelings is NHS (UK) advice for stress. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Get help with stress", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/stress/]
- Self-refer to NHS (UK) talking therapies if low mood, worry or trauma symptoms persist; they list PTSD among what they treat. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Look for a therapist who works with racism and identity; see the Black therapist finder entry for directories. [common advice, untested: BAATN (Black, African and Asian Therapy Network), homepage, https://www.baatn.org.uk/]
- Treat the strain as a health matter: the link to depression, anxiety and stress is seen in a large body of research. [tested: Paradies 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26398658/]

Avoid:
- Assuming it is just you: the association with worse mental health was found across 293 studies. [tested: Paradies 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26398658/]
- Waiting until it is severe before asking for help: the UK's NHS says not to delay seeking help for depression. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]

See someone when:
- Low mood, anxiety, nightmares or flashbacks last more than a couple of weeks (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Stress is affecting sleep, work or relationships (doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Sleep, short sleep and sleep apnoea
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/sleep-and-sleep-apnoea/
Module: Mind
Tier: B moderate (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In a US study Black adults were more likely to sleep under six hours and to have sleep apnoea than white adults, and most people with apnoea had never been told. Discrimination is also linked to shorter sleep. If you snore loudly, gasp or are always tired, see a GP. Regular habits help insomnia.

Do:
- Wake at the same time every day and go to bed only when sleepy. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Insomnia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/]
- Keep the bedroom dark and quiet, and relax for at least an hour before bed. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Insomnia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/]
- Stop tea, coffee, alcohol and smoking at least 6 hours before bed. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Insomnia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/]
- See a doctor if you snore loudly, gasp or choke in your sleep or are always very tired in the day; ask a partner to watch for pauses in breathing. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sleep apnoea", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/]
- Mention it if you have never been tested: most people with sleep apnoea in one US study had no prior diagnosis. [tested: Chen 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25409106/]

Avoid:
- Sleeping in or napping to make up after a bad night. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Insomnia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/]
- Using phones or screens right before bed. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Insomnia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/]
- Assuming constant tiredness is normal for you: apnoea needs treating. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sleep apnoea", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/]

See someone when:
- Loud snoring with gasping or choking, morning headaches, or you are always very tired (doctor; they can refer you for a sleep test).
- Poor sleep for 3 months or more, or sleep problems alongside low mood or anxiety (doctor).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Stigma, talking to family and starting therapy
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/stigma-and-starting-therapy/
Module: Mind
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A London study found stigma, silence and beliefs about causes slow help-seeking in African-descended communities, including in church groups. You can start without a diagnosis: in the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies for anxiety, depression and trauma. Telling one person you trust is a first step.

Do:
- Refer yourself to NHS (UK) talking therapies online if you are 18 or over and registered with a doctor; you do not need a diagnosis. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Tell one person you trust; starting the conversation is what matters. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Help for suicidal thoughts", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/]
- For trauma, note that PTSD is among the problems NHS (UK) talking therapies treat by self-referral. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Ask about help through your employer, university or local charities if the UK's NHS wait is long. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]
- Do not wait: the UK's NHS says the sooner you see a doctor about depression, the sooner you can recover. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Depression in adults: overview", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/]

Avoid:
- Staying silent because of what the community may think: stigma and silencing were what blocked help in the London study. [tested: Mantovani 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27124178/]
- Choosing a private therapist who is not registered with an accredited body. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Talking therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/]

See someone when:
- Low mood, anxiety or trauma symptoms last more than a couple of weeks or stop you functioning (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Eating disorders, bipolar disorder, psychosis or drug and alcohol problems (doctor referral; these usually need a doctor, per NHS in the UK).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## Stress, burnout and blood pressure
URL: https://vilivity.com/mind/stress-burnout-and-blood-pressure/
Module: Mind
Tier: B thin (Tested or observed (see the evidence))
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Reported discrimination is linked to a higher chance of high blood pressure, but the link is small and not proven to be cause. Stress relief such as meditation may add to treatment, not replace it. If stress is wearing you down, talk to someone and get your blood pressure checked.

Do:
- Talk about your feelings with a friend, family member or health professional. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Get help with stress", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/stress/]
- If it is work stress that has not eased, name it: the WHO describes burnout as exhaustion, distance or cynicism about your job and reduced effectiveness, from chronic workplace stress that has not been managed. [clinical guidance: World Health Organization, "Burn-out an occupational phenomenon: International Classification of Diseases", https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases]
- Try the UK's NHS stress busters, including exercise and time management. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Get help with stress", https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/stress/]
- Get your blood pressure checked; stress relief is an addition to guideline treatment. [tested: Levine 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28963100/]
- Ask your doctor before relying on any practice such as meditation: a trial in Black women with hypertension found reductions of up to 7 mmHg with one technique. [tested: Collins 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34606073/]

Avoid:
- Using stress relief as a reason to stop or skip prescribed treatment. [tested: Levine 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28963100/]

See someone when:
- Your blood pressure is high or you have not had it checked in the last year (doctor or pharmacy).
- Stress is affecting sleep, work or relationships (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
- Chest pain, breathlessness or fainting (999, or your local emergency number or A&E in the UK).
- In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

## A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count)
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/low-white-cell-count-duffy-null/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Many people of African ancestry are Duffy-null, an inherited blood-cell variant that gives a lower neutrophil count (the white cells that fight infection). The main study calls it clinically insignificant. The risk is being misread: a normal count for you can be flagged as low.

What it is:
- An inherited variant: red cells do not carry the Duffy antigen. Common in people of African descent. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- Not a disease: it gives a lower neutrophil count without raising infection risk. [tested: Hibbs 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40685916/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A blood test (Duffy testing), done with a full blood count in the main study. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- A haematology review urges clinicians to use Duffy-null reference ranges, so ask your doctor or a haematologist whether yours applies, especially if your count is low and you are well. [tested: Hibbs 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40685916/]

What it changes:
- Your neutrophil count runs lower than other people: median 2,820 against 5,005 per microlitre in one clinic. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- Many cancer trials exclude people whose count is in the Duffy-null range. [tested: Hibbs 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39259539/]
- Standard cut-offs can wrongly label you neutropenic, which can affect treatment and dosing decisions. [tested: Hibbs 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40685916/]

What it does not change:
- It does not raise your risk of infection. [tested: Hibbs 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40685916/]
- It is not a disease and needs no treatment on its own. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]

See someone when:
- You have a low neutrophil count and fevers, repeated infections, mouth ulcers or you feel unwell (doctor, urgently if fever).
- You are about to start chemotherapy or a clinical trial and were told your count is too low (haematologist or oncologist: ask about Duffy-null).
- The count is very low or keeps falling (doctor, then haematologist).

## Alpha-thalassaemia trait: small red cells that are not low iron
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/alpha-thalassaemia-trait-and-low-iron-that-is-not-low-iron/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Alpha-thalassaemia trait means you carry one or two missing copies of the genes that make part of haemoglobin. It is common in people of African descent and can show as small, pale red cells and mild anaemia that looks like low iron. Ask what is behind small red cells before you start iron tablets.

What it is:
- People have four copies of the alpha-globin genes. Losing two causes alpha-thalassaemia trait: unusually small, pale red cells and mild anaemia. Losing one makes a silent carrier, usually with no signs. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Alpha thalassemia", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/alpha-thalassemia/]
- Alpha-thalassaemia is fairly common worldwide, and occurs frequently in people from the Mediterranean, Africa, the Middle East, India and Central Asia. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Alpha thalassemia", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/alpha-thalassemia/]
- More than 100 varieties have been identified; the authors of a review say alpha-thalassaemias deserve higher priority on global public health agendas. [tested: Piel 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25390741/]
- It is inherited, so it is not on you and not caused by your diet. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Alpha thalassemia", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/alpha-thalassemia/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A doctor does a full blood count; if the cause is not clear they may do other tests, and treatment follows once the reason for the anaemia is found. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]
- In one large US study, haemoglobin, red cell size (MCV), transferrin saturation and ferritin were measured alongside a DNA test for the common -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]

What it changes:
- The -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion accounted for about one third of the haemoglobin gap between African Americans and white people. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- Among women, 19.8% of African Americans would be classed as anaemic against 5.3% of white women. With iron-deficient and thalassaemic people removed, the figures were 6.1% and 2.77%. Among men the figures fell from 17.7% and 7.6% to 4.29% and 3.6%. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- Iron tablets replace missing iron, and are advised once a blood test shows low red cells and the cause has been found; the gene change is a separate cause of small red cells. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]

What it does not change:
- Sickle trait and raised creatinine had no effect on the haemoglobin difference in the same study. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- Trait usually means mild anaemia only. The serious forms (HbH disease, Hb Bart syndrome) come from losing three or four copies. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Alpha thalassemia", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/alpha-thalassemia/]
- If both parents are missing at least one alpha-globin copy, their children are at risk of Hb Bart syndrome, HbH disease or trait; the risk depends on how many copies are missing. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Alpha thalassemia", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/alpha-thalassemia/]

See someone when:
- Tiredness, breathlessness or paleness that is new or getting worse (doctor, full blood count).
- You have been told you are anaemic but iron tablets have not helped, or no cause was found (doctor; ask whether thalassaemia trait was considered).
- Planning a pregnancy when you or your partner may carry thalassaemia or sickle genes (doctor, midwife or genetic counselling service; antenatal screening offers differ by country, so ask what is offered where you live).
- Children in the family with severe anaemia from early childhood (doctor or paediatrician, soon).

## Bowel (colon) cancer screening
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/bowel-and-colon-cancer-screening/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In England the NHS posts a home stool test every 2 years from 50 to 74; US guidance starts at 45. Screening works in the general population, and I found no trial of an earlier start for Black adults. Do the test when it arrives, and see a GP about blood in your poo.

Do:
- Do the home FIT test when it arrives: the UK's NHS offers it to people aged 50 to 74 every 2 years, and over-74s can request a kit on 0800 707 6060. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Bowel cancer screening", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bowel-cancer-screening/]
- See a doctor about bowel symptoms you are worried about, whether or not you have had screening. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Bowel cancer screening", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bowel-cancer-screening/]
- If you are in the US, screening from 45 to 49 is recommended (a B recommendation) and from 50 to 75 is strongly recommended (an A recommendation). [tested: US 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34003218/]

Avoid:
- Waiting for a screening invitation when you have symptoms: tell a doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Bowel cancer screening", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bowel-cancer-screening/]
- Assuming screening is only for older people: in the US about one in ten new cases is in people under 50, and cases in 40 to 49 year olds are rising. [tested: US 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34003218/]

See someone when:
- Blood in your poo, or a change in your bowel habit that lasts for weeks (doctor).
- You are 50 or over and have not received a screening kit (your doctor's surgery or the national helpline).
- A close relative had bowel cancer, especially before 50 (doctor: family history can change when screening should start; not covered here).

In other countries:
- In Jamaica, the Ministry of Health 2020 guideline offers average-risk adults a yearly stool test, with colonoscopy if it is positive. (https://www.moh.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/National-Screening-Guidelines-for-Priority-Non-Communicable-Diseases-NCDs-in-Primary-Health-Care.pdf)
- In Kenya, the Ministry of Health 2025 protocol uses a stool blood test (gFOBT or FIT) for average-risk people, repeated after 1 year. (https://health.go.ke/sites/default/files/2025-07/FINAL_NCD%20protocols.pdf)
- In South Africa, the 2026 Adult Primary Care guide says bowel cancer screening is not routinely done; people with symptoms should discuss it with a clinician. (https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2026-10/APC%202026%20E-book.pdf)
- In the US, the USPSTF recommends colorectal cancer screening for adults aged 45 to 49 and, more strongly, for those aged 50 to 75. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening)

## Breast cancer, triple-negative disease and screening
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/breast-cancer-and-cancer-screening/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In England, Black women did not have a higher breast cancer rate than White women, but short-term survival was worse in national data, and one London hospital saw younger, more aggressive cases. Know your own breasts and see a GP about any change. NHS breast screening starts between 50 and 53, bowel screening at 50.

Do:
- See a doctor about a lump, swelling, dimpling or a change in your breast or nipple; on black or brown skin a colour change may look darker than usual. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of breast cancer in women", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/breast-cancer/symptoms/]
- Take up your breast screening invitation, which arrives between 50 and 53 and then every 3 years until your 71st birthday. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Who breast screening is for", https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/breast-screening-mammogram/who-breast-screening-is-for/]
- If no letter has come by 53, contact your local breast screening service. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Who breast screening is for", https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/breast-screening-mammogram/who-breast-screening-is-for/]
- Do the bowel screening home test (FIT kit) when it arrives from age 50, every 2 years to 74. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Bowel cancer screening", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bowel-cancer-screening/]

Avoid:
- Waiting for a screening letter when you have noticed a change: see a doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of breast cancer in women", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/breast-cancer/symptoms/]
- Assuming no pain means no problem: breast pain by itself is not usually a symptom, and you can have these symptoms without pain. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of breast cancer in women", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/breast-cancer/symptoms/]

See someone when:
- A lump or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit (doctor).
- A change in the skin, shape or size of a breast, or in the nipple, including discharge or a rash (doctor).
- You are 50 to 53 and have not had a first screening invitation (breast screening service).
- Blood in your poo or a change in your bowel habit for weeks (doctor).

In other countries:
- In Jamaica, the Ministry of Health 2020 guideline says there is no national mammography screening programme. (https://www.moh.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/National-Screening-Guidelines-for-Priority-Non-Communicable-Diseases-NCDs-in-Primary-Health-Care.pdf)
- In South Africa, the 2026 Adult Primary Care guide offers clinical breast exams twice a year for women aged 40 to 70. (https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2026-10/APC%202026%20E-book.pdf)
- In the US, the USPSTF recommends a mammogram every 2 years for women aged 40 to 74. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-screening)
- WHO describes mammography screening as usually for women aged 50 to 69. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/breast-cancer)

## Creatine supplements: strength, kidneys and your kidney test
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/creatine-supplements/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Creatine helps strength gains when you train with weights, in trials of mostly young men, and reviews found no kidney harm in healthy adults. Our search found no creatine trial in Black participants. It raises the creatinine kidney marker, so tell anyone reading your kidney tests, and check with a doctor first if you have kidney problems.

Do:
- Tell any clinician who reads your kidney blood tests that you take creatine: it can raise serum creatinine without harming your kidneys. [tested: Naeini 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41199218/]
- Pair it with resistance training if strength is your aim: that is where the trial gains were seen. [tested: Wang 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39519498/]
- Check with your health care provider before using it if you are at risk of kidney problems, and expect to be monitored. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Bodybuilding and Performance Enhancement Supplements: What You Need To Know", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/bodybuilding-and-performance-enhancement-supplements]

Avoid:
- Creatine for teenagers: NCCIH says no safety data exist in children, and the American Academy of Pediatrics and American College of Sports Medicine warn against it for teens. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Bodybuilding and Performance Enhancement Supplements: What You Need To Know", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/bodybuilding-and-performance-enhancement-supplements]
- Assuming a "low" kidney reading is real if you take creatine and a creatinine-based test is the only evidence: ask whether another test is needed. [tested: Gray 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42498056/]

See someone when:
- Your creatinine or eGFR result looks abnormal while you take creatine (doctor; ask about repeating it off creatine or a cystatin C test).
- You have kidney disease or a family history of it (doctor or kidney team, before starting).
- Severe muscle pain, swelling or very dark urine after hard exercise (urgent care).

## Fibroids: symptoms, treatment and pregnancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/fibroids-symptoms-treatment-and-pregnancy/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, and by 50 more than eight in ten Black women in one US study had them. Many have no symptoms and need no treatment. If heavy or painful periods, pressure or fertility worries affect your life, see a GP: there are medicines, and several procedures other than hysterectomy.

Do:
- See a doctor if you have heavy or painful periods, tummy or back pain, needing to pee often, or pain during sex. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Expect an ultrasound scan to show how many fibroids there are, where they are and how big. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Ask what options you have before surgery: medicines come first, and some procedures leave the womb in place. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- If you want children, tell the doctor before any treatment: some treatments can stop pregnancy or raise risks in it. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Ask for a blood test for iron deficiency anaemia if bleeding is heavy; see the iron and fibroids entry. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]

Avoid:
- Putting up with heavy periods when painkillers are not helping. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Choosing surgery without asking how it affects having children. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]

See someone when:
- Periods that are heavy or painful enough to affect work, relationships or daily life (doctor).
- Trouble peeing or pooing, or a swollen tummy that is not going down (doctor).
- Difficulty getting pregnant or repeated miscarriages with fibroids known (gynaecologist).
- Bleeding between periods or after sex, or sudden severe pelvic pain (doctor urgently).

## G6PD deficiency: who carries it and what to avoid
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/g6pd-deficiency-what-to-avoid-and-who-carries-it/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: G6PD deficiency is an inherited enzyme shortage, common in people with African, Mediterranean and Asian ancestry. Most carriers feel well. Red blood cells break down only when something stresses them, such as an infection, fava beans or certain medicines. A simple blood test finds it, so ask for one before malaria treatment with primaquine.

What it is:
- An inherited shortage of an enzyme makes red blood cells break down early (haemolysis). The usual problem is haemolytic anaemia, most often set off by infections, some drugs or fava beans. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-deficiency/]
- It is inherited, so nothing you did caused it. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency" (medical encyclopedia), https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000528.htm]
- About 400 million people worldwide have it, most often in parts of Africa, Asia, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-deficiency/]
- The gene sits on the X chromosome. Males have one copy, so one altered copy causes deficiency. Many females with one altered copy are affected much like males, because the normal copy is switched off in most cells. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-deficiency/]
- Many people with it never have symptoms and never know. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency", https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-deficiency/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A blood test measures the G6PD level. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency" (medical encyclopedia), https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000528.htm]
- During a breakdown episode you may have dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, pale skin, tiredness, a fast heartbeat or breathlessness. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency" (medical encyclopedia), https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000528.htm]
- Testing before malaria-area deployment was made mandatory for US Army soldiers; the screening covered 63,302 people. [tested: Chinevere 2006, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17036616/]

What it changes:
- Episodes can be triggered by infections, fava beans, mothball chemicals and some medicines. MedlinePlus lists quinine and other antimalarials, high-dose aspirin, anti-inflammatory painkillers, sulfa medicines and antibiotics such as quinolones and nitrofurantoin. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency" (medical encyclopedia), https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000528.htm]
- A 2023 international guideline sorts medicines into high, medium and low-to-no risk: avoid high risk, use medium risk with caution, and use low-to-no risk with standard precautions. It says official warnings often conflict, so one list on one website can be incomplete. [clinical guidance: CPIC guideline for medication use and G6PD genotype (Gammal et al. 2023, abstract), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36049896/]
- In 63,302 US Army personnel tested, 12.2% of African American males and 4.1% of African American females were deficient, against 4.3% of Asian males and 2.5% of all males. [tested: Chinevere 2006, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17036616/]
- Across ten malaria-endemic African countries, 19 studies found G6PD deficiency from under 1% to 23.9%, higher in men than in women. [tested: Taleb 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40225210/]

What it does not change:
- Most deficient people in the Army screening had only moderate enzyme loss. [tested: Chinevere 2006, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17036616/]
- Episodes are usually brief, because the body keeps making new red cells with normal enzyme activity. [clinical guidance: MedlinePlus, "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency" (medical encyclopedia), https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000528.htm]
- Having it does not mean avoiding all medicines or all malaria care: many drugs fall in the low-to-no-risk class. [clinical guidance: CPIC guideline for medication use and G6PD genotype (Gammal et al. 2023, abstract), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36049896/]

See someone when:
- Dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, sudden paleness or breathlessness after a new medicine, an infection or eating fava beans (urgent same-day care; emergency services if severe).
- Before malaria treatment, travel tablets or any new medicine, if you or a relative has had a reaction or been told they have G6PD deficiency (doctor, pharmacist or travel clinic).
- A newborn whose yellow skin appears early or deepens, especially with a family history (midwife or doctor the same day).

## Glaucoma and eye tests
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/glaucoma-and-eye-tests/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Glaucoma is more common in Black populations at every age, and often has no symptoms until sight is lost. A pooled analysis found the highest prevalence in Black populations at all ages. Have an eye test at least every two years, and ask whether you qualify for a free NHS (UK) test, for example if a close relative has glaucoma.

Do:
- Have an eye test at least every 2 years: glaucoma is usually found during a routine test before any symptoms. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Glaucoma", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/glaucoma/]
- Ask for a free NHS (UK) sight test if you are 40 or over and a parent, brother, sister or child has glaucoma. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Free NHS eye tests and optical vouchers", https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/opticians/free-nhs-eye-tests-and-optical-vouchers/]
- If advised you are at higher risk, have eye tests more often. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Glaucoma", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/glaucoma/]
- If you are diagnosed, go to every follow-up appointment: treatments slow damage but there is no cure. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Glaucoma", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/glaucoma/]

Avoid:
- Waiting for symptoms: it usually has none and develops slowly over years. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Glaucoma", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/glaucoma/]
- Missing follow-up appointments once treatment has started. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Glaucoma", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/glaucoma/]

See someone when:
- Sudden severe eye pain, a red eye, seeing rainbow rings around lights, blurred vision, sickness or a headache (call 999, or your local emergency number or go to A&E in the UK; do not drive).
- You have not had an eye test in the last 2 years (optician).
- A parent, brother, sister or child has glaucoma and you are 40 or over (optician, for a free test).

In other countries:
- In the US, the National Eye Institute says African American people over 40 are at higher risk, and higher-risk people need a dilated exam every 1 to 2 years. (https://www.nei.nih.gov/learn-about-eye-health/eye-conditions-and-diseases/glaucoma)
- In the US, Medicare covers a glaucoma screening once every 12 months if you are African American and 50 or older, after the Part B deductible and 20% cost. (https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/glaucoma-screenings)
- In the US, the USPSTF says evidence is insufficient to judge routine glaucoma screening in adults 40 or older. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/primary-open-angle-glaucoma-screening)

## Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/haemoglobin-and-white-cell-reference-ranges/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Blood test ranges were mostly built from white populations. In large studies, Black adults have lower average haemoglobin and white cell counts, partly from inherited traits such as alpha-thalassaemia and Duffy-null, and partly from low iron. A result outside the range can still be real, so ask what is behind it.

What it is:
- A blood count reports haemoglobin, red cell size (MCV) and white cell counts, each judged against a reference range. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- Benign ethnic neutropenia is the old name for a neutrophil count under 1,500 per microlitre with no extra infection risk; it is most common in people of African ancestry and tracks the Duffy-null trait. [tested: Merz 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33181819/]
- Duffy-null is found in 80% to 100% of people of sub-Saharan African ancestry and under 1% of people of European descent. [tested: Merz 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33181819/]

How to find out if you have it:
- Duffy status is a blood test; in one clinic study it was measured alongside a full blood count with differential. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- Whether low haemoglobin is from low iron or a gene change is sorted by iron tests and sometimes DNA tests; the large US study measured ferritin and transferrin saturation and tested for the alpha-thalassaemia deletion. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]

What it changes:
- Among 120 healthy Black adults at one US primary care centre, 80 (66.7%) were Duffy-null. Their median neutrophil count was 2,820 per microlitre against 5,005 in the others, and 19 of the 80 were under 2,000, against none of the others. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- In 1,491 African American and 31,005 white people, haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV, transferrin saturation and white cell count were lower in African Americans; ferritin was higher. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- In 2024 WHO revised haemoglobin cut-offs for children aged 6 to 23 months, pregnant women in the second trimester and people living at altitude. A review of the guideline lists no ethnicity-based cut-off. [tested: Khurana 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38910369/]

What it does not change:
- The Duffy-null low neutrophil count is clinically insignificant; the study authors want Duffy-null ranges, not a label of disease. [tested: Merz 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/]
- Removing iron-deficient and thalassaemic people narrowed the anaemia gap but did not close it (women 6.1% against 2.77%). [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]
- Whether to adopt group-specific haemoglobin ranges is contested; the Beutler authors argue for them, and my search found no counter-argument I could open. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]

See someone when:
- Tiredness, breathlessness, paleness or a fast heartbeat that is new or getting worse (doctor, full blood count and iron tests).
- Told your white cell or neutrophil count is low: ask whether your Duffy status was considered, and read the Duffy-null entry (doctor or haematologist).
- Fever, chills or an infection that will not clear, whatever your counts say (urgent care).
- Being excluded from a treatment or trial because of a low neutrophil count: ask whether Duffy-null was considered (the doctor running it).

## Heat, sweating and hydration
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/heat-and-hydration/
Module: Body
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: I found no study that shows Black people tolerate heat better or sweat differently. What exists is old, small, and in men who were already acclimatised. Heat risk follows fitness, acclimatisation, body size and exposure. Follow the UK's NHS heat advice, and take extra care if you or your child has sickle cell disease or trait.

Do:
- Drink extra fluids in hot weather, and have cold drinks and cold food. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heatwave: how to cope in hot weather", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/heatwave-how-to-cope-in-hot-weather/]
- Stay in the shade and avoid exercise or hard activity between 11am and 3pm. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heatwave: how to cope in hot weather", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/heatwave-how-to-cope-in-hot-weather/]
- If someone has heat exhaustion: move them somewhere cool, remove extra clothing and give plenty of water. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heat exhaustion and heatstroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heat-exhaustion-heatstroke/]
- If you have sickle cell disease, avoid dehydration and sudden temperature changes: both can trigger a crisis. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]

Avoid:
- Alcohol, caffeine and hot drinks during a heatwave. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heatwave: how to cope in hot weather", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/heatwave-how-to-cope-in-hot-weather/]
- Relying on skin colour to spot heat exhaustion: the UK's NHS says a change in skin colour can be harder to see on brown or black skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heat exhaustion and heatstroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heat-exhaustion-heatstroke/]

See someone when:
- Hot skin without sweating, a very high temperature, fast breathing, confusion or a seizure (call 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number: heatstroke).
- Heat exhaustion that has not eased after 30 minutes of cooling down (NHS 111 in the UK).
- A child or older relative is unwell in the heat (NHS 111 in the UK, or 999, or your local emergency number if they are confused or unresponsive).

## High blood pressure in Black adults
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/high-blood-pressure-in-black-adults/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: The line for high blood pressure is the same for every adult. In England, blood pressure in people of African-Caribbean origin overtakes White people's at around 30 to 40 (about 28 for men's systolic pressure), so being young and fit does not rule it out. Get it checked. If you need tablets, NICE names a different first choice for you.

Do:
- Get your blood pressure checked at a pharmacy or doctor's surgery even if you feel well: it usually causes no symptoms. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure (hypertension)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/]
- Do not wait until 40 to be checked: in one English survey, African-Caribbean blood pressure pulled ahead of White from about 30. [tested: Agyemang 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21881618/]
- Ask for home or 24-hour monitoring to confirm a high clinic reading before any diagnosis. [clinical guidance: NICE NG136, "Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management" (recommendations), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations]
- If tablets are needed, know that NICE suggests a calcium-channel blocker first for Black African or African-Caribbean adults without type 2 diabetes. Your prescriber decides. [clinical guidance: NICE NG136, "Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management" (recommendations), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations]
- Cut down on salt and keep active, as for every adult with high blood pressure. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure (hypertension)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/]

Avoid:
- Taking one clinic reading as the diagnosis: NICE (UK) confirms it with home or 24-hour readings. [clinical guidance: NICE NG136, "Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management" (recommendations), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations]
- Waiting for symptoms: the UK's NHS says high blood pressure does not usually cause any. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure (hypertension)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/]

See someone when:
- A clinic reading of 140/90 or above, or a home average of 135/85 or above (doctor).
- A high reading with a severe headache, blurred vision or chest pain (NHS 111 in the UK urgently; 999, or your local emergency number for chest pain that does not go away).
- You are pregnant or recently gave birth and have a severe headache, vision changes or sudden swelling (call your maternity unit or 111 in the UK straight away).

In other countries:
- In Canada, the 2025 Hypertension Canada primary care guideline defines hypertension as a measured blood pressure of 130/80 or higher. (https://hypertension.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Hypertension-guideline.pdf)
- In Ghana, the 2017 Standard Treatment Guidelines prefer thiazide diuretics or calcium-channel blockers for the general black population; ACE inhibitors are not first choice for uncomplicated cases. (https://www.moh.gov.gh/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/GHANA-STG-2017-1.pdf)
- In Jamaica, the Ministry of Health 2020 interim guideline uses 140/90 and lists a diuretic or calcium-channel blocker for Black patients without heart failure or kidney disease. (https://www.moh.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/HYPERTENSIONGUIDELINES_Interim_final.pdf)
- In Kenya, the Ministry of Health 2025 protocols define hypertension as 140/90 or higher in adults over 18. (https://health.go.ke/sites/default/files/2025-07/FINAL_NCD%20protocols.pdf)
- In South Africa, the national hypertension user guide defines hypertension as 140/90 or higher, confirmed on repeat readings. (https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2021-11/HYPERTENSION%20USER%20GUIDE%20FINAL%20COPY.pdf)
- In the US, the USPSTF advises blood pressure screening for adults aged 18 or older. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/hypertension-in-adults-screening)
- WHO defines hypertension as 140/90 mmHg or higher, confirmed on two different days. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hypertension)

## HIV prevention, testing and PrEP
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/hiv-prevention-testing-and-prep/
Module: Body
Tier: A strong (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: PrEP is a medicine you take before a possible exposure to HIV, and it is highly effective when taken as prescribed. It comes as tablets, injections or a vaginal ring depending on where you live. Get an HIV test first and then regularly. HIV treatment is effective, so knowing your status is a good thing.

Do:
- Get an HIV test at a clinic, an antenatal service or a pharmacy, or order a home testing kit. In the UK you may be eligible for a free one. [clinical guidance: NHS, "HIV and AIDS" (prevention and testing), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hiv-and-aids/prevention/]
- In England, ask a sexual health clinic about PrEP: it is free on the NHS as daily or on-demand tablets, and some people may need an injection every two months. [clinical guidance: NHS, "HIV and AIDS" (prevention and testing), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hiv-and-aids/prevention/]
- In the US, ask a provider or use the HIV.gov services locator: there are two FDA-approved daily oral PrEP medicines and two long-acting injections (every other month and twice a year). [clinical guidance: HIV.gov, Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), https://www.hiv.gov/hiv-basics/hiv-prevention/using-hiv-medication-to-reduce-risk/pre-exposure-prophylaxis]
- Elsewhere ask a local HIV clinic. WHO recommends oral tenofovir-based PrEP, the dapivirine vaginal ring, long-acting injectable cabotegravir and long-acting injectable lenacapavir. [clinical guidance: WHO, HIV and AIDS fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids]
- If you think you were exposed in the last 72 hours, go to a sexual health clinic or emergency department for PEP (post-exposure medicine) in the UK; elsewhere ask an emergency service. [clinical guidance: NHS, "HIV and AIDS" (prevention and testing), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hiv-and-aids/prevention/]

Avoid:
- Taking PrEP on and off: it reduces the risk of HIV from sex by about 99% when taken as prescribed and is much less effective when not taken consistently. [clinical guidance: HIV.gov, Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), https://www.hiv.gov/hiv-basics/hiv-prevention/using-hiv-medication-to-reduce-risk/pre-exposure-prophylaxis]
- Starting PrEP without a clinician: WHO says people should seek advice from a clinician when thinking about PrEP or PEP. [clinical guidance: WHO, HIV and AIDS fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids]
- Dropping condoms and other protection: the UK's NHS calls condoms the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. [clinical guidance: NHS, "HIV and AIDS" (prevention and testing), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hiv-and-aids/prevention/]
- Assuming it is someone else's risk: transmission is ongoing in all countries (WHO). [clinical guidance: WHO, HIV and AIDS fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids]

See someone when:
- You think you were exposed in the last 72 hours (sexual health clinic or emergency department, the same day, for PEP).
- You have not had an HIV test in the last year and have had a new partner or shared needles (sexual health clinic, doctor or a community HIV service).
- A flu-like illness or rash after a possible exposure: ask for an HIV test and tell them if you take PrEP (clinic).
- A positive test: treatment is available and effective; ask for a same-week appointment at an HIV clinic (where you live, ask the testing service).

In other countries:
- In South Africa, the 2026 Adult Primary Care guide cites national lenacapavir PrEP guidelines and says this PrEP needs 6-monthly injections. (https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2026-10/APC%202026%20E-book.pdf)
- In the US, HIV.gov says PrEP is free under almost all health insurance plans under the Affordable Care Act. (https://www.hiv.gov/hiv-basics/hiv-prevention/using-hiv-medication-to-reduce-risk/pre-exposure-prophylaxis/)
- WHO recommends oral tenofovir-based PrEP, the dapivirine ring, and long-acting injectable cabotegravir or lenacapavir. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids)

## How some medicines work differently by gene
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/how-some-medicines-work-differently-by-gene/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Genes change how fast your body breaks down some medicines. The variable is the gene, and some versions are more common in people of African ancestry. Examples are ACE inhibitor tablets, which cause face or throat swelling more often in Black patients, and warfarin, whose dose needs gene variants the first formulas missed.

What it is:
- CYP2D6 is a gene for a drug-processing enzyme. Functional versions make up about 50% of copies in Africans and African Americans, reduced-function versions about 35% (mostly *17), and non-functional versions 14.5% in African Americans against 6.3% in Africans. [tested: Bradford 2002, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11972444/]
- The pattern differs between regions: in Europeans and their descendants functional versions are about 71% and non-functional about 26%. [tested: Bradford 2002, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11972444/]
- Age, allergy history and genes all change the chance of a reaction; in the enalapril trial a past drug rash and seasonal allergies raised the risk of swelling. [tested: Kostis 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043683/]

How to find out if you have it:
- In the enalapril trial, a history of drug rash, age over 65 and seasonal allergies each raised angioedema risk alongside Black race. [tested: Kostis 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043683/]
- Warfarin studies genotype the VKORC1 and CYP2C9 genes; in African Americans these two explain less of the dose variation, so another variant on chromosome 10 was identified. [tested: Perera 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23755828/]

What it changes:
- In 12,557 people with hypertension given enalapril, angioedema occurred in 0.68%; black race raised the odds 2.88 times (95% CI 1.72 to 4.82). [tested: Kostis 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043683/]
- In Cape Town, 237 people with ACE inhibitor angioedema were compared with 466 who tolerated the tablets for two years: 53% of cases had Black genetic ancestry against 29% of controls. [tested: Day 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41189626/]
- In a genetic study of more than 1,000 European patients, the lead risk variants had similar effect sizes and direction in an African-American cohort. [tested: Mathey 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38300190/]
- NICE says that when choosing blood pressure medicine for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, consider an angiotensin II receptor blocker in preference to an ACE inhibitor. [clinical guidance: NICE NG136, "Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management" (recommendation 1.4.30), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations]
- In 533 African American adults on stable warfarin, a new variant in the CYP2C cluster was linked to dose and replicated in 432 more. [tested: Perera 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23755828/]

What it does not change:
- Angioedema from enalapril was uncommon, and none of the 86 cases needed airway protection or died. [tested: Kostis 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043683/]
- ACE inhibitors have proven benefits for mortality and illness in hypertension, heart disease, heart failure and kidney disease; most people tolerate them. [tested: Day 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41189626/]
- The NICE (UK) advice is to consider an ARB in preference; ACE inhibitors stay an option, and NICE says to offer an ACE inhibitor or ARB to adults with type 2 diabetes of any family origin. [clinical guidance: NICE NG136, "Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management" (recommendation 1.4.30), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations]

See someone when:
- Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat, or trouble breathing, while on blood pressure tablets: emergency services now (NHS says throat swelling is a medical emergency; UK 999, US and Canada 911, Australia 000).
- Any past reaction to a medicine, in you or a close relative: tell the prescriber and pharmacist before starting a new one (doctor or pharmacist).
- A medicine that is hard to dose, such as warfarin, or that has not worked as expected: ask whether gene-guided dosing is offered in your service (doctor or anticoagulant clinic).
- A rash, cough or other reaction after starting a new tablet (doctor or pharmacist, before you stop it unless you are told to).

## Ice baths and cold exposure
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/ice-baths-and-cold-exposure/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: yes
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Ice baths eased muscle soreness after exercise in small, low-quality trials that did not report ethnicity. No trial has tested them in people of African descent, and cold injury was far more common in African American soldiers in one British army clinic. Cold shock is a real risk.

Do:
- Enter slowly and give your breathing time to settle before anything else. [clinical guidance: Met Office blog, "Cold water shock: what it is and how to stay safe" (quotes RNLI and RLSS UK), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/blog/2025/cold-water-shock-how-to-stay-safe]
- Get out if you shiver badly, feel weak, disorientated or short of breath, then warm up at once with dry clothes and a hot drink. [clinical guidance: Met Office blog, "Cold water shock: what it is and how to stay safe" (quotes RNLI and RLSS UK), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/blog/2025/cold-water-shock-how-to-stay-safe]
- Go with someone, and tell someone where you are and when you will be back. [clinical guidance: Met Office blog, "Cold water shock: what it is and how to stay safe" (quotes RNLI and RLSS UK), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/blog/2025/cold-water-shock-how-to-stay-safe]
- Skip it straight after strength training if gaining strength or size is your aim. [tested: Roberts 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26174323/]

Avoid:
- Long immersions that leave fingers or toes numb, white or painful: finger cooling was stronger in men of African descent in one lab. [tested: Maley 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25081130/]
- Cold water with a heart condition unless a doctor agrees: cold shock increases arrhythmias. [tested: Barwood 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211547/]
- Believing it treats depression or anxiety. [tested: Ngandeu 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42819812/]

See someone when:
- Fingers or toes stay numb, pale or painful after warming up (doctor).
- You get chest pain, palpitations, fainting or severe breathlessness in cold water (urgent care).
- You have a heart condition (ask your doctor before starting).
- You have sickle cell disease or trait and plan regular cold exposure (ask your haematology team): I did not find specific data.

## Iron, heavy periods and fibroids
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/iron-and-fibroids/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Fibroids are very common in Black women and start earlier than in White women. Heavy periods can drain iron, and in a small US pilot most African American women had low iron. Do not treat tiredness or heavy bleeding yourself: ask a doctor for a blood test.

Do:
- Note how heavy your periods are, and how tired you feel, and take it to your doctor. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]
- Ask for a full blood count if periods are heavy or you are exhausted. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]
- Ask about iron stores (ferritin) too: low iron was common without anaemia. [tested: Bernardi 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27524363/]
- Eat iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, pulses and fortified cereals; tea and coffee with meals reduce absorption. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]

Avoid:
- Taking iron tablets without a blood test: the UK's NHS has a doctor recommend them once a test shows low levels. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]
- Assuming a low haemoglobin means the same thing for everyone: laboratory ranges differed by group. [tested: Beutler 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/]

See someone when:
- Periods are so heavy they affect your daily life, last a long time, or you feel exhausted (doctor).
- Bleeding between periods or after sex, or pelvic pain (doctor).
- A haemoglobin result is flagged low: ask whether iron deficiency or an inherited trait such as alpha-thalassaemia is the cause (doctor).
- Fibroids have been seen on a scan and you have symptoms (gynaecologist: removal is one specialist option).

## Kidney disease, the APOL1 gene and the eGFR race adjustment
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/kidney-disease-apol1-and-egfr/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Two variants of the APOL1 gene, common on African chromosomes, raise the risk of some kidney diseases in African Americans. Early kidney disease usually has no symptoms. UK guidance no longer adjusts the kidney blood test (eGFR) for Black ethnicity. If you have high blood pressure or diabetes, ask about regular kidney checks.

What it is:
- APOL1 is a gene on chromosome 22; two variants common in African chromosomes and absent from European ones raise the risk of some kidney disease. [tested: Genovese 2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20647424/]
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is usually caused by other conditions that strain the kidneys, such as high blood pressure and diabetes. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Chronic kidney disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-disease/]

How to find out if you have it:
- Blood and urine tests find it; if you have high blood pressure or diabetes you may be advised to have regular tests. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Chronic kidney disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-disease/]
- Early CKD usually has no symptoms; later signs include tiredness, swollen ankles, breathlessness and blood in your pee. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Chronic kidney disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-disease/]

What it changes:
