- In African Americans the two APOL1 variants were linked to a 10-fold higher odds of a scarring kidney disease (FSGS) and a 7-fold higher odds of high-blood-pressure-related kidney failure. [tested: Genovese 2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20647424/]
- The old kidney test equation with a Black-race adjustment overestimated true kidney function in Black participants by a median of 3.7 mL/min. [tested: Inker 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34554658/]
- Equations using creatinine and cystatin C, without race, were more accurate than creatinine alone, with smaller gaps between groups. [tested: Inker 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34554658/]

What it does not change:
- NICE (UK) removed the ethnicity adjustment: differences in eGFR are probably partly due to muscle mass, which varies between people of the same ethnicity. [clinical guidance: NICE NG203, "Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management" (recommendations), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations]
- Race is a social, not biological, construct in these equations (the authors' words); the measure that matters is measured GFR. [tested: Inker 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34554658/]

See someone when:
- High blood pressure or diabetes and no kidney blood or urine test in the last year or so (doctor).
- Blood in your pee, swollen ankles or feet, or breathlessness that is new (doctor).
- A kidney result was reported using a race adjustment and you are being assessed for referral or a transplant list: ask whether it was recalculated without it (doctor or kidney doctor).

In other countries:
- In the US, NIDDK lists race-free CKD-EPI equations for estimating kidney function in people 18 and older. (https://www.niddk.nih.gov/research-funding/research-programs/kidney-clinical-research-epidemiology/laboratory/glomerular-filtration-rate-equations/adults)
- In the US, the National Kidney Foundation and American Society of Nephrology recommended a race-free approach to estimate kidney function in September 2021. (https://www.kidney.org/press-room/nkf-and-asn-release-new-way-to-diagnose-kidney-diseases)

## Lactose intolerance and dairy
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/lactose-intolerance-and-dairy/
Module: Body
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Not every Black person is lactose intolerant, and there is no race rule. Whether you keep making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, depends on your genes, and several separate gene variants that keep it switched on are known in East African groups. Symptoms after dairy are checked with a food trial or a breath test.

What it is:
- Symptoms such as tummy pain, bloating and diarrhoea after eating or drinking something with lactose, a sugar in animal milk. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- Usually caused by the body not making enough lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- In Africa, the ability to digest milk as an adult is linked to different gene variants from the European one. [tested: Tishkoff 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17159977/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A doctor may suggest a lactose elimination diet or a hydrogen breath test; blood tests are sometimes used. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- See a doctor if symptoms keep coming back, or you have bloating, loose stools or weight loss for 3 weeks. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]

What it changes:
- Symptoms can be prevented by eating smaller portions of lactose foods or avoiding them; it is important not to cut foods out without advice from a doctor or dietitian. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- A lactase supplement taken before lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]

What it does not change:
- It is not a food allergy, which can cause swelling and breathing difficulty and needs 999. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- It cannot be read from race: the African study found three separate variants in Tanzanians, Kenyans and Sudanese, so group averages do not apply to you. [tested: Tishkoff 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17159977/]

See someone when:
- Tummy pain, bloating or loose stools after dairy that keep happening (doctor).
- Blood in your poo, or weight loss without trying (doctor).
- Lips, mouth, throat or tongue swelling, fast breathing or a tight throat after eating (call 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).

## Lung function tests and race correction in spirometry
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/lung-function-tests-and-race-correction-in-spirometry/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A spirometry test measures how much air you can blow out in one breath. For years the machine compared Black patients with a lower predicted normal than white patients, which can hide lung disease. Guidelines now recommend one race-neutral set of equations. The test is still useful, and your symptoms matter as much as the number.

What it is:
- Spirometry measures how much air you can breathe out in one breath. It is used to check for conditions such as asthma, COPD and pulmonary fibrosis, and to monitor them. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Spirometry test", https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/spirometry/]
- Your result is compared with a predicted normal. Until recently, standards promoted equations that also used self-reported race and ethnicity. [clinical guidance: ATS official statement, "Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation" (Bhakta et al. 2023, abstract), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36973004/]
- Worry grew that this gives a false view of fixed differences between races and may mask the effect of different exposures such as air pollution and work. [clinical guidance: ATS official statement, "Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation" (Bhakta et al. 2023, abstract), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36973004/]

How to find out if you have it:
- The test is done by a healthcare professional at a doctor's surgery, clinic or hospital; they measure your height and weight, which are used to work out your results. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Spirometry test", https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/spirometry/]
- The 2022 GLI-Global race-neutral equations were built by reanalysing the original GLI data from 74,185 people. [tested: Bowerman 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383197/]

What it changes:
- Sitting height, a body-proportion measure, improved the statistics slightly but did not explain the differences in spirometry between race and ethnic groups in 6,984 NHANES III participants. [tested: Bowerman 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383197/]
- The race-neutral GLI-Global equations fitted about as well as the older 'other' equations, with wider limits of normal. [tested: Bowerman 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383197/]
- In 6,107 spirometry tests, switching from race-specific to race-neutral equations reclassified 9% of FEV1 and 10% of FVC results. [tested: Cai 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42741266/]
- Black patients moved to abnormal FEV1 under the race-neutral approach had more medicines, emergency visits and hospital stays than those whose results stayed normal. [tested: Cai 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42741266/]

What it does not change:
- Spirometry stays a useful test for asthma, COPD and pulmonary fibrosis. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Spirometry test", https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/spirometry/]
- The ATS statement cautions that the effects and possible harms of the change are uncertain, and asks for research into the effects. [clinical guidance: ATS official statement, "Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation" (Bhakta et al. 2023, abstract), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36973004/]
- Any equation has limits, so your symptoms and medical history need to be weighed with the number. [tested: Bowerman 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383197/]

See someone when:
- A cough, wheeze or breathlessness that lasts or limits what you do, whatever a breathing test said (doctor).
- You were told your lung function is normal but you are still short of breath: ask which equation was used and whether other tests are needed (doctor or lung specialist).
- A lung function result is being used for a job, insurance or compensation decision: ask whether a race-based equation was used (the ATS statement names these uses).
- A child or teenager with repeated chest symptoms (doctor or paediatrician).

## Lupus: symptoms, risk and getting diagnosed early
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/lupus-in-black-women/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Lupus is a long-term autoimmune condition that causes joint pain, rashes and deep tiredness. It is more common in women of African and Caribbean background and can affect the kidneys, so finding it early matters. See a GP if symptoms keep coming back. Sun protection and regular check-ups help once diagnosed.

Do:
- See a doctor if you often get lupus symptoms: joint and muscle pain, tiredness rest does not fix, or a rash after sun. It is better managed when found and treated early. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Use high-factor sunscreen (at least factor 50) and a hat in the sun. In the UK it can be prescribed if you have lupus. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Go to the regular checks after diagnosis, including blood tests for anaemia and urine tests for kidney problems. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Pace yourself, stay active on better days, and ask family, friends and work for help. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- See a doctor before trying for a pregnancy, so medicines can be checked. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]

Avoid:
- Smoking: it makes lupus worse. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Long spells in direct sun or in rooms with fluorescent lights. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Waiting for one classic rash: lupus has many possible symptoms and is not always easy to diagnose because they resemble other conditions. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lupus", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/]
- Assuming it is unlikely in you: in one Manhattan registry prevalence in Black women was 210.9 per 100,000 against 64.3 in white women. [tested: Izmirly 2017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28891252/]

See someone when:
- Joint pain, a sun-triggered rash or tiredness that keeps returning for weeks (doctor; ask about lupus tests).
- Swollen ankles or face, foamy or dark urine, or new high blood pressure with any lupus symptoms (doctor the same day; kidneys can be affected).
- Chest pain, sudden breathlessness or a severe headache with fever (emergency services; NHS in the UK lists chest or tummy pain among lupus symptoms).
- Low mood or anxiety with lupus (doctor; NHS in the UK lists depression and anxiety among symptoms).

## Magnesium supplements for sleep and cramps
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/magnesium-supplements-for-sleep-and-cramps/
Module: Body
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Magnesium tablets did not clearly prevent leg cramps in older adults, and for sleep three small, low-quality trials in older adults hint at falling asleep a little faster. Our search found no supplement trial in Black participants. Up to four hundred milligrams a day from supplements is unlikely to harm; more can cause diarrhoea.

Do:
- Get magnesium from food first: the UK's NHS says a varied, balanced diet should give you all you need. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamins and minerals: Others" (magnesium), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/others/]
- If you try a supplement, keep it to 400 mg a day or less: the UK's NHS says that is unlikely to cause harm. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamins and minerals: Others" (magnesium), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/others/]

Avoid:
- More than 400 mg a day from supplements: the UK's NHS says high doses can cause diarrhoea, and long-term effects are not known. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamins and minerals: Others" (magnesium), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/others/]
- Relying on magnesium tablets to stop night leg cramps: in older adults the Cochrane review found no clear effect. [tested: Garrison 2020, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32956536/]

See someone when:
- Cramps that are frequent, severe, or come with weakness or swelling (doctor).
- Trouble sleeping most nights for more than a few weeks (doctor; see sleep and sleep apnoea).
- You have kidney disease or take regular medicines and want to start a magnesium supplement (pharmacist).

## PCOS, endometriosis and heavy periods
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/pcos-endometriosis-and-heavy-periods/
Module: Body
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Heavy or painful periods are not something you have to accept. Fibroids are clearly more common in Black women. Endometriosis was the same or lower in US studies, though the data are unclear, and PCOS (now PMOS on the NHS) looked milder in one US trial cohort. See a GP with notes of your symptoms.

Do:
- See a doctor if heavy periods affect your life, you have bleeding between periods or after sex, or severe period pain. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]
- Describe how heavy: changing a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, periods over 7 days, clots larger than a 10p coin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]
- Expect endometriosis to take time to diagnose: symptoms overlap with fibroids, IBS and other conditions. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Endometriosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/]
- Ask about hormone and insulin resistance blood tests, and a scan if over 18, if you have irregular periods, excess hair growth or thick dark skin patches. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS)" (formerly PCOS), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polycystic-ovary-syndrome-pcos/]
- Ask for a blood test for iron deficiency anaemia if bleeding is heavy. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]

Avoid:
- Ruling out endometriosis because it is said to be rarer: data on it are less clear and Black women had worse outcomes. [tested: Katon 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682686/]
- Assuming heavy periods are always normal: they can be a sign of fibroids, endometriosis, PMOS or, rarely, womb cancer. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Heavy periods", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heavy-periods/]

See someone when:
- Heavy periods or severe period pain that stop you doing normal things (doctor).
- Bleeding between periods or after sex (doctor).
- Irregular or missing periods with hair growth, acne or thick dark patches of skin on the neck or armpits (doctor).
- Pain when peeing, pooing or having sex with heavy periods (doctor).

## Pregnancy risk and safe maternity care for Black women
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/pregnancy-and-maternity-care/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In England, Black women are nearly three times as likely to die during pregnancy or within six weeks of it as White women, in the latest national report. A confidential enquiry found bias in the care some received. Go to every antenatal check, learn the warning signs, and call your maternity unit straight away if one appears.

Do:
- Go to your routine antenatal appointments: blood pressure and pee checks are how pre-eclampsia is picked up. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Pre-eclampsia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pre-eclampsia/]
- Know the warning signs: a severe headache that does not go, vision problems, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of face, hands or feet. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Pre-eclampsia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pre-eclampsia/]
- Call your maternity unit if you have the number, or 111 (UK), if you have symptoms in pregnancy or in the weeks after birth. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Pre-eclampsia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pre-eclampsia/]
- Take up the blood test for sickle cell offered by your midwife before 10 weeks. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]

Avoid:
- Waiting to see if a severe headache or vision change settles: the UK's NHS says any of these need checking immediately. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Pre-eclampsia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pre-eclampsia/]
- Assuming it is over after birth: pre-eclampsia can develop in the days or weeks after your baby is born. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Pre-eclampsia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pre-eclampsia/]

See someone when:
- Severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain below the ribs, or sudden swelling in pregnancy or soon after birth (call your maternity unit or 111 in the UK straight away).
- You were not listened to and a symptom is getting worse (ask for the duty midwife or another doctor, or call 111 in the UK).
- Low mood, anxiety or thoughts of harm in pregnancy or the year after (doctor, midwife or NHS 111 in the UK mental health option; 999, or your local emergency number if in danger).

In other countries:
- In the US, the Office on Women's Health says women with high blood pressure have a higher risk of preeclampsia. (https://www.womenshealth.gov/pregnancy/youre-pregnant-now-what/pregnancy-complications)
- WHO lists high blood pressure during pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia) among the main causes of maternal death. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/maternal-mortality)

## Prostate cancer risk and PSA testing
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/prostate-cancer-and-psa-testing/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In England, about one in four Black men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, against about one in eight White men. There is no routine NHS PSA screening for Black men: the UK National Screening Committee advised against it in 2026. You can still ask your GP about a PSA test and weigh the risks and benefits.

Do:
- Ask a doctor about PSA testing if you are worried; the UK's NHS says men can ask and the doctor will discuss risks and benefits. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]
- Go to a doctor if you pee more often, urgently or at night, have blood in your pee, or erection problems. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]
- Know that a high PSA does not mean cancer: an enlarged prostate can cause it. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]
- For 48 hours before a PSA test, avoid ejaculating, exercise that leaves you out of breath, and cycling. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]

Avoid:
- Treating a PSA result as a diagnosis: the test can be inaccurate and lead to tests or treatment you do not need. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]
- Having a PSA test within 4 to 6 weeks after a urine infection has cleared. [clinical guidance: NHS, "PSA test", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prostate-cancer/psa-testing/]

See someone when:
- Peeing more than usual, a sudden urge to pee, or getting up often at night (doctor).
- Blood in your pee (doctor, soon).
- A raised PSA result: expect a repeat test and possibly referral for a biopsy or MRI (doctor, urologist).

In other countries:
- In Kenya, the Ministry of Health 2025 protocol screens men aged 40 or over of African descent with a PSA test, repeated after 2 years if normal. (https://health.go.ke/sites/default/files/2025-07/FINAL_NCD%20protocols.pdf)
- In South Africa, the 2026 Adult Primary Care guide lists African descent as a prostate cancer risk factor and says screening is not routinely done. (https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2026-10/APC%202026%20E-book.pdf)
- In the US, the USPSTF says men aged 55 to 69 should make an individual decision about PSA screening after discussing benefits and harms. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/prostate-cancer-screening)

## Pulse oximeters and dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/pulse-oximeters-and-dark-skin/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Pulse oximeters shine light through the skin, and melanin changes how that light behaves. In a large US hospital study, readings that looked safe hid low blood oxygen more often in Black patients. A UK review says the devices are valuable and should not be dropped, but need to be tested on darker skin tones.

What it is:
- A device that estimates oxygen in the blood by sending light through the skin; the light reacts differently with different levels of melanin. [clinical guidance: GOV.UK, "Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report" (March 2024), https://gov.uk/government/publications/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-final-report/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-summary-report]
- Devices were commonly tested on people with light skin, so those readings were taken as the norm. [clinical guidance: GOV.UK, "Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report" (March 2024), https://gov.uk/government/publications/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-final-report/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-summary-report]

How to find out if you have it:
- You cannot check it at home: the study compared finger readings with arterial blood gas tests taken within 10 minutes in hospital. [tested: Valbuena 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35793817/]

What it changes:
- Among readings of 92% or more, about 1 in 5 hid dangerously low blood oxygen in Black patients (19.6%), against about 1 in 6 in White patients (15.6%). [tested: Valbuena 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35793817/]
- An inaccurate reading could delay finding dangerously low oxygen levels and so referral for more intensive care. [clinical guidance: GOV.UK, "Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report" (March 2024), https://gov.uk/government/publications/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-final-report/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-summary-report]

What it does not change:
- The review says pulse oximeters are valuable and does not advise curtailing their use in patients with darker skin tones. [clinical guidance: GOV.UK, "Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report" (March 2024), https://gov.uk/government/publications/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-final-report/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-summary-report]
- The evidence of harm to care is so far only from the US healthcare system. [clinical guidance: GOV.UK, "Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report" (March 2024), https://gov.uk/government/publications/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-final-report/equity-in-medical-devices-independent-review-summary-report]

See someone when:
- You are breathless at rest, your chest is tight, or you feel very unwell, whatever the reading says (NHS 111 in the UK, or 999, or your local emergency number if severe).
- Your lips, tongue or skin turn blue, grey or pale; on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms or soles (999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).
- A clinician is relying on an oximeter reading and you feel worse than it suggests: say so and ask what else they can check.

## Sarcoidosis: symptoms, risk and follow-up
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/sarcoidosis-in-black-adults/
Module: Body
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Sarcoidosis is a rare condition where small patches of swollen tissue form, most often in the lungs, skin and lymph nodes. In studies it is more common, and in some studies more severe, in Black adults. Many cases settle without treatment, but a lasting cough, breathlessness or sore red eyes need a doctor.

Do:
- See a doctor about a persistent dry cough, breathlessness, tender bumps on the skin or red, sore eyes. Symptoms depend on which organs are affected. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]
- Keep monitoring appointments: X-rays, breathing tests and blood tests show whether it is settling or getting worse. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]
- If treatment is recommended, expect steroid tablets first and ask about side effects such as weight gain, mood changes and bone thinning. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]
- If other organs may be involved, ask about scans or examinations of the skin, heart and eyes. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]

Avoid:
- Taking calcium or vitamin D supplements on your own: take them only if a doctor advises, because sarcoidosis can raise the risk of kidney stones. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]
- Assuming it is only a lung problem: it can also affect skin, glands, joints, eyes and the heart. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]
- Waiting years with symptoms because many cases clear on their own: a few people become severely affected, so follow-up matters. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sarcoidosis", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/]

See someone when:
- A dry cough or breathlessness lasting more than a few weeks (doctor; ask whether a chest X-ray is needed).
- A red, painful eye or a change in vision (same-day eye care or urgent doctor).
- Palpitations, an irregular heartbeat or fainting (urgent medical care; NHS in the UK lists abnormal heart rhythm as a possible sarcoidosis symptom).
- Kidney-stone pain or tender lumps on the legs and arms with feeling unwell (doctor).

## Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/sauna-and-heat-bathing/
Module: Body
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Frequent sauna use went with fewer heart deaths in Finnish men, a link that falls short of proof, and Black participants were tested only in one tiny heat study. Keep sessions to fifteen or twenty minutes, skip alcohol, watch for dehydration, and ask a doctor first if you have heart or blood pressure problems or sickle cell trait.

Do:
- Keep sessions to about 15 to 20 minutes, starting with about five if you are new to it. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Sauna Benefits", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sauna-benefits]
- Watch for dehydration, and leave if you feel faint or confused: the weight lost is water. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Sauna Benefits", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sauna-benefits]

Avoid:
- Sauna after alcohol. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Sauna Benefits", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sauna-benefits]
- Sauna if you have heart disease, heart failure, severe aortic stenosis or high or low blood pressure, unless your doctor agrees. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Sauna Benefits", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sauna-benefits]
- Sauna if you are trying to get pregnant. [clinical guidance: Cleveland Clinic, "Sauna Benefits", https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sauna-benefits]
- Staying in heat until you feel unwell if you have sickle cell trait: one sauna visit triggered severe muscle breakdown and kidney failure in one reported case. [tested: Eisenbach 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15786826/]

See someone when:
- Chest pain, palpitations, fainting or severe breathlessness in the heat (urgent care).
- Severe muscle pain, weakness or very dark urine after a sauna or hard exercise (urgent care).
- You have heart or blood pressure problems, sickle cell trait or disease, or are pregnant and want to use a sauna (doctor or haematology team).

## Sickle cell disease, trait and pregnancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/sickle-cell-disease-trait-and-pregnancy/
Module: Body
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Sickle cell disease is a lifelong inherited blood condition; trait means you carry one copy of the gene and do not have the disease and cannot develop it. If both parents carry it, a child can have the disease. In pregnancy, carriers had low risks in a review, but more anaemia and bacteria in the urine, so ask about checks.

Do:
- Drink plenty of fluids and avoid sudden temperature changes, including very cold water, to help prevent a crisis. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Try gentle to moderate exercise such as walking or yoga; the UK's NHS says avoid high-intensity exercise for disease. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Keep up to date with vaccinations and go to your regular check-ups. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- If pregnant, take the blood test your midwife offers before 10 weeks; anyone can ask a doctor for a carrier test at any time. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- If you carry the trait and are pregnant, tell your midwife and ask about checks for anaemia and urine infection. [tested: Jans 2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20946275/]

Avoid:
- Alcohol and smoking: the UK's NHS says they can raise the risk of acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Driving yourself to A&E (UK) in a crisis: call your local emergency number (999 in the UK, 911 in the US and Canada, 112 in the EU) for severe pain, breathing difficulty or a high temperature. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]

See someone when:
- Severe sudden pain, breathing difficulty or being sick with sickle cell disease (call 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).
- A high temperature, or a painful erection that will not go away, with sickle cell disease (call 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).
- You are not sure whether you carry the gene and are planning a pregnancy (doctor, for a blood test).
- You carry the trait and have heavy exertion, heat or altitude planned (see the trait and hard exercise entry).

In other countries:
- In Ghana, the Ghana Health Service said in June 2025 it is pursuing newborn screening initiatives for sickle cell disease. (https://ghs.gov.gh/news-and-events/ghana-health-service-marks-world-sickle-cell-day-with-hope-and-action)
- In Kenya, a Ministry of Health policy (June 2023) sets out how to carry out universal infant screening for sickle cell disease. (https://www.health.go.ke/sites/default/files/2023-06/Policy%20guidelines%20on%20infant%20screening%20of%20Sickle%20Cell%20Disease.pdf)
- WHO says early diagnosis, for example through newborn screening, is essential for managing sickle-cell disease. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sickle-cell-disease)

## Sickle cell trait and hard exercise
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/sickle-cell-trait-and-hard-exercise/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Sickle cell trait is one copy of the sickle gene, not sickle cell disease. It raises the risk of serious muscle breakdown in very hard exercise. A soldiers' study found no clear difference in deaths (a wide margin of error); a US college football study found far more exertional deaths. Know your status and train with care.

What it is:
- You carry one copy of the sickle gene: you do not have sickle cell disease and cannot develop it, but you can pass the gene on. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease" (carrier section), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Largely a benign carrier state, and a risk factor for a few outcomes. [tested: Naik 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30383109/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A blood test shows it: ask your doctor. Pregnant people are usually offered screening by a midwife. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease" (carrier section), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Some sports bodies test at the pre-participation exam. [clinical guidance: NCAA, "Sickle cell trait" (athlete precautions), http://www.ncaa.org/what-we-do/health-safety-and-performance/sickle-cell-trait]

What it changes:
- Raises the risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis, muscle breakdown in very hard exercise, by about half in the largest cohort. [tested: Nelson 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27518662/]
- Build training up slowly, set your own pace, and rest between hard efforts. [clinical guidance: NCAA, "Sickle cell trait" (athlete precautions), http://www.ncaa.org/what-we-do/health-safety-and-performance/sickle-cell-trait]
- Drink plenty, especially in heat and humidity; take extra care when changing altitude. [clinical guidance: NCAA, "Sickle cell trait" (athlete precautions), http://www.ncaa.org/what-we-do/health-safety-and-performance/sickle-cell-trait]
- Stop at once with muscle pain, unusual weakness, exhaustion or breathlessness, and tell your coach. [clinical guidance: NCAA, "Sickle cell trait" (athlete precautions), http://www.ncaa.org/what-we-do/health-safety-and-performance/sickle-cell-trait]
- NCAA data, 2004-2008: exertional death in Division I football players with the trait was 1 in 827, 37 times higher than in players without it. [tested: Harmon 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22442191/]

What it does not change:
- It is not sickle cell disease. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease" (carrier section), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/]
- Among soldiers training under precautions, no clear difference in death risk (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.13, a wide interval that cannot rule out a higher or lower risk). [tested: Nelson 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27518662/]

See someone when:
- You collapse, have severe muscle pain or weakness, or dark urine after exercise (urgent care today).
- You have the trait and heavy exertion, heat or high altitude is planned (haematologist or sports doctor beforehand).
- You are unsure of your status (doctor: a blood test answers it).
- Persistent protein in urine or kidney concerns (doctor).

## Starting training, rest days and recovery
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/starting-training-rest-days-and-recovery/
Module: Body
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Nothing I found says Black adults need a different programme or rest days, so the NHS targets apply: strength work on two days, plus moderate or vigorous activity most days. One US survey found creatine kinase, a muscle blood marker, runs higher in Black adults, so a high result may be normal.

Do:
- Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week or 75 minutes of vigorous, spread over 4 to 5 days or every day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- Do strengthening work for all the major muscle groups on at least 2 days a week. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- Speak to your doctor first if you have not exercised for some time or have a medical condition, and match intensity to your fitness. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- Use a beginner plan such as the UK's NHS Couch to 5K, a 9-week running programme. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- If a blood test shows a high creatine kinase, ask whether it is high for a Black adult, not only for the standard range. [tested: George 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27537560/]

Avoid:
- Jumping straight to hard training after a long break: the UK's NHS says to make intensity appropriate to your fitness. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- Long unbroken spells of sitting or lying down: break them up with some activity. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]

See someone when:
- Severe muscle pain, weakness or dark urine after hard exercise (urgent care today).
- Chest pain, pressure or being very short of breath during exercise (999 in the UK, or your local emergency number if it does not settle).
- You know you carry sickle cell trait and plan very hard training, heat or altitude (see the trait entry; doctor or sports doctor).

## Stroke: signs to act on and what raises the risk
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/stroke-signs-and-risk/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A stroke is an emergency: a drooping face, a weak arm, slurred speech, then call emergency services at once, even if it passes. Black adults have strokes more often and younger in the studies we found, and high blood pressure is the biggest risk. Having your blood pressure checked and treated is the most useful step.

Do:
- Learn FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech problems, Time to call the emergency number. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of a stroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/symptoms/]
- Call straight away even if the signs stop: symptoms can pass after a short time, and a mini-stroke still needs urgent care. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of a stroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/symptoms/]
- Get your blood pressure checked, and treat high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol and an irregular heartbeat, all of which raise stroke risk. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Causes of a stroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/causes/]
- Quit smoking, eat a balanced diet, be active and cut down on alcohol; take medicines for underlying conditions every day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Causes of a stroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/causes/]
- Do not wait for symptoms to check your risk: in one South London register, 12% of strokes in Black African participants, at a median age of 59, came with no earlier risk factor diagnosis. [tested: Emmett 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42472283/]

Avoid:
- Waiting to see if the signs pass, or driving yourself to hospital: the emergency call handler gives advice on what to do. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of a stroke", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/symptoms/]
- Adding salt at the table: in a West African study it was linked to about double the odds of stroke. [tested: Owolabi 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29496511/]
- Smoking: in the same study current smokers had over four times the odds of stroke. [tested: Owolabi 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29496511/]
- Leaving a diagnosed risk factor untreated: in South London 36% of strokes happened in people with diagnosed but untreated risk factors. [tested: Emmett 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42472283/]

See someone when:
- Any sign of a stroke, even one that passes: call your emergency number now. UK 999, US and Canada 911, Australia 000; elsewhere your local emergency number.
- Sudden weakness or numbness down one side, blurred vision or loss of sight, trouble finding words, confusion, dizziness, or a sudden severe headache (emergency number).
- High blood pressure readings, diabetes or an irregular heartbeat with no regular review in the last year (doctor or local clinic).
- A child with sickle cell disease who has any stroke sign (emergency number; sickle cell stroke risk is not covered in this card).

## Type 2 diabetes risk and blood sugar
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/type-2-diabetes-risk/
Module: Body
Tier: B moderate (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In south London, people with Black African or Black Caribbean backgrounds had two to three times the risk of type 2 diabetes of White British people, and the gap was only partly explained by weight, blood pressure or deprivation. The NHS says check your risk from 25. Weight, activity and blood tests are where you act.

Do:
- Check your risk from age 25 if you are Black African or Black Caribbean, rather than waiting until 40. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how it's diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-2-diabetes/symptoms/]
- Use the Diabetes UK Know Your Risk tool, and ask for a free NHS Health Check once you are 40 to 74. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how it's diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-2-diabetes/symptoms/]
- Know that health risks from weight start at a lower BMI for you: the UK's NHS calls 23 to 27.4 overweight and 27.5 or more obese. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Build up to at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, spread over 4 to 5 days. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/]
- If you are overweight, aim to lose weight steadily, about half to one kilogram a week. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]

Avoid:
- Waiting for symptoms: not everyone with type 2 diabetes has any. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how it's diagnosed", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-2-diabetes/symptoms/]
- Using bitter gourd (cerasee) tea or tablets in place of diabetes treatment: the Cochrane review found insufficient evidence. [tested: Ooi 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22895968/]

See someone when:
- You are very tired, very thirsty, peeing more than usual or losing weight without trying (doctor, for a blood glucose test).
- You are 25 or over, from a Black African or Black Caribbean background, and have never been checked (GP or pharmacy).
- A parent, brother or sister has diabetes and you have not been tested (doctor).

In other countries:
- In Jamaica, the Ministry of Health 2020 guideline says average-risk adults should start diabetes screening at 45; higher-risk adults from 30. (https://www.moh.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/National-Screening-Guidelines-for-Priority-Non-Communicable-Diseases-NCDs-in-Primary-Health-Care.pdf)
- In Kenya, the Ministry of Health 2025 protocol says testing should be considered for adults who are overweight or obese and have a risk factor. (https://health.go.ke/sites/default/files/2025-07/FINAL_NCD%20protocols.pdf)
- In the US, the USPSTF recommends diabetes screening for adults aged 35 to 70 who have overweight or obesity. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/screening-for-prediabetes-and-type-2-diabetes)

## Vitamin D and dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/vitamin-d-and-dark-skin/
Module: Body
Tier: A moderate (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Total vitamin D in the blood is lower in Black Americans, but so is the protein that carries it, and one study found the usable amount similar. Two trials in older Black American women found supplements did not slow bone loss. UK advice still says dark-skinned people should consider a daily supplement. They disagree.

What it is:
- The blood measure is 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Total levels were lower in Black than White adults in Baltimore, as was the vitamin D-binding protein. [tested: Powe 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24256378/]
- Skin makes vitamin D from sunlight; the NHS says dark skin may not make enough in the UK. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]

How to find out if you have it:
- A blood test measures it: ask your doctor if you are concerned. The UK's NHS lists no routine symptom check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- Interpret a total result with care: binding protein differed too. [tested: Powe 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24256378/]

What it changes:
- The NHS advises people of African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds to consider a 10 microgram supplement all year. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- In 260 older Black American women, supplements did not slow bone loss. [tested: Aloia 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29905969/]
- A 208-woman trial also found no bone-density benefit. [tested: Aloia 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043680/]

What it does not change:
- A low total result does not on its own show too little usable vitamin D. [tested: Powe 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24256378/]
- It does not make a high dose safe: the UK's NHS says not to exceed 100 micrograms a day. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take other medicines or calcium: supplements are not tested with other medicines. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Taking bendroflumethiazide with other medicines and herbal remedies" (the herbal-remedy wording applies generally), https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/bendroflumethiazide/taking-bendroflumethiazide-with-other-medicines-and-herbal-remedies]

See someone when:
- You have a long-term condition or take regular medicines and are unsure whether to supplement (pharmacist or doctor).
- A very low result on a blood test (doctor: follow the lab's and doctor's advice).
- A child or pregnant woman and you are unsure what to take (doctor, midwife, health visitor in the UK).

In other countries:
- In the US, the USPSTF found evidence insufficient to judge screening for vitamin D deficiency in adults without symptoms. (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/vitamin-d-deficiency-screening)

## Weight, BMI and losing weight safely
URL: https://vilivity.com/body/weight-bmi-and-ethnicity/
Module: Body
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: The NHS says people from Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds are at risk of health problems at a slightly lower BMI: 23 to 27.4 is overweight and 27.5 or more is obese. Lose weight steadily, about half to one kilogram a week, with a balanced diet and activity. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat.

Do:
- Check your BMI against the lower cut-offs: 23 to 27.4 overweight, 27.5 or more obese for Black African or African-Caribbean adults. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables and fewer high-fat or sugary foods. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Aim to lose weight steadily, about 0.5 to 1 kg a week. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Get active for 45 to 60 minutes a day if you are aiming to lose weight; shorter sessions count. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Cut down on alcohol, which is high in calories. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]

Avoid:
- Fast weight loss: the UK's NHS advice is to lose weight steadily. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]
- Relying on BMI alone if you carry a lot of muscle: it may put you in the overweight or obese category without much body fat. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]

See someone when:
- Your BMI is in the obese range for your background, or you have high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes with extra weight (doctor, for a weight-management plan).
- You have gained weight quickly without a clear reason (doctor).

In other countries:
- In the US, NIDDK defines overweight as a BMI of 25 to 29.9 and obesity as 30 or above for adults. (https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/adult-overweight-obesity/definition-facts)
- WHO defines adult overweight as a BMI of 25 or more and obesity as 30 or more. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/obesity-and-overweight)

## Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/apple-cider-vinegar/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Apple cider vinegar may lower blood sugar and weight slightly in short trials, but the trials are small and varied, and one well-known weight trial was retracted. Our search found no trial of apple cider vinegar in Black participants. Dilute it or use it in food, and avoid the tablets: one injured a throat.

Do:
- If you use it, put it in food or dilute it in water: drinking it undiluted can erode tooth enamel over time. [clinical guidance: Harvard Health, "Can apple cider vinegar curb appetite?", https://www.health.harvard.edu/staying-healthy/can-apple-cider-vinegar-curb-appetite]
- Treat a lower blood sugar claim as a small, short-term effect seen in trials, and keep taking any diabetes medicine as prescribed. [tested: Hadi 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34187442/]

Avoid:
- Apple cider vinegar tablets: oesophageal injury was reported, and tablet products varied widely in what they contained. [tested: Hill 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15983536/]
- Drinking it at bedtime: Harvard Health notes its acidity makes that a poor time. [clinical guidance: Harvard Health, "Can apple cider vinegar curb appetite?", https://www.health.harvard.edu/staying-healthy/can-apple-cider-vinegar-curb-appetite]
- Expecting weight loss: Harvard Health says the scientific evidence does not support drinking it to curb appetite or lose weight. [clinical guidance: Harvard Health, "Can apple cider vinegar curb appetite?", https://www.health.harvard.edu/staying-healthy/can-apple-cider-vinegar-curb-appetite]

See someone when:
- Pain on swallowing, or a feeling that something is stuck in your throat (doctor or urgent care).
- You have diabetes and are thinking of using it alongside your medicine (diabetes nurse or pharmacist).
- Tooth sensitivity or enamel wear (dentist).

## Baobab fruit: blood sugar, iron and vitamin C
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/baobab-fruit/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Baobab fruit is a traditional African food and a source of vitamin C. Two small trials in healthy adults in Europe found it lowered the blood sugar rise after a sugary or starchy load. A trial in Kenyan schoolchildren found no significant effect on iron or haemoglobin. My search found no trial in people with diabetes.

Do:
- Eat it as a food; do not rely on it for blood sugar or iron: the evidence is small and short. [tested: Evang 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33355689/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Using baobab instead of iron tablets or other treatment for anaemia: the Kenyan trial found no significant effect. [tested: Evang 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33355689/]
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- You are often tired, pale or short of breath and think it could be iron (doctor, for a blood test).
- You take diabetes medicine and want to add baobab (pharmacist or doctor).

## Black seed oil (Nigella sativa)
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/black-seed-oil-nigella-sativa/
Module: Food
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: A 2025 review of 82 studies of black seed (Nigella sativa) found small improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body fat, and called it a promising add-on. The trials were not in Black people, and I did not read how sure the authors were. It is not a cure, and not a replacement for medicine.

Do:
- Check with a pharmacist before taking black seed products if you take other medicines, including blood pressure and diabetes medicines. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Treat it as an add-on to treatment, not a substitute: the authors describe it only as a promising adjunct. [tested: Jafari 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40714301/]

Avoid:
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Stopping or skipping prescribed medicine for black seed oil. [tested: Jafari 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40714301/]

See someone when:
- You take blood pressure or diabetes medicine and want to add black seed (pharmacist or doctor).
- You have a high blood pressure reading or high blood sugar symptoms (doctor).
- A reaction such as rash, swelling or tummy pain after taking it (doctor; 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number for swelling of the face or throat or breathing difficulty).

## Bovine colostrum supplements for immunity and gut health
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/bovine-colostrum-supplements/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Bovine colostrum, the first milk from cows, has small, mixed trials in athletes and a few other groups, with little effect on immune markers. Our search found no trial of colostrum in Black participants. It is a cow's milk product, so check first if dairy upsets you, and do not use it to treat an infection.

Do:
- Check first if dairy upsets you: bovine colostrum comes from cow's milk, and lactose is found in milk from cows, goats and sheep. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Lactose intolerance", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lactose-intolerance/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any supplement you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Relying on it to stop colds or infections: in athletes it made little difference to immune markers or illness. [tested: Mizelman 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40640599/]
- Giving it to children for illness without advice: the evidence in children was conflicting. [tested: Guberti 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34202206/]

See someone when:
- A rash, swelling or breathing difficulty after taking it (urgent care).
- Tummy pain, bloating or diarrhoea that follows each dose (pharmacist or doctor; see lactose intolerance).
- An infection that is not clearing (doctor). A supplement does not replace treatment.

## Bush teas and herbal remedies (cerasee, bitter leaf) with medicines
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/bush-teas-cerasee-bitter-leaf-and-medicines/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Natural does not mean safe with medicine. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that bitter melon (cerasee) helps type 2 diabetes. Memorial Sloan Kettering warns it can add to diabetes medicines and reports case reports of serious harm. The UK's NHS says do not mix herbal medicines with certain medicines, and always check with a pharmacist.

Do:
- Check first with a pharmacist before taking a herbal medicine if you already take other medicine, including over-the-counter medicine. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about every tea or remedy you use. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Talk to your provider if you use bitter melon and take insulin or diabetes medicines: it may have additive effects. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Bitter Melon" (About Herbs, updated 23 May 2025), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/bitter-melon]
- Read the leaflet in your medicine packet for herbal warnings. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Using cerasee in place of diabetes treatment: the Cochrane review found insufficient evidence. [tested: Ooi 2012, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22895968/]
- Bitter melon if you are pregnant: animal studies suggest it may cause birth defects. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Bitter Melon" (About Herbs, updated 23 May 2025), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/bitter-melon]
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have kidney or liver problems, or take statins, antidepressants, diabetes, blood pressure or blood-thinning medicines, or the combined pill, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- You use bush tea and have diabetes, high blood pressure or take blood thinners (pharmacist or doctor).
- Irregular heartbeat, severe tummy pain or vomiting after a herbal drink (urgent care or 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or tummy swelling after months of a herbal tea (doctor urgently).

## Caribbean and West African diets and health
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/caribbean-and-west-african-diet-and-health/
Module: Food
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No trial has tested a traditional Caribbean or West African diet for blood pressure or diabetes, so nobody can say whether it is better or worse. What is tested is the pattern: more fruit and vegetables, less salt and saturated fat lowered blood pressure in a mostly Black US trial. Judge your own plate on that pattern.

Do:
- Aim for the tested pattern: plenty of fruit and vegetables and low-fat dairy, with less salt, as in the DASH trial. [tested: Hussain 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42429484/]
- Base meals on starchy foods, and eat plenty of fruit and veg, some protein and fish, with less saturated fat and sugar. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]
- Keep salt to no more than 6g a day, remembering salt in stock, sauces, bread and processed foods. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]
- Weigh yourself against the lower BMI cut-offs the NHS uses for Black African and African-Caribbean adults. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Overweight and obesity in adults", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/]

Avoid:
- Judging a dish as good or bad by where it comes from: the UK's NHS advice is about amounts of salt, saturated fat and sugar. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]

See someone when:
- You have high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes or kidney disease and want to change your diet a lot (doctor, or a dietitian by referral).
- You have lost weight without trying, or have bloating or diarrhoea for weeks (doctor).

## Cod liver oil: vitamin D, vitamin A and colds
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/cod-liver-oil/
Module: Food
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Cod liver oil is a source of vitamin D, which the UK's NHS says people with dark skin should consider taking all year. A large trial in Norwegian adults found it did not prevent covid or other chest infections. It is also high in vitamin A, so too much, or liver products in pregnancy, can do harm.

Do:
- Consider a daily 10 micrograms vitamin D supplement all year if you have dark skin. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D" (vitamins and minerals), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- Keep vitamin A from food and supplements, fish liver oil included, to 1.5mg a day or less. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin A" (vitamins and minerals; page reviewed 3 August 2020), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-a/]
- If you eat liver once a week, take no supplements containing vitamin A, fish liver oil included. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin A" (vitamins and minerals; page reviewed 3 August 2020), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-a/]

Avoid:
- Relying on cod liver oil to prevent colds or chest infections: a large trial found no effect. [tested: Brunvoll 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36215222/]
- Liver and liver products if you are pregnant: they are high in vitamin A, which can harm the baby. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Foods to avoid in pregnancy", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/foods-to-avoid/]
- More than 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) of vitamin D a day as an adult: it could be harmful. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D" (vitamins and minerals), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]

See someone when:
- You are pregnant or planning to be and take fish liver oil (midwife or doctor).
- You give a child cod liver oil every day and are not sure of the amount (pharmacist or health visitor in the UK).
- You get repeated chest infections, whatever you take (doctor).

## Does diet cause acne? Sugar, dairy and foods linked to spots
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/diet-and-acne-on-dark-skin/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No diet is proven to treat acne, and the British Association of Dermatologists says a healthy, balanced diet is all it advises. Some studies link sugary, refined foods and dairy to more spots. A 12-week trial in 43 Australian men found a low-glycaemic diet reduced spots. In Nigerian teenagers, milk, fried beef and cake were linked to more acne.

Do:
- Eat a healthy, well-balanced diet: there is not enough evidence to support specific diets for acne. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Acne", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/acne/]
- Check hair and skin products first: the UK's NHS says products that make skin greasy can cause acne. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Acne: causes", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acne/causes/]
- If you try cutting back on sugary, refined foods, give it about 12 weeks: that was the length of the one trial. [tested: Smith 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17616769/]

Avoid:
- Strict or cut-everything diets for acne: the BAD says there is not enough evidence for specific diets. [clinical guidance: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Acne", https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/condition/acne/]
- Assuming milk causes your acne: the dairy evidence is observational and mixed. [tested: Meixiong 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35373155/]

See someone when:
- Spots are deep, painful, many, or leaving scars or dark marks (doctor, then dermatologist).
- Acne is affecting your mood or confidence (doctor).
- You are thinking of cutting out whole food groups because of acne (doctor or dietitian).

## Fasting in Ramadan with diabetes or sickle cell
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/ramadan-and-religious-fasting-with-diabetes-or-sickle-cell/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: With diabetes, fasting in Ramadan can cause low blood sugar and dehydration, and the evidence on sickle cell disease is small and mixed. None of the studies was of Black Muslims as a group. Diabetes UK says do not fast if your diabetes is poorly controlled. Agree a plan with your diabetes or sickle cell team before Ramadan.

Do:
- Talk to your diabetes team before Ramadan about your medicines and a plan: they may change the type, dose or timing. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]
- Test your blood sugar more often during the fast, and break the fast if it falls below 4 mmol/l. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]
- Carry hypo treatment and water with you. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]
- If you have sickle cell disease, drink plenty of fluids when you can: not drinking enough is a listed trigger for a crisis. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Sickle cell disease: living with", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/living-with/]
- Speak to an Imam about alternatives to fasting if you are advised not to fast for health reasons. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]

Avoid:
- Fasting if your diabetes was not well controlled before Ramadan: Diabetes UK says it would not be a safe option. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]
- Pre-mixed insulin during fasting: it is not recommended. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]
- Changing your diabetes medicines yourself, or fasting when you cannot reach your doctor or diabetes team. [clinical guidance: Diabetes UK, "Ramadan and diabetes", https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/ramadan]

See someone when:
- Before Ramadan, if you take insulin or tablets for diabetes (doctor or diabetes team, with time to adjust).
- Before Ramadan, if you have sickle cell disease, or sickle cell trait and are not sure how to fast safely (haematology team or doctor).
- During the fast: blood sugar below 4 mmol/l, or above your team's limit (break the fast, then get advice).
- Severe pain, trouble breathing, being sick, or a high temperature with sickle cell disease (999 in the UK, or your local emergency number).

## Fibroids, food and supplements
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/fibroids-and-diet/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: No food has been shown to shrink fibroids. In Black women, a high glycaemic index diet was only weakly linked to fibroid risk. Five trials of vitamin D in other populations found smaller fibroids, and one tiny trial of green tea extract found the same; both need larger trials. See a doctor for heavy bleeding.

Do:
- See a doctor if fibroids cause heavy or painful periods; treatment is not needed without symptoms. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Ask about a vitamin D supplement: the NHS says people with African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds should consider one through the year. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, as for everyone. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]
- Know that being overweight is a risk factor the UK's NHS lists for fibroids. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]

Avoid:
- Treating heavy bleeding with food or supplements alone: iron deficiency anaemia is a known complication. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Fibroids", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/]
- Taking green tea extract tablets as a fibroid treatment: the only trial I found was a pilot of 39 women in Egypt. [tested: Roshdy 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23950663/]

See someone when:
- Heavy periods, pain or pressure from fibroids that affect daily life (doctor).
- Tiredness, breathlessness or pale skin with heavy periods (doctor, for a blood count).
- Bleeding between periods or after sex (doctor).

## Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/hibiscus-sorrel-blood-pressure/
Module: Food
Tier: A thin (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Hibiscus tea lowered blood pressure a little in several trials, including one in Nigerian adults. A stricter review found too little reliable evidence, so the effect is contested. It is a reasonable drink, not a replacement for blood-pressure medicine.

Do:
- Drink it if you like it, alongside the UK's NHS basics: less salt, regular exercise, alcohol within limits. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure: prevention", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/prevention/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist you drink it if you take blood-pressure tablets. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Taking bendroflumethiazide with other medicines and herbal remedies" (the herbal-remedy wording applies generally), https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/bendroflumethiazide/taking-bendroflumethiazide-with-other-medicines-and-herbal-remedies]

Avoid:
- Stopping or skipping prescribed medicine because you drink hibiscus. [tested: Pattanittum 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34837382/]
- Treating a high reading as something a drink will fix. [tested: Pattanittum 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34837382/]

See someone when:
- A home reading is repeatedly high (doctor).
- A reading is very high with headache, chest pain, vision change or confusion (urgent care today).
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding and want to take it regularly (midwife or doctor): I did not find safety data in what I read.

## Intermittent fasting for weight and health
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/intermittent-fasting-for-weight-and-health/
Module: Food
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Intermittent fasting lost weight in trials, about the same as ordinary calorie cutting, and one small pilot of Black adults in churches found it workable. Avoid it if you have had an eating disorder or are pregnant or breastfeeding, and plan it with your care team if you have diabetes. Religious fasting has its own guidance.

Do:
- Choose a plan written by a dietitian that is built on healthy, balanced eating. [clinical guidance: NHS My Health London, "Intermittent fasting", https://www.myhealthlondon.nhs.uk/be-healthier/lose-weight/which-diet-is-right-for-me/intermittent-fasting/]
- Protect fruit, vegetables and fibre on eating days: the fasting group in the church pilot ate less of them. [tested: Yeary 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38986868/]
- Treat it as one way to eat less, not a special effect: against ordinary calorie cutting it gave about the same weight loss, except alternate-day fasting, which gave a little more. [tested: Semnani-Azad 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40533200/]

Avoid:
- Intermittent fasting if you have had an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. [clinical guidance: NHS My Health London, "Intermittent fasting", https://www.myhealthlondon.nhs.uk/be-healthier/lose-weight/which-diet-is-right-for-me/intermittent-fasting/]
- Delaying or skipping meals if you have diabetes, unless your diabetes team has planned it with you. [clinical guidance: NHS My Health London, "Intermittent fasting", https://www.myhealthlondon.nhs.uk/be-healthier/lose-weight/which-diet-is-right-for-me/intermittent-fasting/]

See someone when:
- You have diabetes, especially on insulin or tablets that can cause low blood sugar (diabetes team, before changing meal times).
- You get dizziness, fainting, palpitations or confusion while fasting (doctor).
- Food is taking over your thoughts, or you are eating very little (doctor or an eating disorder service).
- You are fasting for religious reasons with diabetes or sickle cell (see the Ramadan and religious fasting entry).

## Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/kola-nut/
Module: Food
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Kola nut is a traditional stimulant chewed and shared across West Africa. My search found no human study of what it does to health. Its main active ingredient is caffeine, so normal caffeine cautions apply, including a daily limit in pregnancy. Lab and animal findings on the heart and on nitrosamines are untested in people.

Do:
- If you are pregnant, keep total caffeine to 200mg a day or less: kola nut contains caffeine, but its amount per nut is not sourced here. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Foods to avoid in pregnancy", https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/foods-to-avoid/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- Palpitations, a racing or irregular heartbeat after chewing kola nut (doctor; 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number with chest pain or collapse).
- You are pregnant and chew or drink kola products often (midwife or doctor).
- You take heart or blood pressure medicine and chew it daily (pharmacist or doctor).

## Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/lions-mane-and-reishi-mushroom-supplements/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Lion's mane and reishi have only small trials behind them, mostly low quality, in older Japanese adults with memory loss, healthy adults, and cancer patients on treatment. Our search found no trial of these mushrooms in Black participants. Treat claims for memory or immunity as untested for you, and tell your doctor or pharmacist you take them.

Do:
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist you take mushroom supplements, especially if you are on cancer treatment or any regular medicine. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Treat memory or immunity claims as unproven for you: the trials were small and in older Japanese adults with memory problems, or cancer patients. [tested: Mori 2009, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18844328/]

Avoid:
