- Using reishi or lion's mane as a replacement for cancer treatment: the Cochrane review found only poor-quality trials of reishi alongside treatment. [tested: Jin 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27045603/]
- Mushroom supplements if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- Itching, rash, swelling or breathing trouble after taking one (urgent care).
- Stomach pain or headache that continues while taking it (doctor or pharmacist).
- You are having cancer treatment and want to add reishi (your oncology team).

## Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/moringa-leaf-and-blood-sugar/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Moringa leaf is a nutritious food, but a 2025 review of nine trials found no consistent benefit for blood sugar, weight or cholesterol, and rated the evidence very low certainty. A small trial in Nigerian adults with type 2 diabetes found no difference in blood sugar after two weeks. Do not swap it for medicine.

Do:
- Treat it as a food or an add-on: the review found no consistent benefit. [tested: Crisan 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41305552/]
- Check first with a pharmacist before taking moringa capsules or powder if you take other medicine, including diabetes or blood pressure tablets. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Stopping or skipping prescribed medicine for moringa: trials show no consistent benefit. [tested: Crisan 2025, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41305552/]
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- You take diabetes or blood pressure medicine and want to add moringa (pharmacist or doctor).
- You have high blood sugar symptoms such as thirst, passing a lot of urine or tiredness (doctor).
- A rash, swelling or tummy pain after taking it (doctor; 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number for swelling of the face or throat or trouble breathing).

## Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/plantain-yam-and-cassava-and-blood-sugar/
Module: Food
Tier: B thin (Observed in Black populations)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: In glucose tests, cassava, pounded yam and several West African staples raised blood sugar quickly, while breadfruit, white yam, eddoes and tannia were in the middle. Plantain results vary by ripeness and cooking. Cassava must be fully processed, since undercooked bitter cassava has caused paralysis. No trial shows that swapping staples prevents diabetes.

Do:
- Try intermediate staples such as white yam, eddoes, tannia or breadfruit more often: the Trinidad authors say a swap may bring health benefits. [tested: Ramdath 2004, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15182400/]
- Choose higher-fibre cereal foods: more cereal fibre was linked to lower diabetes rates in US Black women. [tested: Krishnan 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039988/]
- Process cassava fully, by grating, soaking and cooking as taught: processing methods prevented cyanide poisoning. [tested: Cliff 2011, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20654676/]

Avoid:
- Treating pounded yam, cassava or white rice as low-sugar: most staples tested had a high glycaemic index. [tested: Kouame 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690417/]
- Ready-to-eat cassava chips or under-processed bitter cassava as a daily food: cyanide levels can be high. [tested: Quinn 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35626954/]

See someone when:
- Constant thirst, passing a lot of urine, tiredness or blurred vision (doctor, for a blood sugar test).
- Sudden weakness or stiffness in the legs after a diet heavy in cassava (urgent doctor or A&E in the UK).
- You have diabetes and want to change your staples (diabetes team or dietitian).

## Probiotics and gut health
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/probiotics-and-gut-health/
Module: Food
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Probiotics reduced diarrhoea caused by antibiotics in trials, and the UK's NHS says they may ease some IBS symptoms, but evidence for most other claims is thin. Our search found one small safety pilot in Black women, for vaginal health, and no gut trial in Black participants. Avoid them if your immune system is weak unless your doctor agrees.

Do:
- If you are on antibiotics and want to try one, ask your pharmacist or doctor: trials found less antibiotic-related diarrhoea. [tested: Liao 2021, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33234881/]
- Treat the label with caution: the UK's NHS says we cannot always be sure a product contains the bacteria stated, enough of them, or that they survive to your gut. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Probiotics", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/probiotics/]
- Food counts too: the UK's NHS describes probiotics as live bacteria and yeasts found in yoghurts and supplements. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Probiotics", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/probiotics/]

Avoid:
- Probiotics if you have a weakened immune system or are very unwell, unless your doctor agrees: NCCIH, in its review of use with antibiotics, excludes people who are very weak or have poorly functioning immune systems from the safe group. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Probiotics: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety]
- Giving them to premature babies unless the hospital team prescribes them: severe and fatal infections have been reported. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Probiotics: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety]
- Using them to treat eczema: the UK's NHS says there is no evidence they help. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Probiotics", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/probiotics/]

See someone when:
- Fever, chills or feeling very unwell after starting one (urgent care).
- Diarrhoea that lasts more than a few days, or blood in your stool (doctor).
- You have a weakened immune system, are pregnant, or are caring for a premature baby and want to use one (your clinical team).

## Salt and blood pressure
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/salt-and-blood-pressure/
Module: Food
Tier: A moderate (Tested in people like you)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Cutting salt lowers blood pressure in Black and non-Black adults alike, and the DASH eating pattern did too in a large US feeding trial that was mostly Black. Salt matters, but a special inherited salt gene is not established, and historians dispute the slavery-era theory behind it. Aim for no more than 6g a day, like every adult.

Do:
- Eat no more than 6g of salt a day as an adult: about three-quarters of the salt we eat is already in the food we buy. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]
- Check food labels: more than 1.5g of salt per 100g means a food is high in salt. [clinical guidance: NHS, "8 tips for healthy eating", https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eight-tips-for-healthy-eating/]
- Combine less salt with the DASH pattern (fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy): together they lowered blood pressure in the trial. [tested: Hussain 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42429484/]
- Get your blood pressure checked, even if you feel well. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure (hypertension)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/]

Avoid:
- Believing salt is only a problem for you or that you are immune: reducing sodium lowered blood pressure in both Black and non-Black participants. [tested: Hussain 2026, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42429484/]
- Stopping or changing blood pressure medicine because you have cut salt: tell your doctor or pharmacist first. [clinical guidance: NHS, "High blood pressure (hypertension)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure-hypertension/]

See someone when:
- A home reading above 135/85 on average or a clinic reading of 140/90 or above (doctor).
- A high reading with headache, blurred vision or chest pain (NHS 111 in the UK; 999, or your local emergency number for chest pain that does not go away).

## Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/sea-moss-irish-moss/
Module: Food
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: My search found no human study showing sea moss improves health. It contains iodine, which in excess can upset the thyroid, and seaweed can carry heavy metals such as arsenic and cadmium. Avoid it while breastfeeding, and ask your doctor first if you have a thyroid condition.

Do:
- Ask your doctor before taking sea moss if you have a thyroid condition: excess iodine can upset the thyroid. [tested: Farebrother 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30891786/]
- Check any supplement label for iodine: the UK's NHS says 0.5mg or less a day of iodine supplements is unlikely to cause harm. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iodine" (vitamins and minerals), https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/iodine/]
- Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbal product you take. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Sea moss while breastfeeding, unless its iodine and heavy metal levels are shown to be low: excess iodine from seaweed has suppressed infants' thyroids. [clinical guidance: Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed), "Sea Moss" (NICHD, updated 15 Feb 2026), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41730053/]
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver problems, without a pharmacist check. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- A swelling at the front of your neck, a racing heart, or unexplained weight change after regular use (doctor).
- You have a thyroid condition or take thyroid tablets and use sea moss (doctor or pharmacist).
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding and have been taking it (midwife or doctor).

## Soursop (graviola): cancer cure, blood sugar and safety
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/soursop-graviola/
Module: Food
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: There is no proof that soursop treats cancer; human studies are lacking. The fruit is eaten as food. In Guadeloupe, regular soursop consumption was closely linked to a rare, severe parkinsonism, with a plant chemical called annonacin as the probable cause. Do not use it instead of cancer treatment, and tell your doctor if you take it.

Do:
- Tell your healthcare providers about any soursop or graviola you take, including tea and capsules. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Graviola" (About Herbs, updated 14 April 2026), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola]
- Talk to your provider before using graviola if you take blood sugar or blood pressure medicines: graviola can lower both. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Graviola" (About Herbs, updated 14 April 2026), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola]
- Avoid graviola if you are having imaging such as a PET scan: it can affect results. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Graviola" (About Herbs, updated 14 April 2026), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola]

Avoid:
- Using graviola as a cancer treatment: Memorial Sloan Kettering says there is no proof it benefits cancer patients. [clinical guidance: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, "Graviola" (About Herbs, updated 14 April 2026), https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola]
- Regular use of soursop fruit or leaf tea: regular consumption was linked to atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe. [tested: Lannuzel 2008, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18816693/]

See someone when:
- You have cancer and are thinking of stopping or delaying treatment for a herbal remedy (your cancer team, first).
- New tremor, stiffness, balance problems, hallucinations or memory loss in someone who uses soursop regularly (doctor, urgently).
- You take diabetes or blood pressure medicine and drink soursop leaf tea (pharmacist or doctor).

## Turmeric and curcumin supplements
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/turmeric-and-curcumin-supplements/
Module: Food
Tier: B moderate (Tested, but not in people like you)
Harm signal: yes
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-16
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: Turmeric and curcumin supplements may ease joint pain a little in low-quality trials, but NCCIH says we do not know enough to say they help. Our search found no trial of turmeric or curcumin in Black participants. Rare serious liver injury is reported, and some loose turmeric powder carries lead. Stop and see a doctor if you turn yellow.

Do:
- Stop it and talk to a health care provider if you get fatigue, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine or jaundice. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Turmeric: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/turmeric]
- If you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, tell your prescriber about any supplement first: the UK's NHS says some supplements and remedies do not mix well with it. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Warfarin: medicine used to prevent and treat blood clots", https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/warfarin/]
- Prefer turmeric as a food spice from a source you trust to concentrated capsules: the liver injury cases were linked to supplement products. [tested: Halegoua-DeMarzio 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36252717/]

Avoid:
- Turmeric supplements in pregnancy: NCCIH says they may be unsafe. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Turmeric: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/turmeric]
- Highly bioavailable curcumin products, which NCCIH says may harm your liver. [clinical guidance: NCCIH, "Turmeric: Usefulness and Safety", https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/turmeric]
- Assuming loose turmeric powder is clean: lead chromate was found in 14 per cent of samples in a South Asian survey. [tested: Forsyth 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39053552/]

See someone when:
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching or marked tiredness while using it (doctor or urgent care).
- You take a blood thinner, diabetes medicine or any regular medicine and want to start a supplement (pharmacist).
- Persistent joint pain, swelling or stiffness (doctor; a supplement does not replace a diagnosis).

## Vitamins and supplements: what the NHS says
URL: https://vilivity.com/food/vitamins-and-supplements-basics/
Module: Food
Tier: D (Untested)
Harm signal: no
Founder's own practice: no
Last checked: 2026-11-12
Clinical review: not yet clinically reviewed

Answer: The NHS says most people get all the nutrients they need from a varied, balanced diet. The main exception for you is vitamin D: people with African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds should consider a daily supplement all year. Do not take iron without a blood test, and tell a pharmacist about any herbal remedy if you take other medicines.

Do:
- Aim to get your nutrients from a varied and balanced diet first. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamins and minerals", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/]
- Consider a daily vitamin D supplement all year if your background is African, African-Caribbean or South Asian; everyone should consider one in autumn and winter. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Vitamin D", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/]
- Ask for a full blood count if you are tired, short of breath or have heavy periods, before any iron tablets. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]
- Check with a pharmacist before taking a herbal medicine if you already take other medicines. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

Avoid:
- Taking iron tablets without a blood test: the UK's NHS has a doctor recommend treatment once the cause is found. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Iron deficiency anaemia", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/]
- Herbal medicines if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have kidney or liver problems, or take medicines such as statins, diabetes or blood pressure tablets, unless a pharmacist has checked. [clinical guidance: NHS, "Herbal medicines and complementary therapies", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/herbal-medicines/]

See someone when:
- Tiredness, breathlessness, headaches or paler skin that is not settling (doctor, for a blood test).
- Heavy periods with tiredness (doctor).
- You take prescribed medicine and want to add a herbal remedy (pharmacist).

# Generational practices

## African black soap
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/african-black-soap/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: C thin
Harm: possible (Soaps are alkaline and can dry or irritate sensitive or eczema-prone skin (general dermatology, not from the review abstract).)
What people do: Wash the face and body, and sometimes hair, with a soft soap made from plantain-skin and cocoa-pod ash with palm oil and shea; known as dudu osun or ose dudu.
Why they say it works: Said to clear acne, soothe eczema and fade marks, and to be gentler than shop soap.

## Aloe vera (sinkle bible)
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/aloe-vera-sinkle-bible/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean, East and Southern Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Putting aloe, or any plant material, in the eye risks infection and corneal damage (Somalia commentary); oral aloe latex is a laxative.)
What people do: Cut a leaf and use the gel on burns, skin and scalp, or drink it for "sugar"; in rural Somalia aloe gel is also put in the eye.
Why they say it works: The gel is cooling and healing; the bitter drink is believed to treat diabetes.

## Ash, cow dung or heat on the baby's umbilical cord
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/umbilical-cord-ash-cow-dung-and-hot-compress/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B moderate
Harm: yes (Ash and dung on a cord stump are linked by the authors to fatal infection; chlorhexidine gel is the replacement.)
What people do: Birth attendants and relatives cut the cord with a razor blade and dress the stump with ash, cow dung or a hot compress.
Why they say it works: To dry the stump quickly and prevent bleeding or "spirits".

## Being strong and hiding distress
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/the-strong-black-woman-and-hiding-distress/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Black British, African American
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Delayed help-seeking is the harm identified.)
What people do: Carry on, keep distress private, and avoid asking for help; a cultural legacy of strength.
Why they say it works: Strength was needed to survive; showing weakness is seen as risky or shameful.

## Bitter leaf (Vernonia amygdalina)
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/bitter-leaf/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Malaria treated with a leaf instead of an antimalarial is dangerous; the trial does not support that.)
What people do: Wash the leaves to remove bitterness and cook them in soup, or squeeze and drink the bitter juice, for malaria, "sugar" and stomach complaints.
Why they say it works: Bitterness is read as strength; it is said to clean the blood and treat fever.

## Bush medicine taken alongside diabetes and blood pressure tablets
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/bush-medicine-alongside-diabetes-and-blood-pressure-drugs/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: C thin
Harm: possible (Interaction risk is predicted (computer modelling), not observed in patients. The practical point: tell the doctor or pharmacist what you are drinking.)
What people do: Take bush teas or herbal remedies for "sugar" and "pressure" in addition to, or sometimes instead of, prescribed medicines; about a third of Barbadian church-goers use herbal remedies.
Why they say it works: Plants are "natural", familiar, cheap and passed on by older relatives.

## Bush tea for a "washout" or "blood cleanse"
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/bush-tea-washout-and-blood-cleanse/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: C thin
Harm: possible (Bitter and purgative teas can cause diarrhoea and dehydration (general pharmacology, not sourced here). A search summary links Jamaican "bush tea" made from Crotalaria to veno-occlusive liver disease (Bras 1954/1957); I did not open the primary papers, so UNVERIFIED.)
What people do: Drink a bitter or purgative bush tea (cerasee and others), often as a regular tonic or at the turn of the year, to "wash out" or "clean the blood".
Why they say it works: The body is said to collect "dirt" or "bad blood" that a bitter tea flushes out; it is also taken to prevent illness.

## Cerasee (bitter melon) tea
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/cerasee-tea-bitter-melon/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Bitter melon can lower blood sugar; people on diabetes tablets or insulin using it alongside risk going too low (general pharmacology, not found in the Cochrane abstract). MSK says safety data are sparse (agent4).)
What people do: Boil the vine leaves of cerasee (Momordica charantia) and drink the bitter tea, for "sugar" (diabetes), colds, skin and as a cleansing tonic.
Why they say it works: It is bitter, so it is "strong medicine"; it is believed to lower blood sugar and clear the system.

## Chebe powder
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/chebe-powder/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, Central Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Powder-coated braids can be tight; traction concerns apply.)
What people do: Mix roasted chebe seed powder with oil or fat and coat the lengths (not scalp) before plaiting, repeating every few days.
Why they say it works: Said to stop breakage so hair grows very long, as Basara Arab women of Chad are known for.

## Chemical relaxers, often started in childhood
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/chemical-relaxers-from-childhood/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American, East and Southern Africa, West Africa, Black British
Tier: B moderate
Harm: yes (Associated with traction alopecia when combined with tight styling; a cancer association is reported but unsettled.)
What people do: Use a lye or no-lye relaxer to straighten the hair every few weeks to months, often starting as a girl.
Why they say it works: Straight hair is easier to manage and long seen as "professional"; family tradition.

## Cocoa butter on stretch marks
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/cocoa-butter-on-stretch-marks/
Counted as documented: no (reported, not yet documented)
Regions: Caribbean, African American, Black British, West Africa
Tier: A moderate
Harm: none (No harm identified; wasted money more than harm.)
What people do: Rub cocoa butter cream or butter into the belly, hips and breasts in pregnancy, and onto scars.
Why they say it works: Said to keep skin supple and stop or fade stretch marks.

## Cooking with shea butter
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/shea-butter-as-cooking-fat/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: none (No harm identified; it is a saturated-fat food and this is a cross-sectional association.)
What people do: Use shea butter as a cooking fat in northern Ghana and the savanna belt of West Africa.
Why they say it works: It is the traditional local fat, regarded as healthy and "medicinal".

## Eating clay (geophagy) and ice (pagophagia) in pregnancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/clay-eating-geophagy/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American
Tier: B moderate
Harm: yes (Pica is tied in these studies to lower iron stores in pregnancy; clay may raise blood pressure (Vermeer). Tell the midwife.)
What people do: Some women, especially in the rural South, eat white or red clay, and some pregnant women eat large amounts of ice or freezer frost.
Why they say it works: A cultural and family habit; women describe cravings and say it settles the stomach or helps the baby.

## Eating patterns of Somali families in the UK
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/somali-diet-in-the-uk/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Black British, East and Southern Africa
Tier: D
Harm: low (Low fruit and vegetables is a general dietary risk, not a Somali-specific finding.)
What people do: Eat mainly rice, pasta and red meat with little fruit or vegetable; cultural beliefs about food shape the diet.
Why they say it works: Familiar, filling foods; unsure what counts as healthy.

## Epsom salt baths
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/epsom-salt-baths/
Counted as documented: no (reported, not yet documented)
Regions: African American, Caribbean, Black British
Tier: C thin
Harm: low (A case report exists of hypermagnesaemia after swallowing a bath agent; not a bathing risk.)
What people do: Soak in hot water with Epsom salt for aches, colds and "drawing out" illness.
Why they say it works: Magnesium is said to be absorbed through the skin and relax the muscles.

## Fever grass (lemongrass) tea for fever
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/fever-grass-lemongrass-tea/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: D
Harm: low (Fever in a baby or a fever that lasts needs a doctor; a tea is no substitute (general advice).)
What people do: Drink fever grass (Cymbopogon citratus) tea to bring down a fever, often for children, with a shared home tradition of "sweating it out".
Why they say it works: It is a cooling, aromatic herb believed to break a fever.

## Food taboos in pregnancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/dietary-taboos-in-pregnancy/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: East and Southern Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Restriction of nutritious food in pregnancy can lower birth weight, per the authors' view; 1988, one community.)
What people do: Pregnant women avoid certain foods because of family rules and beliefs about the baby and about witchcraft.
Why they say it works: Foods are believed to harm or mark the baby or ease labour.

## Garlic and ginger for high blood pressure
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/garlic-and-ginger-for-blood-pressure/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Authors advise clinicians to ask about and counsel on CAM use; garlic and ginger effects on BP tablets not read.)
What people do: People with hypertension take raw garlic or ginger, in food or water, alongside or instead of tablets.
Why they say it works: Garlic is believed to thin the blood and lower pressure; ginger to warm and open the vessels.

## Greasing the scalp (and pressing with a hot comb)
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/greasing-the-scalp-and-hot-combing/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American, Caribbean, Black British
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Heavy products on a scalp with seborrhoeic dermatitis can feed yeast (dermatology guidance in the bank's scalp-oiling entry).)
What people do: Part the hair and rub a grease, pomade or oil onto the scalp, often as a weekly routine before braiding or pressing.
Why they say it works: Said to moisturise, heal the scalp and help growth.

## Hair threading (irun kiko)
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/threading-irun-kiko/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, Central Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Tight threading pulls on the roots, so the traction-alopecia warning applies (extrapolated from braids, not threading-specific).)
What people do: Wrap sections of hair in black or coloured thread from root to tip to stretch and style it, often for girls and women.
Why they say it works: It keeps hair stretched without heat, protects the ends and looks neat for weeks.

## Herbal concoctions in pregnancy and to start labour
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/herbal-concoctions-in-pregnancy-and-to-start-labour/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, East and Southern Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Non-disclosure to clinicians means reactions are missed. The Cochrane castor oil review is a different herb from the concoctions studied.)
What people do: Women drink herbal mixtures through pregnancy, to induce labour or to boost health, often from family or friends, and often without telling the clinic.
Why they say it works: To keep the pregnancy "strong", ease labour and avoid medicines.

## Herbal teas, ginger, lime and spices for colds and flu
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/herbal-teas-and-spices-for-colds-and-flu/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: D
Harm: low (Hot drinks are low risk; the harm is delay when a child or older person has breathing difficulty (general advice, not from these sources).)
What people do: Drink hot infusions, decoctions and "punch" made from local herbs (mint family especially), often with ginger, lime or honey, at the first sign of a cold; Haitian families did this in the COVID period.
Why they say it works: Heat, sweating and the plant itself are believed to "break" the cold.

## Hot compress on the abdomen after birth
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/postpartum-hot-compress-on-the-abdomen/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Burn risk on a numb, tired post-delivery body is plausible but I found no source quantifying it. The Nnewi authors call some postpartum practices "out rightly dangerous" without naming which in the abstract.)
What people do: After delivery a mother presses hot cloths or hot water bottles to the lower abdomen, often daily for weeks.
Why they say it works: To help the womb drain (lochia) and shrink back, and to keep the body "warm" after birth.

## Hot salt-water sitz bath after birth
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/postpartum-hot-sitz-bath/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: low (Warm (not scalding) sitz baths are standard postnatal advice in many places; I did not open guidance, so this is UNVERIFIED as clinical guidance.)
What people do: Sit in a bowl or bath of hot water (sometimes with salt) in the first days and weeks after delivery.
Why they say it works: To speed healing of tears and stitches, help the womb drain and "tighten" the vagina.

## Hot water fomentation of the baby's soft spot
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/hot-fomentation-of-newborn-fontanelle/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: yes (Listed with scalp moulding, scarification and ano-genital irrigation as newborn practices that "pose a threat" to the neonate. Scald risk is plain; rates not read.)
What people do: Press hot cloths or heated water to a newborn's fontanelle (and body) to "mould" the head or soothe the baby.
Why they say it works: Believed to close the fontanelle, protect the baby's head and ward off illness.

## Hot water, hot food and pepper soup after birth
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/postpartum-hot-water-hot-food-and-pepper/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (The Nnewi authors judged some of the practices in their list to be dangerous; the abstract does not say which, and I did not read the full text.)
What people do: For weeks after birth the mother drinks hot water, eats hot (temperature) and very peppery food and bathes in hot water.
Why they say it works: Birth is believed to leave the body "cold" and "open"; heat restores it and helps the milk.

## Irish moss (sea moss) drink
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/irish-sea-moss-drink/
Counted as documented: no (reported, not yet documented)
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Contamination in commercial products (microbes and metals).)
What people do: Boil dried sea moss with milk, spices and sweetener for a thick drink; now sold as a gel supplement.
Why they say it works: Believed to build strength and stamina, treat colds, and boost libido.

## Isihlambezo, umhlabelo and imbiza in pregnancy and infancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/zulu-isihlambezo-umhlabelo-and-imbiza/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: East and Southern Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Contents vary by healer; nothing opened quantifies harm.)
What people do: Zulu women take isihlambezo during pregnancy, umhlabelo for postpartum recovery and imbiza for babies.
Why they say it works: To keep pregnancy healthy, speed recovery and protect the baby; passed down and used alongside free clinics.

## Jamaican black castor oil on the scalp and edges
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/jamaican-black-castor-oil-on-scalp-and-edges/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean, African American, Black British
Tier: C thin
Harm: low (Hair felting and contact dermatitis reported; thick oil on a damaged scalp can trap product.)
What people do: Massage black castor oil into the scalp and hairline for growth, thickness and edges.
Why they say it works: The roasted-ash oil is thick and "strong"; it is said to grow hair and thicken edges.

## Kola nut
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/kola-nut-chewing/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Contains caffeine-type stimulants (general); linked here only to social and school correlates, not to a physical harm.)
What people do: Chew kola nut for alertness and stamina, offer it in hospitality and ritual, and (in one Nigerian custom) rub a kola paste on a pregnant belly.
Why they say it works: It is a stimulant and a symbol of welcome; some say it stops hunger and fatigue.

## Moringa
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/moringa-for-health-and-milk/
Counted as documented: no (reported, not yet documented)
Regions: West Africa, Caribbean
Tier: B moderate
Harm: low (Large doses untested.)
What people do: Drink moringa leaf tea or powder for energy, blood pressure and breast milk.
Why they say it works: Called a "miracle tree".

## Oiling and massaging newborns
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/newborn-oil-massage-and-petroleum-jelly/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, East and Southern Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: low (Oils can irritate and some cooking oils may harm fragile skin (not sourced here); for preterm babies clinics now offer emollient therapy.)
What people do: Rub cooking oil, other natural oils or petroleum jelly into a newborn after bathing; massage the belly with a kola paste in some Nigerian communities.
Why they say it works: To keep the baby's skin supple, strengthen the limbs and, in the kola-paste custom, prevent thrush and skin infection.

## Orthodox Christian fasting
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/ethiopian-orthodox-fasting/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: East and Southern Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (People on diabetes medicines who change their eating risk going low; the abstract does not discuss hypoglycaemia.)
What people do: Observe the Orthodox fasts (no animal products on many days, including Wednesdays, Fridays and long seasons such as the Assumption fast).
Why they say it works: It is a religious duty and a spiritual discipline; many also see it as healthy.

## Palm wine, alcohol and tea to bring in milk
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/postpartum-lactation-drinks-palm-wine-and-tea/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Alcohol passes into breast milk (general pharmacology, not from these sources). The Nnewi authors flagged dangerous practices without detail in the abstract.)
What people do: Mothers drink tea, hot water, palm wine or other alcoholic drinks to "improve the flow" of breast milk.
Why they say it works: Warm or fermented drinks are believed to open the milk.

## Planning exercise around your hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/planning-exercise-around-hair/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American
Tier: B thin
Harm: low (The practice protects the style at a cost to exercise; low-manipulation styles and swim caps are the usual compromise.)
What people do: Change hairstyle for exercise or skip workouts to protect a style that took hours and money.
Why they say it works: Sweat and water ruin straightened or braided styles; washing and restyling takes too long.

## Plants for childbirth recovery and vaginal "cleansing" (Haitian and Caribbean women)
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/haitian-and-caribbean-plants-for-childbirth-and-vaginal-cleansing/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Authors raise the possibility of vaginal dysbiosis (hypothesised, not demonstrated in these sources).)
What people do: Women use food plants as teas, baths and vaginal preparations after childbirth and for gynaecological infections or "cleansing"; the practice continues after migration.
Why they say it works: Plants are believed to clean the womb, heal after birth and prevent infection.

## Prayer and the church as mental health support
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/prayer-and-faith-as-coping/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American, Caribbean, Black British
Tier: B thin
Harm: low (Positive as support; risk is when prayer replaces treatment for severe illness.)
What people do: Turn to prayer, scripture, the pastor or the congregation when distressed, instead of or before therapy.
Why they say it works: God is a source of strength; church is trusted, free and close.

## Prayer camps, faith and traditional healers for mental illness
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/traditional-and-faith-healing-for-mental-illness/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, East and Southern Africa
Tier: D
Harm: yes (Shackling, flogging and forced fasting are documented in these centres. Collaboration with clinics is possible and wanted by many healers.)
What people do: Families take people with psychosis or severe distress to a traditional healer, prayer camp or church; some centres use shackling, flogging and forced fasting.
Why they say it works: Illness is seen as spiritual, so prayer, ritual and herbs are the first treatment; healers are trusted and close by.

## Putting mascara, kohl, aloe, honey or breast milk in babies' eyes
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/traditional-eye-remedies-for-babies-and-children/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, East and Southern Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: yes (The ocular surface is easily infected or scarred; "natural does not mean sterile". Seek an eye clinic for any red or painful eye.)
What people do: Apply mascara-type eye cosmetics to a newborn's eyes, or instil aloe, honey, plant sap or breast milk for red or sore eyes.
Why they say it works: To "clear" or strengthen the eyes and treat redness.

## Root work and Gullah herbal remedies
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/root-work-and-gullah-herbal-remedies/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Unknown: no individual plant or recipe examined.)
What people do: Families in the South and Sea Islands use teas, poultices and spiritual practice drawn from herbal lore; the tradition is documented in books.
Why they say it works: Remedies handed down from enslaved ancestors; belief that plants and spiritual work treat illness.

## Satin bonnet, scarf or pillowcase at night
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/satin-bonnet-and-scarf-at-night/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American, Caribbean, Black British, West Africa
Tier: D
Harm: none (No harm identified.)
What people do: Cover the hair with a satin or silk bonnet or scarf, or sleep on a satin pillowcase.
Why they say it works: Cotton "steals moisture" and rubs hair, causing breakage; a cover keeps a style and edges neat.

## Shea butter on skin, hair and babies
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/shea-butter-on-skin-hair-and-babies/
Counted as documented: no (reported, not yet documented)
Regions: West Africa, Caribbean, African American, Black British
Tier: B thin
Harm: low (Latex allergy with raw shea (Cleveland Clinic, in the bank entry).)
What people do: Rub raw or whipped shea butter on skin, scalp, hair and babies as a daily moisturiser.
Why they say it works: Traditional West African emollient, called gentle and healing.

## Skin lightening and bleaching creams
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/skin-lightening-and-bleaching/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, Caribbean, African American, Black British
Tier: B moderate
Harm: yes (Mercury, potent steroids and hydroquinone cause kidney, skin and cancer harm; WHO calls mercury products hazardous (agent4).)
What people do: Apply lightening creams, soaps or injections (hydroquinone, steroids, sometimes mercury) to the face or whole body, often for years, often from a young age.
Why they say it works: Lighter skin is linked to beauty and status; people also use the products for dark marks and "even" skin.

## Sorrel (hibiscus) drink
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/sorrel-drink/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean, West Africa
Tier: B moderate
Harm: low (Can add to blood pressure drugs; sweetened versions add sugar; a minor, clinically insignificant rise in AST was noted in one analysis. The Gleaner claims about cancer are uncited.)
What people do: Steep dried sorrel calyces (Hibiscus sabdariffa) with ginger and cloves, sweeten and chill; a Christmas staple in Jamaica and drunk through the year; known as zobo or sobolo in West Africa.
Why they say it works: It is said to be cooling, good for the heart and "pressure", and rich in vitamin C.

## Soursop leaf tea
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/soursop-leaf-tea/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean
Tier: C thin
Harm: yes (Neurotoxicity signal from the Guadeloupe work (associational) and no human evidence of cancer benefit. Soursop as a cancer treatment is a harm practice in the bank rules.)
What people do: Steep soursop (graviola) leaves, or eat or juice the fruit, for sleep, nerves, "sugar", and increasingly as a cancer remedy.
Why they say it works: Said to calm the nerves and, in recent social media, to kill cancer cells.

## Tight braids, weaves and extensions on relaxed hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/braids-and-extensions-on-relaxed-hair/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa, East and Southern Africa, African American, Black British
Tier: B moderate
Harm: yes (Traction alopecia can become permanent scarring hair loss; tightness and hairline pain are the early signs.)
What people do: Put in tight cornrows, braids or extensions as a protective, low-maintenance style for weeks at a time.
Why they say it works: Protects the ends, saves daily styling and keeps hair "tucked away".

## Traditional birth attendants' herbal remedies
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/traditional-birth-attendant-herbs/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: East and Southern Africa
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Bleeding and retained placenta are emergencies; relying on herbs delays hospital care (authors stress referral).)
What people do: Traditional birth attendants give herbal remedies for threatened miscarriage, labour complications, retained placenta and postpartum bleeding.
Why they say it works: Long experience: attendants have delivered hundreds of women and trust the local plants.

## Treating "high blood" by how you feel
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/high-blood-and-high-pertension/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Adjusting tablets by symptoms rather than by readings is unsafe for a condition that is often silent.)
What people do: Older Black women describe "high blood" or "high-pertension" as something felt in the blood and nerves, and manage medication by those symptoms.
Why they say it works: The illness is understood through symptoms and life stress rather than a number on a cuff.

## Tying cloth tightly around the abdomen after birth
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/postpartum-abdominal-binding/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: West Africa
Tier: B thin
Harm: possible (Evidence is for caesarean recovery only. Very tight binding after vaginal birth has no source I opened for or against.)
What people do: Tie a wrapper or cloth tight across the belly after delivery, for days or weeks.
Why they say it works: To "close" the body, flatten the stomach and support the womb.

## Vaginal steaming and herbal feminine cleansing
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/vaginal-steaming-and-feminine-cleansing/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: African American, West Africa, Caribbean
Tier: D
Harm: possible (Framed as medically risky in the paper; Caribbean ethnobotany authors hypothesise microbiome disruption. No injury data opened.)
What people do: Sit over herbal steam or use herbal washes to "clean" the womb after periods or birth; promoted through wellness networks.
Why they say it works: To detox the womb, ease cramps, restore the vagina after birth or treat infection.

## Vicks VapoRub on the chest, feet and nose
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/vicks-vaporub-on-chest-and-feet/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Caribbean, African American, Black British, West Africa
Tier: B moderate
Harm: possible (Tested only in children aged 2 to 11; more irritation than petrolatum. Not tested in babies under two. The "feet" version has no source I opened.)
What people do: Rub Vicks on the chest, back, soles of the feet (under socks) or under the nose for colds, coughs and asthma, including on children.
Why they say it works: The menthol "opens the chest"; rubbing the feet is believed to pull the cold down.

## Washing hair every few weeks
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/infrequent-hair-washing-and-long-gaps-between-wash-days/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Black British, African American
Tier: B thin
Harm: low (Long gaps may let scalp disease build up; the exact interval has no tested threshold I found.)
What people do: Keep a style in for weeks and wash only now and then, often once every two to four weeks, longer in braids or weaves.
Why they say it works: Frequent washing dries the hair and undoes styles; the scalp "does not get dirty".

## Wearing hair natural in later life
URL: https://vilivity.com/practices/natural-hairstyles-and-wellbeing-in-older-black-women/
Counted as documented: yes
Regions: Black British
Tier: B thin
Harm: none (No harm identified.)
What people do: Stop relaxing and wearing complex styles; wear the natural texture.
Why they say it works: Confidence, identity and less time and cost; resistance to Eurocentric standards.

# Studies

## Absolute neutrophil count by Duffy status among healthy Black and African American adults
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/merz-2023-35994632/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35994632/
Citation: Merz LE, Story CM, Osei MA, Jolley K et al (2023), Blood Advances
- In A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count): 120 healthy self-identified Black and African American adults at one US primary care centre (n=120). 66.7% (80 of 120) were Duffy-null. Median absolute neutrophil count was 2,820 cells per microlitre in Duffy-null people against 5,005 in Duffy non-null (P<.001). 23.8% (19 of 80) of Duffy-null people had a count below 2,000, against none of the non-null. The authors state the Duffy-null phenotype is clinically insignificant and advocate Duffy-null-specific reference ranges.
- In Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test: 120 healthy self-identified Black adults at one primary care centre (n=120). 66.7% (80 of 120) were Duffy-null. Median absolute neutrophil count was 2,820 per microlitre in Duffy-null and 5,005 in Duffy non-null (P under .001); 19 of 80 Duffy-null adults had counts under 2,000 and none of the others did. The authors call the Duffy-null phenotype clinically insignificant and advocate Duffy-null-specific ranges and replacing the term benign ethnic neutropenia.

## Reduced neutrophil count in people of African descent is due to a regulatory variant in the Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines gene
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/reich-2009-19180233/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19180233/
Citation: Reich D, Nalls MA, Kao WH, Akylbekova EL et al (2009), PLoS Genetics
- In A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count): 6,005 African Americans from three cohort studies (n=6005). The Duffy Null variant (rs2814778) predicted white cell and neutrophil count in African Americans beyond the previously described admixture association, establishing a new phenotype for the variant.

## Cancer Trial Eligibility and Therapy Modifications for Individuals With Duffy Null-Associated Neutrophil Count
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hibbs-2024-39259539/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39259539/
Citation: Hibbs SP, Aiken L, Vora K, Mowete C et al (2024), JAMA Network Open
- In A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count): Phase 3 cancer trials for prostate, breast, melanoma, colorectal and lung cancers, 2021-2023 (n=382). Of 289 eligible trials, 221 (76.5%, 95% CI 71.1-81.2) excluded patients whose neutrophil counts were within the Duffy-null reference range. Colorectal trials had the highest exclusion proportion (86.4%), prostate the lowest (47.8%).

## The Duffy antigen: A narrative review of testing, epidemiology, neutrophil counts and clinical consequences
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hibbs-2025-40685916/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40685916/
Citation: Hibbs SP, Jones J, Hantel A, Merz LE (2025), British Journal of Haematology
- In A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count): Narrative review (n=not stated). The Duffy null variant is a non-pathological mutation that is partly protective against Plasmodium vivax and gives a lower neutrophil count without increasing infection risk. In many regions neutropenia has been defined by the counts of Duffy-positive people, which may be unsuitable for decisions in Duffy-null people.

## Febrile neutropenia in patients with Duffy-null-associated neutrophil counts and multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/abdallah-2024-39348709/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39348709/
Citation: Abdallah M, Arters F, Patel J, Edwards C et al (2024), Blood Advances
- In A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count): Duffy-null Black people and dose decisions (n=0). I found papers on febrile neutropenia in Duffy-null patients with myeloma (Abdallah 2024, abstract not retrievable) and on CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer (Ferri 2025, not opened). I could not confirm trial evidence for safe use of Duffy-specific thresholds. UNVERIFIED.

## A subgroup analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of adapalene-benzoyl peroxide topical gel in black subjects with moderate acne
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/alexis-2014-24509968/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24509968/
Citation: Alexis AF, Johnson LA, Kerrouche N, Callender VD (2014), Journal of Drugs in Dermatology
- In Acne on dark skin: Black subjects with moderate acne, pooled from three randomised trials (3,855 people in total) (n=subgroup size not in abstract). More Black participants had treatment success with adapalene-benzoyl peroxide than with vehicle at week 12, with lower lesion counts from week 1. It was well tolerated and no treatment-related dark marks were seen.

## Treatment recommendations for acne-associated hyperpigmentation: Results of the Delphi consensus process and a literature review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/taylor-2023-36924935/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924935/
Citation: Taylor S, Elbuluk N, Grimes P, Chien A et al (2023), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Acne on dark skin: Ten US dermatologists (consensus), plus a literature review, for acne with dark marks (n=10). Most people with acne and acne-related dark marks should get early, effective acne treatment with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide. Hydroquinone, azelaic acid, chemical peels or antioxidants may be added. The authors say large randomised trials are lacking, so evidence-based recommendations cannot be made.
- In Dark marks after acne (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation): 10 board-certified dermatologists (n=10 experts). Large randomised trials of acne and acne-marks treatment are lacking, so evidence-based recommendations cannot be made. The panel agreed that most patients with acne and marks should get early, effective acne treatment with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide. Hydroquinone, azelaic acid, chemical peel or antioxidants may be added.

## Effects of Topical Retinoids on Acne and Post-inflammatory Hyperpigmentation in Patients with Skin of Color: A Clinical Review and Implications for Practice
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/callender-2022-34751927/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34751927/
Citation: Callender VD, Baldwin H, Cook-Bolden FE et al (2022), American Journal of Clinical Dermatology
- In Acne on dark skin: Patients with skin of colour (mixed groups) (n=not stated). Topical retinoids treat acne and have been shown to reduce dark marks in skin of colour, so should be started early unless contraindicated; moisturisers and novel formulations may cut irritation; acne spots improve weeks before the marks do.

## African black soap: Physiochemical, phytochemical properties, and uses
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ogunbiyi-2021-33571401/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33571401/
Citation: Ogunbiyi A, Enechukwu NA (2021), Dermatologic Therapy
- In African black soap: Review of physical, chemical and plant-chemical properties (West Africa focus) (n=not stated). Traditional black soap is made from ash-derived alkali and plant oils. It is described as gentle, super-fatted and hypoallergenic and advertised as antimicrobial, anti-acne, exfoliating, toning and scar-fading, but the authors say some claims remain anecdotal. Studies have shown it has antimicrobial properties against Staphylococcal and some Streptococcal organisms (in the laboratory, per the authors' wording 'studies have shown').
- In African black soap: Survey of skin-lightening practices (context) (n=not applicable). Black soap is sometimes sold or marketed as lightening or scar-fading. Nothing in the sources opened shows it lightens skin; it is a claim to treat with caution given the harms in the skin lightening entry.

## Hematologic differences between African-Americans and whites: the roles of iron deficiency and alpha-thalassemia on hemoglobin levels and mean corpuscular volume
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/beutler-2005-15790781/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15790781/
Citation: Beutler E, West C (2005), Blood
- In Alpha-thalassaemia trait: small red cells that are not low iron: 1,491 African American and 31,005 white people with routine blood results and stored samples, about half men and half women (n=32496). Haematocrit, haemoglobin, MCV, transferrin saturation and white cell count were lower in African Americans; ferritin was higher. The -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion accounted for about one third of the haemoglobin difference; sickle trait and raised creatinine had no effect. Of women, 19.8% of African Americans and 5.3% of white women would be called anaemic; without iron-deficient or thalassaemic people the figures were 6.1% and 2.77% (men 17.7% and 7.6%, then 4.29% and 3.6%). The authors say the same reference standards do not apply to all ethnic groups.
- In Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test: 1,491 African American and 31,005 white people with routine laboratory results, about half men and half women (n=32496). Haematocrit, haemoglobin, MCV, transferrin saturation and white cell count were lower in African Americans and ferritin higher. The -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion accounted for about a third of the haemoglobin difference. With iron-deficient and thalassaemic people removed, the share classed anaemic was 6.1% against 2.77% in women and 4.29% against 3.6% in men.
- In Iron, heavy periods and fibroids: 1,491 African-American and 31,005 White laboratory subjects (n=32496). Haemoglobin, haematocrit and MCV were lower in African-Americans. Among all subjects 19.8% of African-American women would be classed as anaemic against 5.3% of White women; after removing iron-deficient and thalassaemic subjects the gap narrowed to 6.1% and 2.77%. The alpha-thalassaemia deletion explained about a third of the haemoglobin difference. The authors say the same reference standards do not apply to all ethnic groups.

## The α-thalassemias
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/piel-2014-25390741/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25390741/
Citation: Piel FB, Weatherall DJ (2014), New England Journal of Medicine
- In Alpha-thalassaemia trait: small red cells that are not low iron: Reviewed literature on the alpha-thalassaemias worldwide (n=not applicable). More than 100 varieties of alpha-thalassaemia have been identified. The authors say their geographic distribution, and the challenges of screening, diagnosis and management, suggest they should have a higher priority on global public health agendas. The abstract gives no more detail.

## Racism as a Determinant of Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/paradies-2015-26398658/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26398658/
Citation: Paradies Y, Ben J, Denson N et al (2015), PLoS One
- In Anxiety, depression and what helps: 293 studies (333 articles), mainly US (n=293 studies). Reported racism was linked to poorer mental health (negative mental health r = -0.23, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.21, 227 studies), including depression, anxiety and psychological stress, and to poorer general (r = -0.13) and physical health (r = -0.09). Effects were stronger in cross-sectional than longitudinal data. Ethnicity moderated some effects; the abstract text I read was cut off before the Black-specific comparison.
- In Racism, racial stress and mental health: 293 studies (333 articles), mainly US (n=293 studies). Reported racism was linked to poorer mental health (negative mental health r = -0.23, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.21, 227 studies), including depression, anxiety and psychological stress, and to poorer general (r = -0.13) and physical health (r = -0.09). Effects were stronger in cross-sectional than longitudinal data. Ethnicity moderated some effects; the abstract text I read was cut off before the Black-specific comparison.

## The effect of apple cider vinegar on lipid profiles and glycemic parameters: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hadi-2021-34187442/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34187442/
Citation: Hadi A, Pourmasoumi M, Najafgholizadeh A, Clark CCT et al (2021), BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies
- In Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety: Adults in nine randomised trials (ten study arms) of apple cider vinegar for at least two weeks (ethnicity not stated in the abstract) (n=not stated in the abstract). Apple cider vinegar lowered total cholesterol by about 6 mg/dL, fasting glucose by about 8 mg/dL and HbA1c by 0.5 points. There was no effect on LDL, HDL, insulin or HOMA-IR. Results were stronger in people with type 2 diabetes and with longer use, and variation between studies was moderate to high.

## Effect of Apple Cider Vinegar Intake on Body Composition in Humans with Type 2 Diabetes and/or Overweight: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/castagna-2025-41010525/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41010525/
Citation: Castagna A, Ferro Y, Noto FR, Bruno R et al (2025), Nutrients
- In Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety: Adults with overweight, obesity or type 2 diabetes in ten randomised trials of daily apple cider vinegar for at least 4 weeks (n=789). Daily apple cider vinegar reduced body weight, BMI and waist circumference slightly in the pooled results, with large differences between studies. Effects held when high-risk-of-bias trials were removed and were seen up to 12 weeks, at about 30 mL a day. The authors call it a possible short-term adjunct.

## Esophageal injury by apple cider vinegar tablets and subsequent evaluation of products
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hill-2005-15983536/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15983536/
Citation: Hill LL, Woodruff LH, Foote JC, Barreto-Alcoba M (2005), Journal of the American Dietetic Association
- In Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety: One adult who reported an adverse event, and eight apple cider vinegar tablet products tested (n=8). Apple cider vinegar tablets injured the oesophagus in one reported case. The eight products varied widely in tablet size, acidity, acid content and label claims, and the authors doubted whether apple cider vinegar was actually an ingredient in some of them.

## Retraction: Apple cider vinegar for weight management in lebanese adolescents and young adults with overweight and obesity: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bmj-2025-41789013/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41789013/
Citation: BMJ Nutrition, Prevention and Health (retraction notice) (2025), BMJ Nutrition, Prevention and Health
- In Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety: Lebanese adolescents and young adults with overweight and obesity (a 2024 randomised trial of apple cider vinegar for weight) (n=not applicable). BMJ Nutrition, Prevention and Health retracted its 2024 trial of apple cider vinegar for weight management in Lebanese young people. The notice I opened gives the DOI of the retracted article and no reasons in the part I read.

## Does Ashwagandha supplementation have a beneficial effect on the management of anxiety and stress? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/akhgarjand-2022-36017529/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36017529/
Citation: Akhgarjand C, Asoudeh F, Bagheri A, Kalantar Z et al (2022), Phytotherapy Research
- In Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions: Adults aged 25 to 48 in 12 randomised trials (country and ethnicity not stated in the abstract) (n=1002). Ashwagandha lowered anxiety and stress scores compared with placebo. The studies disagreed a lot with each other (heterogeneity above 80 per cent), so the size of the effect is uncertain.

## Effect of Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/cheah-2021-34559859/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34559859/
Citation: Cheah KL, Norhayati MN, Husniati Yaacob L, Abdul Rahman R (2021), PLoS One
- In Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions: Adults aged 18 and over in five randomised trials (insomnia subgroup included) (n=400). Ashwagandha extract gave a small but significant improvement in overall sleep (standardised mean difference -0.59). Effects were larger in people diagnosed with insomnia, at 600 mg a day or more, and over eight weeks or more.

## Ashwagandha-induced liver injury: A case series from Iceland and the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bjornsson-2020-31991029/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31991029/
Citation: Bjornsson HK, Bjornsson ES, Avula B, Khan IA et al (2020), Liver International
- In Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions: Five adults (mean age 43, three men) with liver injury attributed to ashwagandha supplements, from Iceland and the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (n=5). All five became jaundiced with nausea, lethargy, itching or abdominal discomfort after 2 to 12 weeks. The injury was cholestatic or mixed. Itching and raised bilirubin lasted 5 to 20 weeks, no one developed liver failure, and liver tests returned to normal within 1 to 5 months in four of the five.

## Efficacy and Safety of Ashwagandha Root Extract in Subclinical Hypothyroid Patients: A Double-Blind, Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/sharma-2018-28829155/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28829155/
Citation: Sharma AK, Basu I, Singh S (2018), Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
- In Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions: Adults aged 18 to 50 with subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH), one hospital in Varanasi, India (n=50). TSH, T3 and T4 improved compared with placebo over 8 weeks. Four people withdrew (two from each group).

## Bridging diagnostic safety and mental health: a systematic review highlighting inequities in autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/srivarathan-2026-40854799/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40854799/
Citation: Srivarathan A, Bradford A, Shearkhani S, Heimlich L et al (2026), BMJ Quality & Safety
- In Autism and ADHD: being missed, delayed or misdiagnosed: 20 US studies of inequities in diagnosing mental disorders; 17 were about autism (n=20 studies). Most diagnostic errors were delayed diagnosis. Eleven factors contributed: limited health literacy was the leading cause in recognising symptoms, insurance coverage delayed engagement, provider bias during history-taking was a key cause of delays and misdiagnoses, and culturally inequivalent assessment measures might cause misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis for Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino people.

## Racial Differences in the Prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gallin-2025-38941049/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38941049/
Citation: Gallin Z, Kolevzon AM, Reichenberg A, Hankerson SH et al (2025), Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
- In Autism and ADHD: being missed, delayed or misdiagnosed: 17 US population-based birth-cohort studies of autism prevalence by race, at least 1,000 cases each (n=17 studies). Before 2010, prevalence was highest in White children in nearly all birth cohorts. In the 2010 birth cohort, prevalence per 1,000 was 22.3 for Black, 22.5 for Hispanic, 22.2 for Asian/Pacific Islander and 21.2 for White children, and the gap grew in 2012. Possible drivers include changes in screening and diagnosis, insurance policy and education.

## Determinants of marginal traction alopecia in African girls and women
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khumalo-2008-18694677/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18694677/
Citation: Khumalo NP, Jessop S, Gumedze F, Ehrlich R (2008), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Babies' and children's hair: 574 African schoolgirls (6-21 years) and 604 women (18-86 years), South Africa (n=1178). Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).

Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).
- In Chemical relaxers and hair straighteners: 574 African schoolgirls and 604 women, South Africa (n=1178). Traction added to relaxed hair carried the highest odds of traction alopecia (odds ratio 3.47, 95% CI 1.94-6.20) against natural hair.

Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).

- In Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles: 574 African schoolgirls (6-21 years) and 604 women (18-86 years), South Africa (n=1178). TA was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20). Odds were higher with braiding-related than chemical-related symptoms. Only 18.9% of people with TA had never had hairdressing-related symptoms.
- In Wigs, weaves and lace glue: 574 African schoolgirls (6-21 years) and 604 women (18-86 years), South Africa (n=1178). Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).

## Hair care practices and their association with scalp and hair disorders in African American girls
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rucker-2011-20728245/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20728245/
Citation: Rucker Wright D, Gathers R, Kapke A, Johnson D et al (2011), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Babies' and children's hair: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.
- In Braids, twists and extensions: tension, how long, itch: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.
- In Dry, itchy, flaky scalp and dandruff: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.
- In Locs: starting, washing and keeping them healthy: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.
- In Scalp oiling and greasing: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). 99% reported using hair oils or grease. Infrequent hair oil use was associated with seborrheic dermatitis (adjusted odds ratio 3.69, 95% CI 1.07-12.7). No association was found between hair grease use and tinea capitis, or between washing frequency and either condition.
- In Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US dermatology and non-dermatology clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). 99% used hair oils or grease, 80% hot combs and 42% chemical relaxers.
- In Wash day and routine for 4c hair: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics (n=201). Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.

## Interventions for infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (including cradle cap)
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/victoire-2019-30828791/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30828791/
Citation: Victoire A, Magin P et al (2019), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Babies' and children's hair: 310 children aged 0 to 24 months, six trials (n=310). Six trials compared oral biotin against placebo, proprietary products against placebo or control shampoo, and topical steroids against other products; the trials were short (10 to 42 days) and the results were based on very low-quality evidence.

## Skin care interventions in infants for preventing eczema and food allergy
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kelleher-2022-36373988/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36373988/
Citation: Kelleher MM, Phillips R, Brown SJ et al (2022), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Baby skin care (newborns and infants): Infants, mostly newborns, 8 of the 11 meta-analysed trials in babies at high risk of eczema or food allergy (33 trials, 25,827 babies identified; the eczema result rests on 7 trials, 3,075 infants); ethnicity not given in the abstract (n=3075). Skin care interventions during infancy probably do not change the risk of eczema by 1 to 3 years (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.31; moderate-certainty; 7 trials, 3,075 infants). They may increase IgE-mediated food allergy (RR 2.53, 0.99 to 6.49; low-certainty; 1 trial, 976 infants) and probably increase skin infection (RR 1.33, 1.01 to 1.75). Only 17 of 33 trials reported prespecified outcomes.
- In Eczema on dark skin (atopic eczema, including babies): Healthy infants, mostly newborns (33 randomised trials, 25,827 babies); ethnicity not given in the abstract (n=25827). With low to moderate certainty, emollients in the first year of life in healthy infants are probably not effective for preventing eczema, may increase food allergy and probably increase skin infection.

## Adansonia digitata L. (Baobab Fruit) Effect on Postprandial Glycemia in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rita-2022-35057579/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35057579/
Citation: Rita K, Bernardo MA, Silva ML, Brito J et al (2022), Nutrients
- In Baobab fruit: blood sugar, iron and vitamin C: 31 healthy adults in Portugal (n=31). The rise in blood glucose (incremental area under the curve) and the peak glucose were significantly lower in the baobab group than in the control group after a glucose load. The extract had high polyphenol content.

## The polyphenol-rich baobab fruit (Adansonia digitata L.) reduces starch digestion and glycemic response in humans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/coe-2013-24176228/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24176228/
Citation: Coe SA, Clegg M, Armengol M, Ryan L (2013), Nutrition Research
- In Baobab fruit: blood sugar, iron and vitamin C: Healthy adults in the UK (numbers not in the abstract) (n=not stated in the abstract). Baobab fruit extract at both low and high doses significantly reduced the glucose response to white bread. It had no significant effect on satiety or energy expenditure. In the lab it also reduced starch digestion.

## Can the supplementary consumption of baobab (Adansonia digitata L.) fruit pulp improve the hemoglobin levels and iron status of schoolchildren in Kenya? Findings of a randomized controlled intervention trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/evang-2021-33355689/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33355689/
Citation: Evang EC, Habte TY, Owino WO, Krawinkel MB (2021), European Journal of Nutrition
- In Baobab fruit: blood sugar, iron and vitamin C: 58 Kenyan schoolchildren aged 6 to 12 with haemoglobin below 12.2 g/dl (n=58 (29 per group)). Haemoglobin, ferritin and soluble transferrin receptor did not differ significantly between the groups. Haemoglobin rose 2.2% with baobab and fell 1.2% in the control group, a difference the authors did not find significant.

## Racial bias in pain assessment and treatment recommendations, and false beliefs about biological differences between blacks and whites
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hoffman-2016-27044069/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044069/
Citation: Hoffman KM, Trawalter S, Axt JR, Oliver MN (2016), PNAS
- In Being believed by doctors, and pain: White laypeople and white medical students and residents, US (n=not stated in the abstract (two studies)). Half of a sample of white medical students and residents endorsed false beliefs about biological differences between Black and white people. Those who did rated the Black patient's pain lower and made less accurate treatment recommendations; those who did not rated the Black patient's pain higher and showed no bias in treatment recommendations.

## Racial and ethnic disparities in the management of acute pain in US emergency departments: Meta-analysis and systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lee-2019-31186154/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31186154/
Citation: Lee P, Le Saux M, Siegel R et al (2019), American Journal of Emergency Medicine
- In Being believed by doctors, and pain: 7,070 white, 3,125 Black, 1,538 Hispanic patients across 14 US emergency department studies (n=14 studies). Black patients were less likely than white patients to receive analgesia for acute pain (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.83).

## Racial Disparities in Opioid Prescribing in the United States from 2011 to 2021: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hirani-2024-39529944/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39529944/
Citation: Hirani S, Benkli B, Odonkor C et al (2024), Journal of Pain Research
- In Being believed by doctors, and pain: 12 studies in the meta-analysis, 43 in the review, US adult patients (n=12 and 43 studies). Compared with white patients, Black patients were less likely to receive opioid analgesia (odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.94). The authors describe persistent disparities despite a decade since the previous review.

## Masculinity and Race-Related Factors as Barriers to Health Help-Seeking Among African American Men
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/powell-2016-27337619/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27337619/
Citation: Powell W, Adams LB, Cole-Lewis Y et al (2016), Behavioral Medicine
- In Black men, depression and getting support: 458 African American men, recruited mainly from US barbershops (n=458). More frequent everyday racism and higher masculinity norm salience went with higher barriers to health help-seeking. Everyday racism's link to barriers was partly explained by a lower sense of control and more depressive symptoms. The authors say interventions should address masculinity norms and also threats to sense of control and the effects of everyday racism.
