Estimated prevalence above age 70 was 6% in white, 16% in black and 3% in Asian populations. Men were 1.37 times more likely than women to have it.

## When non-Whiteness becomes a condition
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/merz-2021-33181819/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33181819/
Citation: Merz LE, Achebe M (2021), Blood
- In Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test: People of African ancestry and the haematology reference-range literature (n=not applicable). Benign ethnic neutropenia (neutrophils under 1,500 per microlitre with no extra infection risk) is most common in people of African ancestry, and African reference ranges say counts under 1,500 are common and harmless. Duffy-null explains it and is seen in 80% to 100% of people of sub-Saharan African ancestry and under 1% of those of European descent. The authors say labelling common non-White phenotypes abnormal contributes to systemic racism in haematology.

## Revised WHO Guidelines on Hemoglobin Cutoffs to Define Anemia in Individuals and Populations
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khurana-2024-38910369/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38910369/
Citation: Khurana R, Kanvinde P, Mudaliar S (2024), Indian Pediatrics
- In Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test: WHO 2024 guideline on haemoglobin cut-offs (n=not applicable). WHO proposed revised haemoglobin cut-offs for children aged 6 to 23 months, pregnant women in the second trimester and people living at elevated altitude, to raise sensitivity and make diagnosis uniform; there were no major changes in other domains.

## African hair growth parameters
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/loussouarn-2001-11531795/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11531795/
Citation: Loussouarn G (2001), British Journal of Dermatology
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: 38 adults from Central and West Africa (n=38). Mean growth 256 micrometres a day against 396 in Caucasian volunteers (comparison from earlier work); density 190 against 227 hairs per cm squared. By my arithmetic that is about 0.8 cm a month against 1.2.

## Diversity in human hair growth, diameter, colour and shape. An in vivo study on young adults from 24 different ethnic groups observed in the five continents
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/loussouarn-2016-27019510/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27019510/
Citation: Loussouarn G et al (2016), European Journal of Dermatology
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: 2,249 young adults from 24 ethnic groups (n=2249). African hair had lower density and slower growth than the other groups; Asian hair was thicker and faster.

## What is normal black African hair? A light and scanning electron-microscopic study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khumalo-2000-11050586/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11050586/
Citation: Khumalo NP et al (2000), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: 12 African volunteers, Oxford; over 2,000 hairs (n=12). Afro-textured shafts knotted and fractured far more often when combed: 10 to 16% of shafts knotted against 0.15% in other groups.

## Apparent fragility of African hair is unrelated to the cystine-rich protein distribution: a cytochemical electron microscopic study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khumalo-2005-15810890/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15810890/
Citation: Khumalo NP, Dawber RP, Ferguson DJ (2005), Experimental Dermatology
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: African hair samples, electron microscopy (n=not stated). Cystine-rich proteins were distributed as in other hair types, so fragility was not explained by a protein defect; the authors read the damage as grooming trauma rather than inherent weakness.
- In Wash day and routine for 4c hair: African hair samples, electron microscopy (n=not stated). Cystine-rich proteins were distributed as in other hair types, so fragility was not explained by a protein defect; the authors read the damage as grooming trauma rather than inherent weakness.

## Quantifying the impact of braiding and combing on the integrity of natural African hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/molamodi-2021-33605448/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33605448/
Citation: Molamodi et al (2021), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: 30 women (15 frequent braiders against 15 comparison women); hair fibres studied in the laboratory (n=30). Cuticle damage rose in a linear trend with the number of combing strokes; 480 strokes did more cuticle damage than frequent braiding. Frequent braiders had weaker, thinner fibres.
- In Wash day and routine for 4c hair: 30 women (15 frequent braiders against 15 comparison women); hair fibres studied in the laboratory (n=30). Cuticle damage rose in a linear trend with the number of combing strokes; 480 strokes did more cuticle damage than frequent braiding. Frequent braiders had weaker, thinner fibres.

## How different is human hair? A critical appraisal of the reported differences in global hair fibre characteristics and properties towards defining a more relevant framework for hair type classification
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/daniels-2023-36374002/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36374002/
Citation: Daniels G, Fraser A, Westgate G (2023), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Hair breakage, growth and keeping length: Review of hair-fibre studies across hair types (n=not stated). Curlier hair has a smaller, elliptical cross-section. Fragility is attributed to knotting and cracking rather than to a structural weakness. Sources disagree on water uptake. The review calls the eight-type curl system possibly too complex to reproduce.
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: Review of hair-fibre studies across hair types (n=not stated). Curlier hair has a smaller, elliptical cross-section. Fragility is attributed to knotting and cracking rather than to a structural weakness. Sources disagree on water uptake. The review calls the eight-type curl system possibly too complex to reproduce.

## Rosemary oil vs minoxidil 2% for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia: a randomized comparative trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/panahi-2015-25842469/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25842469/
Citation: Panahi Y, Taghizadeh M et al (2015), Skinmed
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: 100 Iranian patients with androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) (n=100). No significant change at 3 months in either group. At 6 months both groups had a significant rise in hair count, with no significant difference between them. Scalp itching was higher in both groups than at baseline and more frequent with minoxidil.

## Rosmagain™ as a Natural Therapeutic for Hair Regrowth and Scalp Health: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Three-Armed, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/patel-2025-40656290/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40656290/
Citation: Patel et al (2025), Cureus
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: 90 healthy adults (18 to 55) in India (n=90). The rosemary blends improved phototrichogram hair growth rate, thickness, density and length against coconut oil (p<0.0001); growth rate rose from 0.22 to 0.34 mm a day in the rosemary-lavender arm.

## An Exploratory Preclinical In Vivo Pilot Study Evaluating the Hair Growth-Promoting Effects of Rosmarinus officinalis and Ricinus communis Combination
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mathenge-2026-42112722/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42112722/
Citation: Mathenge et al (2026), BioMed Research International
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: 15 mice (n=15). A combination of rosemary and castor oils was tested for hair growth in mice (three animals per group).

## Herbal Remedies for Hair Loss: A Review of Efficacy and Safety
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ahmed-2025-40771449/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40771449/
Citation: Ahmed et al (2025), Skin Appendage Disorders
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: Review of herbal remedies for hair loss (n=not stated). Studies suggest potential benefits for some herbs in androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium and alopecia areata, but many studies have small samples, short treatment periods and no long-term follow-up; larger randomised trials are needed.

## A Review of the Use of Biotin for Hair Loss
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/patel-2017-28879195/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28879195/
Citation: Patel DP, Swink SM et al (2017), Skin Appendage Disorders
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: Published case reports and randomised trials of biotin for hair and nails (n=not stated). Eighteen reported cases of biotin use for hair and nail changes; in all of them the patient had an underlying cause of poor hair or nail growth and improved. The authors found limited research showing biotin works in healthy people and propose there is insufficient evidence for supplementation in healthy individuals.

## Evaluating the Effectiveness of Commercial Oral Supplements for Hair Growth: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/alanazi-2026-41954038/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41954038/
Citation: Alanazi et al (2026), Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: 967 adults with alopecia or hair thinning, 14 studies (n=967). Branded supplements (such as Nutrafol and Viviscal) improved anagen hair density against placebo, but total hair count showed no significant difference (p=0.06). The authors say more rigorous, independent research is needed.

## The implications of biotin supplementation on multiple sclerosis, hair loss conditions, and thyroid disorders
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bhimireddy-2026-42933321/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42933321/
Citation: Bhimireddy et al (2026), Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders
- In Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin: Review of biotin supplementation (n=not stated). Over-the-counter biotin doses of 5 to 20 mg a day can interfere with thyroid function tests and other lab immunoassays, causing falsely abnormal results and potential misdiagnoses.

## True porosity measurement of hair: a new way to study hair damage mechanisms
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hessefort-2008-18818850/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18818850/
Citation: Hessefort Y, Holland BT, Cloud RW (2008), Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Hair porosity and moisture: Hair fibre samples (laboratory) (n=not stated). Bleach damage and UV damage change hair porosity by different pathways; bleach nearly triples surface area in the first minute, then it falls, while UV damage shows an immediate loss then gradual increase. This defines porosity as a measurable pore property of the fibre.

## Methods adapted to evaluate products for textured hair: Shine, curl shrinkage, flexibility and consumer-perceived hair porosity
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/sorrells-2026-42971783/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42971783/
Citation: Sorrells L, Senak L, Kang X, Abegunde A et al (2026), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Hair porosity and moisture: Textured hair tresses (laboratory, industry methods paper) (n=not stated). The authors describe a refined contact-angle method to measure consumer-perceived hair porosity in textured hair. It is a method paper and tests no routine.

## Use of single fibre fatiguing experiments to understand breakage in textured hair Part I
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/evans-2026-42971788/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42971788/
Citation: Evans TA (2026), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Hair porosity and moisture: Very curly textured hair against straight Caucasian hair (laboratory) (n=not stated). Textured hair showed a far greater tendency to break under fatigue than straight hair, some fibres failed after very few cycles, and higher grooming forces produced exponentially faster breakage.

## Current research on ethnic hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/franbourg-2003-12789163/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12789163/
Citation: Franbourg A, Hallegot P, Baltenneck F, Toutain C et al (2003), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Hair porosity and moisture: Hair from Caucasian, Asian and African subjects (laboratory) (n=not stated). No differences in the intimate structure of the fibres were observed among the three hair types, whereas geometry, mechanical properties and water swelling differed by ethnic origin.

## Classification of High Curl Pattern Hair: A Systematic Review and Clinical Perspective
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/callender-2026-41928381/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41928381/
Citation: Callender V, Burgess C, Harvey VM, Heath C et al (2026), Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology
- In Hair porosity and moisture: Hair shape classification systems (n=4 systems). Four mainstream classification systems exist (Andre Walker, LOIS, FIA, L'Oreal). The authors state hair type classification is under-used in clinical practice and argue it should be based on shape criteria rather than race.
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: Systematic review of curl classification (n=not stated). Curl classification may have predictive value for scalp disease such as seborrhoeic dermatitis, but further validation is required.

## Postpartum Telogen Effluvium Unmasking Additional Latent Hair Loss Disorders
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/galal-2024-38779373/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38779373/
Citation: Galal et al (2024), Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
- In Hair shedding after pregnancy, illness or stress: 200 women with postpartum hair loss, Egypt (n=200). Only 9.5% had telogen effluvium alone; 56.0% also had androgenetic alopecia, 6.5% also had traction alopecia and 28.0% had all three. The authors say postpartum telogen effluvium may be associated with other hair loss disorders.
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: 200 women with postpartum hair loss, Egypt (n=200). Only 9.5% had telogen effluvium alone; 56.0% also had androgenetic alopecia, 6.5% also had traction alopecia and 28.0% had all three. The authors say postpartum telogen effluvium may be associated with other hair loss disorders.

## Postpartum hair loss is associated with anxiety
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hirose-2024-39462180/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39462180/
Citation: Hirose et al (2024), Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
- In Hair shedding after pregnancy, illness or stress: Postpartum women, Japan (n=not stated). Postpartum hair loss was associated with anxiety symptoms.

## Comparative Study of a Novel Tool for Follicular Unit Extraction for Individuals with Afro-textured Hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/umar-2016-27757365/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27757365/
Citation: Umar S et al (2016), Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open
- In Hair transplants in afro-textured hair: 18 patients with tightly curled afro-textured hair (n=18). Sharp and dull conventional rotary punches failed or had excessive transection rates in 8 patients; a 2-pronged curved non-rotary punch had the best transection rate, below 5%, in all instances.

## Hair transplantation in the surgical treatment of central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/callender-2014-25207763/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25207763/
Citation: Callender VD et al (2014), Dermatologic Surgery
- In Hair transplants in afro-textured hair: 2 African American women with end-stage CCCA (n=2). Hair grew at the recipient sites from 4 to 5 months, with no scarring in recipient or donor areas; the authors call transplantation safe and well tolerated in end-stage CCCA with no inflammation on biopsy.

## Advances and challenges in hair restoration of curly Afrocentric hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rogers-2014-24680003/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24680003/
Citation: Rogers N, Callender V (2014), Dermatologic Clinics
- In Hair transplants in afro-textured hair: Review of hair restoration surgery in curly Afrocentric hair (n=not stated). Hair structure differs between groups, and curly hair poses specific challenges and special considerations when surgery is considered, including curvature, grooming techniques, instruments and complications. The abstract gives no success rates.
- In Receding hairline and hair transplants in Black men: Review of hair restoration surgery in curly Afrocentric hair (n=not stated). Hair structure differs between groups, and curly hair poses specific challenges and special considerations when surgery is considered, including curvature, grooming techniques, instruments and complications. The abstract gives no success rates.

## Reimagining Hair Science: A New Approach to Classify Curly Hair Phenotypes via New Quantitative Geometric and Structural Mechanical Parameters
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gaines-2023-37212612/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37212612/
Citation: Gaines et al (2023), Accounts of Chemical Research
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: Review of hair classification, including the Walker system (n=not stated). The Walker 1 to 4C system is described as the existing gold standard in practice but "relies upon qualitative classification measures, making the system vague and ambiguous".

## Shape variability and classification of human hair: a worldwide approach
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/de-2007-18078200/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18078200/
Citation: De la Mettrie R et al (2007), Human Biology
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: 1,442 people from 18 countries (n=1442). Eight curl types were defined from three measured descriptors, deliberately without reference to ethnicity.

## All hairstyles are not created equal: What the dermatologist needs to know about black hairstyling practices and the risk of traction alopecia (TA)
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/haskin-2016-27114262/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27114262/
Citation: Haskin A et al (2016), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: Black hairstyling practices and traction alopecia (n=not stated). The review stratifies hair care and styling practices into high-, moderate- and low-risk categories for traction alopecia, with a diagnostic approach and conservative management guidance.

## Hairstyling Practices to Prevent Hair Damage and Alopecia in Women of African Descent
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/geisler-2022-35659800/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35659800/
Citation: Geisler AN et al (2022), Cutis
- In Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you: Women of African descent, hairstyling and hair damage (n=not stated). Highly textured hair is more susceptible to breakage because of an increased proportion of spirals and fewer elastic fibres anchoring follicles to the dermis; the review gives an overview of hairstyles so physicians can spot high-risk ones and suggest safer alternatives.

## A study of head lice among primary schoolchildren in Kenya
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/chunge-1986-3726995/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3726995/
Citation: Chunge RN et al (1986), Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
- In Head lice in afro-textured hair and locs: 1,270 schoolchildren, 33 urban and rural primary schools, Kenya (n=1270). 17.1% were infested (8% with living lice or nits). Negroid children had lower infestation rates than non-Negroid children, and the authors say the criterion seems to be hair type. Infestation was higher in older children, in children with longer hair and in those who washed less; most had one or two lice.

## Pediculosis capitis risk factors in schoolchildren: hair thickness and hair length
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/valero-2024-37967666/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37967666/
Citation: Valero MA et al (2024), Acta Tropica
- In Head lice in afro-textured hair and locs: 310 schoolchildren aged 1 to 13, Paraná, Brazil (n=310). Prevalence of head lice was 49.35%. Longer and thicker hair raised the risk; hair colour, shape and scale type also changed the risk when added to the model.

## Over-the-counter Pediculus humanus capitis treatment: The nit comb is not appropriate for all hair types!
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/shea-2023-36241488/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36241488/
Citation: Shea LA et al (2023), Journal of the American Pharmacists Association
- In Head lice in afro-textured hair and locs: US over-the-counter head lice products (n=not stated). The authors say the nit comb would not suit an individual with African hair, yet all OTC product instructions require it and do not address African hair. They suggest pharmacists counsel applying the active formulation and not using the nit comb afterwards.

## Characterization of formaldehyde exposure resulting from the use of four professional hair straightening products
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/pierce-2011-22035353/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22035353/
Citation: Pierce JS et al (2011), Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene
- In Heat, silk press, keratin treatments and colour: Four professional keratin smoothing products applied to wigs on mannequins in a simulated salon (n=88). Airborne formaldehyde averaged 0.08 to 3.47 ppm during blow-drying and 0.08 to 1.05 ppm during flat-ironing. Bulk samples held 11.5% formaldehyde in Brazilian Blowout, 8.3% in Global Keratin, 3% in Coppola and 0% in La Brasiliana, and other products that break down into formaldehyde were found in three of the four.
- In Relaxer, texturiser, perm and keratin: what is the difference: Four professional keratin smoothing products applied to wigs on mannequins in a simulated salon (n=88). Airborne formaldehyde averaged 0.08 to 3.47 ppm during blow-drying and 0.08 to 1.05 ppm during flat-ironing. Bulk samples held 11.5% formaldehyde in Brazilian Blowout, 8.3% in Global Keratin, 3% in Coppola and 0% in La Brasiliana, and other products that break down into formaldehyde were found in three of the four.

## Tolerance of very hot humid environments by highly acclimatized Bantu at rest
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/wyndham-1968-5642646/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/5642646/
Citation: Wyndham CH, Williams CG, Morrison JF, Heyns AJ et al (1968), British Journal of Industrial Medicine
- In Heat, sweating and hydration: Groups of 10 highly acclimatised Bantu men resting in hot, humid rooms (n=groups of 10 men). Rectal temperature rose steadily at 102 and 104 F wet bulb and reached a plateau at lower temperatures. Sweat rate rose from 130 ml per hour at 96 F to 875 ml per hour at 104 F; water intake lagged behind sweating at the highest temperatures. There was no comparison group in the abstract.

## Ethnicity and temperature regulation
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lambert-2008-19209002/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19209002/
Citation: Lambert MI, Mann T, Dugas JP (2008), Medicine and Sport Science
- In Heat, sweating and hydration: Narrative review of ethnicity and temperature regulation (n=not applicable). Phenotypic differences between groups living in different climates are very clear, but genotypic differences are less easy to discern because of the difficulty of controlling environmental and lifestyle factors. The authors say it is reasonable to assume more genetic differences will be found as data become available.

## Effect of Hibiscus sabdariffaon blood pressure and electrolyte profile of mild to moderate hypertensive Nigerians: A comparative study with hydrochlorothiazide
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/nwachukwu-2015-26289514/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26289514/
Citation: Nwachukwu DC, Aneke E, Nwachukwu NZ, Obika LF et al (2015), Nigerian Journal of Clinical Practice
- In Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure: 80 newly diagnosed, untreated Nigerian adults with mild to moderate hypertension, Enugu (n=80). Both hibiscus and the drug lowered blood pressure compared with placebo. The authors reported hibiscus as more effective than the drug and without electrolyte imbalance, and the fall persisted after withdrawal. No side effects were reported.

## Hibiscus sabdariffa L. tea (tisane) lowers blood pressure in prehypertensive and mildly hypertensive adults
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mckay-2010-20018807/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20018807/
Citation: McKay DL, Chen CY, Saltzman E, Blumberg JB (2010), Journal of Nutrition
- In Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure: 65 pre- and mildly hypertensive US adults aged 30 to 70, not on blood-pressure drugs (n=65). Systolic pressure fell 7.2 mmHg on hibiscus against 1.3 mmHg on placebo (P=0.030). Diastolic did not differ from placebo.

## Efficacy and safety of Hibiscus sabdariffa in cardiometabolic health: An overview of reviews and updated dose-response meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/norouzzadeh-2025-39870328/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39870328/
Citation: Norouzzadeh M, Hasan Rashedi M, Azizi MH, Teymoori F et al (2025), Complementary Therapies in Medicine
- In Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure: 1,797 people across 26 randomised trials (Iran, Mexico, Egypt, Nigeria and others) (n=1797). Hibiscus lowered systolic and diastolic pressure compared with placebo and other teas, dose-dependently, with no significant difference from antihypertensive drugs. The authors rated the credibility of a fall of more than 10 mmHg as moderate. The authors note long-term and therapeutic-dose safety needs monitoring.

## Roselle for hypertension in adults
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/pattanittum-2021-34837382/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34837382/
Citation: Pattanittum P, Ngamjarus C, Buttramee F, Somboonporn C (2021), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure: Adults with high blood pressure; strict Cochrane criteria (n=52). Only one trial met the criteria (60 people with type 2 diabetes, 8 weeks, capsules). Effect on systolic pressure was 1.65 mmHg (95% CI -7.89 to 11.19), very low certainty. The review concludes evidence is insufficient to say whether roselle lowers blood pressure.

## Is the blood pressure of people from African origin adults in the UK higher or lower than that in European origin white people? A review of cross-sectional data
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/agyemang-2003-12874609/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12874609/
Citation: Agyemang C, Bhopal R (2003), Journal of Human Hypertension
- In High blood pressure in Black adults: 14 UK studies, mostly London, of adults of African descent against White adults (n=14 studies). Most studies found higher mean blood pressure and higher rates of hypertension in men and women of African descent. Ethnic group differences in blood pressure were not present in the younger age groups. The authors say differences in age, definitions and the mix of Afro-Caribbean and West African groups explain much of the inconsistency between studies.

## Divergence with age in blood pressure in African-Caribbean and white populations in England: implications for screening for hypertension
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/agyemang-2012-21881618/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21881618/
Citation: Agyemang C, Humphry RW, Bhopal R (2012), American Journal of Hypertension
- In High blood pressure in Black adults: 22,723 adults in the Health Surveys for England (1,379 African-Caribbean, 21,344 White) (n=22723). African-Caribbean blood pressure crossed above White at about 30-40 years. At 20-29 African-Caribbean men were advantaged, but not after that. African-Caribbean women had higher BMI than White women; men did not differ much. The authors advise extra vigilance in screening African-Caribbean patients from age 30 and call the mechanism "still mysterious".
- In Weight, BMI and losing weight safely: 22,723 adults in the Health Surveys for England (1,379 African-Caribbean) (n=22723). African-Caribbean women had higher BMI than white women; there was little difference in BMI in men.

## Antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV prevention in heterosexual men and women
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/baeten-2012-22784037/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22784037/
Citation: Baeten JM, Donnell D, Ndase P, Mugo NR et al (2012), New England Journal of Medicine
- In HIV prevention, testing and PrEP: 4,758 heterosexual HIV-serodiscordant couples in Kenya and Uganda; the HIV-negative partner (62% male) took tenofovir, tenofovir-emtricitabine or placebo (n=4758). Of 82 HIV infections in the HIV-negative partners, 17 were in the tenofovir group (0.65 per 100 person-years), 13 in the tenofovir-emtricitabine group (0.50) and 52 in the placebo group (1.99). That is a 67% reduction with tenofovir (95% CI 44 to 81) and 75% with the combination (95% CI 55 to 87).

## Twice-Yearly Lenacapavir or Daily F/TAF for HIV Prevention in Cisgender Women
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bekker-2024-39046157/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39046157/
Citation: Bekker LG, Das M, Abdool Karim Q, Ahmed K et al (2024), New England Journal of Medicine
- In HIV prevention, testing and PrEP: 5,338 HIV-negative adolescent girls and young women in South Africa and Uganda (n=5338). 55 HIV infections occurred: none among 2,134 on lenacapavir (0 per 100 person-years; 95% CI 0.00 to 0.19), 39 among 2,136 on F/TAF (2.02) and 16 among 1,068 on F/TDF (1.69). Background incidence in the screened population was 2.41 per 100 person-years. Lenacapavir was significantly lower than background and than F/TDF; F/TAF did not differ significantly from background. The authors note gaps in uptake, adherence and persistence of PrEP among cisgender women.

## Rosacea in black South Africans with skin phototypes V and VI
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dlova-2017-28639713/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28639713/
Citation: Dlova NC, Mosam A (2017), Clinical and Experimental Dermatology
- In How skin conditions look on dark skin (redness, rashes, rosacea, sunburn): 15 Black South Africans (phototypes V and VI) diagnosed with rosacea among 6,700 patients over 8 years (n=15). Rosacea was rare in this clinic (0.2% of patients). Those with phototype VI mostly had skin-coloured papules; those with phototype V had erythema, telangiectasia and red papules; 10 of 15 (67%) had granulomatous rosacea on histology and 5 (33%) declined a facial biopsy. 5 (33%) were HIV positive and 5 (33%) had used topical steroids, so the group is not a clean picture of rosacea alone. The authors say a high index of suspicion is needed because classic erythema and telangiectasia are hard to discern.

## Rosacea in skin of color: not a rare diagnosis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/al-dabagh-2014-25526008/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25526008/
Citation: Al-Dabagh A, Davis SA, McMichael AJ, Feldman SR (2014), Dermatology Online Journal
- In How skin conditions look on dark skin (redness, rashes, rosacea, sunburn): US national ambulatory care survey 1993-2010 (n=not stated). 2.0% of patients with a rosacea diagnosis were Black. When Black patients attended with "other diseases of the skin", rosacea was the diagnosis for 2.2% against 8.3% of White patients; the authors suggest underdiagnosis in skin of colour.

## Skin Tone Analysis for Representation in Educational Materials (STAR-ED) using machine learning
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/tadesse-2023-37596324/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37596324/
Citation: Tadesse GA et al (2023), npj Digital Medicine
- In How skin conditions look on dark skin (redness, rashes, rosacea, sunburn): Dermatology textbooks (machine-learning audit) (n=not stated). Fitzpatrick V-VI images made up only 10.5% of all skin images.

## Incidence and characteristics of angioedema associated with enalapril
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kostis-2005-16043683/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043683/
Citation: Kostis JB, Kim HJ, Rusnak J, Casale T et al (2005), Archives of Internal Medicine
- In How some medicines work differently by gene: 12,557 people with hypertension in a randomised, double-blind trial of enalapril 5 to 40 mg daily (n=12557). Angioedema occurred in 86 people (0.68%). Black race (odds ratio 2.88, 95% CI 1.72 to 4.82), history of drug rash (3.78), age over 65 (1.60) and seasonal allergies (1.79) were independent risk factors. Incidence was 3.6 per 1,000 patients per month soon after starting and fell to 0.4. Fatal angioedema or angioedema needing airway protection did not occur.

## Risk factors for angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor angioedema in a South African population
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/day-2025-41189626/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41189626/
Citation: Day C, Mapahla L, Ribeiro M, Deetlefs M et al (2025), Frontiers in Allergy
- In How some medicines work differently by gene: 237 people with ACE inhibitor angioedema and 466 drug-tolerant controls in Cape Town, South Africa (n=703). Cases more often had Black genetic ancestry than controls (53% against 29%, P under 0.001). Only 31.1% of angioedema occurred within 30 days of starting, and the median time to angioedema was 6.9 years, so it can start long after starting treatment. The authors describe ACE inhibitors as having proven mortality and morbidity benefit.

## Meta-analysis of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema identifies novel risk locus
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mathey-2024-38300190/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38300190/
Citation: Mathey CM, Maj C, Eriksson N, Krebs K et al (2024), Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
- In How some medicines work differently by gene: More than 1,000 European patients with ACE inhibitor angioedema from 8 cohorts, plus an African-American cohort (n=more than 1000). Three genome-wide significant risk loci were found, one new (20q11.22). Highlighted genes included BDKRB2 and F5. Lead variants showed similar effect sizes and direction in an African-American cohort.

## CYP2D6 allele frequency in European Caucasians, Asians, Africans and their descendants
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bradford-2002-11972444/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11972444/
Citation: Bradford LD (2002), Pharmacogenomics
- In How some medicines work differently by gene: Published allele-frequency studies of CYP2D6 in European, Asian and African populations (n=not stated in the abstract). Functional alleles are about 71% in European Caucasians, about 50% in Asians and about 50% in Africans and African Americans. Reduced-function alleles are about 35% in African populations (mainly *17); non-functional alleles are 14.5% in African Americans and 6.3% in Africans. Non-functional and reduced-function alleles make up about half of alleles in Black populations, with greater variety.

## Genetic variants associated with warfarin dose in African-American individuals: a genome-wide association study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/perera-2013-23755828/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23755828/
Citation: Perera MA, Cavallari LH, Limdi NA, Gamazon ER et al (2013), Lancet
- In How some medicines work differently by gene: 533 African American adults on stable warfarin (discovery) and 432 (replication) (n=965). VKORC1 and CYP2C9 explain less dose variation in people of African descent than in Europeans or Asians. A novel variant in the CYP2C cluster (rs12777823) reached genome-wide significance in the discovery cohort and was confirmed in the replication cohort.

## Cold-water immersion (cryotherapy) for preventing and treating muscle soreness after exercise
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bleakley-2012-22336838/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22336838/
Citation: Bleakley C, McDonough S, Gardner E, Baxter GD et al (2012), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 366 participants in 17 small trials, mainly athletes and active adults (not selected by ancestry) (n=366). Compared with rest, cold-water immersion reduced muscle soreness at 24, 48, 72 and 96 hours (for example standardised mean difference -0.55 at 24 hours). The authors rate study quality as low; the trials varied in temperature, duration and exercise, and most did not report active surveillance of adverse events.

## Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/roberts-2015-26174323/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26174323/
Citation: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, Figueiredo VC et al (2015), Journal of Physiology
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 21 physically active men (12-week study) and 9 men (muscle biopsy study) (n=30). Strength and muscle mass increased more with active recovery than with cold-water immersion, and several markers of muscle growth signalling were lower after cold-water immersion.

## Cold-water exposure and psychological outcomes in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ngandeu-2026-42819812/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42819812/
Citation: Ngandeu Schepanski S, Batta F, Schroter M, Ngoumou GB et al (2026), Frontiers in Physiology
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 13 studies, 4,105 adults (cold showers, immersion, winter swimming) (n=4105). Pooled estimates generally favoured cold exposure for depressive symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, but confidence intervals were wide, several estimates shrank in controlled-only analyses, and most studies had serious or critical risk of bias. The authors state the evidence does not establish that cold-water exposure improves mood or stress and that it should not be regarded as a standalone psychological treatment. Anxiety showed little consistent benefit.

## The effect of ethnicity on the vascular responses to cold exposure of the extremities
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/maley-2014-25081130/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25081130/
Citation: Maley MJ, Eglin CM, House JR, Tipton MJ (2014), European Journal of Applied Physiology
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 10 Caucasian, 10 Asian and 10 men of African descent (AFD), UK laboratory (n=30). Men of African descent had more intense and prolonged finger vasoconstriction during hand immersion than Caucasian men; skin blood flow during immersion was 24% (AFD) against 42% (Caucasian), and rewarming was slower (2.5 against 3.2 degrees C per minute). Cold sensation thresholds were similar. The authors note cold injuries are more prevalent in people of African descent and suggest this sensitivity may explain it.

## Retrospective analysis of the ethnic origins of male British army soldiers with peripheral cold weather injury
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/burgess-2009-19817081/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19817081/
Citation: Burgess JE, Macfarlane F (2009), Journal of the Royal Army Medical Corps
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 311 male British Army soldiers assessed at a cold injury clinic; the paper compares "African Americans", Pacific Islanders and Gurkhas with Caucasians (n=311). Those classed as African Americans (the paper's own term, in the British Army; the abstract does not say how ethnicity was assigned) had a relative incidence of cold injury of 30.36 (95% CI 25.82-35.70) against Caucasian soldiers and were more severely affected (mean score 5.39 against 4.24).

## Habituation of the cold shock response: A systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/barwood-2024-38211547/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211547/
Citation: Barwood MJ, Eglin C, Hills SP, Johnston N et al (2024), Journal of Thermal Biology
- In Ice baths and cold exposure: 17 groups, 145 participants in cold-shock response analyses (n=145). Cold-water immersion triggers a reflex cold shock response with hyperventilation, increased cardiac arrhythmias and increased drowning risk. Repeated immersions reduced these responses after about four immersions.

## Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/semnani-azad-2025-40533200/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40533200/
Citation: Semnani-Azad Z, Khan TA, Chiavaroli L, Chen V et al (2025), BMJ
- In Intermittent fasting for weight and health: Adults in 99 randomised trials (720 healthy, 5,862 with health conditions) (n=6582). All fasting and calorie-restriction diets reduced weight compared with eating freely. Compared with continuous calorie restriction, only alternate-day fasting gave extra weight loss (1.29 kg, moderate certainty). In trials of 24 weeks or longer, strategies only beat eating freely.

## An Intermittent Fasting Intervention for Black Adults Can Be Feasibly Implemented in Black Churches: A Cluster Randomized Controlled Pilot Study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/yeary-2025-38986868/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38986868/
Citation: Yeary KHK, Johnson D, Harris N, Yu H et al (2025), Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
- In Intermittent fasting for weight and health: Black adults with BMI of 25 or more, from five Black churches in Western New York State (n=42). Weight fell in both arms (fasting -3.5 kg, calorie reduction -2.9 kg). The fasting group ate about 414 kcal a day less than the calorie-reduction group, but ate less fruit, vegetables and fibre. Satisfaction was high. The authors conclude it is feasible and larger studies are needed.

## Do the Effects of Early Time-Restricted Eating Vary by Cardiometabolic Phenotype, Age, Sex, or Race? A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rehman-2026-41941962/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41941962/
Citation: Rehman Z, Altonji OM, Steger FL, Jamshed H et al (2026), Journal of Nutrition
- In Intermittent fasting for weight and health: Adults aged 25 to 75 with obesity (BMI 30 to 60) in a 14-week weight-loss trial; the race analysis used 13 Black participants (n=not stated for the whole trial). Early time-restricted eating lowered blood pressure in adults with hypertension and HbA1c in prediabetes, and raised cholesterol in people with severe obesity. Blood pressure and glucose measures improved more in Black than in White participants, but the authors say the Black group was small and the result needs further investigation.

## Uterine fibroid incidence and growth in an ultrasound-based, prospective study of young African Americans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/baird-2020-32105679/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32105679/
Citation: Baird DD, Patchel SA, Saldana TM, Umbach DM et al (2020), American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
- In Iron, heavy periods and fibroids: 1,693 African American women aged 23-35 with no prior fibroid diagnosis (n=1693). Among 1,123 fibroid-free women with follow-up, incidence was 9.4% over about 18 months, rising from 6% at ages 23-25 to 13% at 32-35. Women with existing fibroids were more than twice as likely to develop new ones (relative risk 2.3). Average fibroid growth was 89% per 18 months.

## The association between subjective assessment of menstrual bleeding and measures of iron deficiency anemia in premenopausal African-American women: a cross-sectional study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bernardi-2016-27524363/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27524363/
Citation: Bernardi LA, Ghant MS, Andrade C, Recht H et al (2016), BMC Women's Health
- In Iron, heavy periods and fibroids: 44 premenopausal African American women, a pilot (n=44). Iron deficiency was present in 68.2% and anaemia in 18.2%. Women who reported heavy or very heavy periods had lower haemoglobin, haematocrit and ferritin and more anaemia symptoms. Of those reporting heavy periods, 35% were anaemic. The authors recommend evaluation for iron deficiency and anaemia whenever African American women report heavy bleeding.

## Multi-ancestry meta-analysis of keloids uncovers novel susceptibility loci in diverse populations
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/greene-2025-40835838/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40835838/
Citation: Greene CA, Hampton G, Jaworski J, Shuey MM et al (2025), Nature Communications
- In Keloids and piercings: 7,837 keloid cases and 1,593,009 controls across continental ancestry groups (n=7837). 26 genetic loci were found, 12 replicated. Estimated heritability was 6% in European, 21% in East Asian and 34% in African ancestry analyses. The authors state keloids are more likely in darker-skinned people of African and Asian descent than in Europeans.

## Admixture mapping identifies a locus at 15q21.2-22.3 associated with keloid formation in African Americans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/velez-2014-25280642/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25280642/
Citation: Velez Edwards DR, Tsosie KS, Williams SM, Edwards TL et al (2014), Human Genetics
- In Keloids and piercings: 478 African Americans (122 keloid cases, 356 controls) (n=478). A region on chromosome 15 and variants in two myosin genes were associated with keloid risk. The authors give the figure that keloids occur about 20 times more often in people of African than of European descent.

## Relationship between age of ear piercing and keloid formation
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lane-2005-15867040/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15867040/
Citation: Lane JE, Waller JL, Davis LS (2005), Pediatrics
- In Keloids and piercings: 32 patients with keloids resulting from ear piercing (n=32). Of those who had piercings at age 11 or older, 80% developed keloids against 23.5% of those pierced before 11. Half developed a keloid after their first piercing. The authors advise people with a family history to consider avoiding ear piercing.

## Does ear keloid formation depend on the type of earrings or piercing jewellery?
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hochman-2015-25715880/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25715880/
Citation: Hochman B, Isoldi FC, Silveira TS, Borba GC et al (2015), Australasian Journal of Dermatology
- In Keloids and piercings: 141 ear keloids, Brazil (n=141). Most keloids sat on the back of the earlobe and most earrings had metallic backs. The authors suggest the back of the earring may worsen local neurogenic inflammation.

## Updated international clinical recommendations on scar management: part 2--algorithms for scar prevention and treatment
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gold-2014-25068544/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25068544/
Citation: Gold MH, McGuire M, Mustoe TA, Pusic A et al (2014), Dermatologic Surgery
- In Keloids and piercings: International advisory panel (n=panel). A combination of multiple treatments gives the best chance of success for hypertrophic scars and keloids. The panel advocates earlier, more aggressive initial management of keloids, including earlier 5-fluorouracil.

## Comorbidities of Keloid and Hypertrophic Scars Among Participants in UK Biobank
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ung-2023-36598763/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36598763/
Citation: Ung CY et al (2023), JAMA Dermatol
- In Keloids and piercings: listed as a source, no finding recorded.

## Association of trypanolytic ApoL1 variants with kidney disease in African Americans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/genovese-2010-20647424/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20647424/
Citation: Genovese G, Friedman DJ, Ross MD, Lecordier L et al (2010), Science
- In Kidney disease, the APOL1 gene and the eGFR race adjustment: African Americans with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and hypertension-attributed end-stage kidney disease (H-ESKD), and controls (n=not stated in the abstract). Two independent APOL1 sequence variants were associated with FSGS (odds ratio 10.5, 95% CI 6.0-18.4) and H-ESKD (odds ratio 7.3, 95% CI 5.6-9.5). The variants are common in African chromosomes but absent from European chromosomes, and sit within haplotypes showing positive selection. Only the kidney-disease variants lysed Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense in vitro; the authors speculate a survival factor against sleeping sickness may have contributed to high kidney disease rates.

## New Creatinine- and Cystatin C-Based Equations to Estimate GFR without Race
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/inker-2021-34554658/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34554658/
Citation: Inker LA, Eneanya ND, Coresh J, Tighiouart H et al (2021), New England Journal of Medicine
- In Kidney disease, the APOL1 gene and the eGFR race adjustment: 8,254 participants (31.5% Black) for the creatinine equation and 5,352 (39.7% Black) for creatinine plus cystatin C; validated in 4,050 (14.3% Black) (n=4050 in validation). The current equation with a race term overestimated measured GFR in Black participants by a median of 3.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 and slightly in others (0.5). Omitting the race term underestimated it in Black participants by 7.1. A new race-free creatinine equation underestimated in Black participants by 3.6 and overestimated in non-Black by 3.9. Creatinine plus cystatin C equations were more accurate with smaller differences between groups.

## A Unifying Approach for GFR Estimation: Recommendations of the NKF-ASN Task Force on Reassessing the Inclusion of Race in Diagnosing Kidney Disease
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/delgado-2021-34556489/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34556489/
Citation: Delgado C, Baweja M, Crews DC, Eneanya ND et al (2021), Journal of the American Society of Nephrology
- In Kidney disease, the APOL1 gene and the eGFR race adjustment: NKF-ASN Task Force on race in diagnosing kidney disease (n=not applicable). The Task Force recommended a unified approach to estimating GFR without race; the abstract in my copy was cut off before the recommendations themselves.

## Prevalence and associated risk factors of Kola nut chewing among secondary school students in Osogbo, Nigeria
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/erinfolami-2011-25478098/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25478098/
Citation: Erinfolami A, Eegunranti A, Ogunsemi O, Oguntuase A et al (2011), Mental Illness
- In Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims: 385 randomly chosen secondary school students in Osogbo, Nigeria (n=385). Kola nut use was common: 11.2% in the past 30 days, 29.1% in the past year and 74.8% over a lifetime, most starting at 14 or younger. Use was associated with younger age and poor school attendance. The authors suggest awareness programmes about dangers.

## Some preliminary observations on the effects of kola nut on the cardiovascular system
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/agatha-1978-753053/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/753053/
Citation: Agatha M, Breckenridge C, Soyemi EA (1978), Nigerian Medical Journal
- In Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims: Anaesthetised cats (n=not stated). Low doses raised blood pressure by 8 to 9% and high doses lowered it by 18 to 71%. With larger doses a slow heart rate developed and cardiac arrhythmias occurred as a terminal event. The authors say the effects are probably due to caffeine and that the role of habitual chewing in heart disease needs discussion.

## Nitrosatable amines and nitrosamide formation in natural stimulants: Cola acuminata, C. nitida and Garcinia cola
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/atawodi-1995-7672735/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7672735/
Citation: Atawodi SE, Mende P, Pfundstein B, Preussmann R et al (1995), Food and Chemical Toxicology
- In Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims: Kola nut samples of Nigerian origin (Cola acuminata, C. nitida, Garcinia cola) (n=not applicable). Primary and secondary amines were found in all varieties. Methylating activity after nitrosation was higher in kola nuts than ever reported for a fresh plant product, which the authors say suggests the possible role of kola nut chewing in human cancer causes should be explored in countries where it is widely used.

## Caffeine - rich infusion from Cola nitida (kola nut) inhibits major carbohydrate catabolic enzymes; abates redox imbalance; and modulates oxidative dysregulated metabolic pathways and metabolites in Fe(2+)-induced hepatic toxicity
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/erukainure-2017-29223552/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29223552/
Citation: Erukainure OL, Oyebode OA, Sokhela MK, Koorbanally NA et al (2017), Biomedicine and Pharmacotherapy
- In Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims: Laboratory models (cell-free assays and rat liver tissue) (n=not applicable). The concentrated infusion was 80.08% caffeine by HPLC, scavenged free radicals and inhibited carbohydrate-digesting enzymes (alpha-glucosidase and alpha-amylase) in the lab. The authors suggest antioxidative and antidiabetic properties, with caffeine the major constituent.

## Convergent adaptation of human lactase persistence in Africa and Europe
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/tishkoff-2007-17159977/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17159977/
Citation: Tishkoff SA, Reed FA, Ranciaro A, Voight BF et al (2007), Nature Genetics
- In Lactose intolerance and dairy: 470 Tanzanians, Kenyans and Sudanese (n=470). Three SNPs (G/C-14010, T/G-13915 and C/G-13907) were associated with lactase persistence and raised transcription from the LCT promoter in vitro. They arose on different haplotype backgrounds from the European C/T-13910 variant and from each other. Haplotype homozygosity extended more than 2 Mb on chromosomes carrying C-14010, consistent with a selective sweep over about 7,000 years. The authors describe convergent evolution driven by animal domestication and adult milk consumption.

## Lasers for reduction of unwanted hair in skin of colour: a systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dorgham-2020-31587390/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31587390/
Citation: Dorgham NA, Dorgham DA (2020), Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
- In Laser hair removal on dark skin: Participants with Fitzpatrick skin types III-VI in 12 comparative trials (9 randomised) (n=12 trials). Alexandrite laser was superior to IPL for hair count; Nd:YAG and diode were not significantly different from IPL for hair count. Nd:YAG had fewer dark marks than IPL (OR 0.26). Diode and alexandrite had comparable safety to IPL, with more pain.

## Laser and energy-based device use in skin of color: A clinical review of safety, efficacy, and best practices
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dreifus-2026-42660430/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42660430/
Citation: Dreifus EM, Burke OM, Alexis AF et al (2026), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Laser hair removal on dark skin: Fitzpatrick IV-VI (mixed groups) (n=not stated). Melanin competes for laser energy in skin of colour, raising the risk of dark or pale marks, blisters and scarring; optimal outcomes need careful pre- and post-treatment care, strict photoprotection and sequential, lower-energy treatments; large prospective trials in darker skin are lacking.
- In Stretch marks and fading scars: Fitzpatrick IV-VI skin (mixed groups) (n=not stated). In skin of colour, melanin competes for the laser energy and raises the risk of dark or pale marks, blisters and scarring. Low-fluence Q-switched and picosecond Nd:YAG are favourable; non-ablative fractional lasers can be used conservatively; ablative devices carry more complications. The authors say large prospective trials in darker skin are lacking.

## Improving effects of the mushroom Yamabushitake (Hericium erinaceus) on mild cognitive impairment: a double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mori-2009-18844328/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18844328/
Citation: Mori K, Inatomi S, Ouchi K, Azumi Y et al (2009), Phytotherapy Research
- In Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements: Japanese men and women aged 50 to 80 with mild cognitive impairment (n=30). Cognitive scores rose more in the lion's mane group at weeks 8, 12 and 16, then fell back four weeks after stopping. Laboratory tests showed no adverse effect.

## The Acute and Chronic Effects of Lion's Mane Mushroom Supplementation on Cognitive Function, Stress and Mood in Young Adults: A Double-Blind, Parallel Groups, Pilot Study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/docherty-2023-38004235/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38004235/
Citation: Docherty S, Doughty FL, Smith EF (2023), Nutrients
- In Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements: Healthy adults aged 18 to 45 (country not stated in the abstract) (n=41). One dose was followed by faster Stroop task performance at 60 minutes. A trend to lower self-rated stress after 28 days did not reach significance (p = 0.051). The authors say null and limited findings were also seen and call for larger studies.

## Benefits, side effects, and uses of Hericium erinaceus as a supplement: a systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/menon-2025-40959699/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40959699/
Citation: Menon A, Jalal A, Arshad Z, Nawaz FA et al (2025), Frontiers in Nutrition
- In Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements: Humans and laboratory models: five randomised trials, three pilot trials, one cohort study and a case report on lion's mane, plus 15 laboratory studies (n=5 randomised trials and 3 pilot trials). The authors report cognitive benefits in the trials, including a combined Mini-Mental State Examination gain of about 1 point. Side effects are commonly unreported; those that were reported include stomach discomfort, headache and allergic reactions.

## Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi mushroom) for cancer treatment
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/jin-2016-27045603/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27045603/
Citation: Jin X, Ruiz Beguerie J, Sze DM, Chan GC (2016), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements: Cancer patients in five randomised trials of reishi (Ganoderma lucidum), mostly as an add-on to chemotherapy or radiotherapy (n=5). Methodological quality was generally unsatisfying and reporting poor. People given reishi alongside chemotherapy or radiotherapy were more likely to respond than with the treatment alone (relative risk 1.50, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.51), and reishi on its own did not match that. No trial reported long-term survival, and adverse events were reported in only one study.

## Lipid distribution on ethnic hairs by Fourier transform infrared synchrotron spectroscopy
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/barba-2022-34549464/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34549464/
Citation: Barba C et al (2022), Skin Research and Technology
- In LOC and LCO: layering liquid, oil and cream: Virgin hair fibres of African, Asian and Caucasian origin (n=not stated). African virgin hair had more lipids, mainly in the medulla, which the authors link to hydrophobicity, and its cuticle lipids were highly disordered, which they link to high water-vapour diffusion. They say the lipid differences may account for how African hair moisturises and swells.

## A systematic review on the lipid composition of human hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/csuka-2023-35218566/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35218566/
Citation: Csuka EA et al (2023), International Journal of Dermatology
- In LOC and LCO: layering liquid, oil and cream: Review of 59 articles on lipid content of human hair (n=59 articles). Hair lipid composition varies by ethnic hair type and by hair layer; lipids affect water permeability, hydration, strength and texture.

## Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation: An Official American Thoracic Society Statement
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bhakta-2023-36973004/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36973004/
Citation: Bhakta NR, Bime C, Kaminsky DA, McCormack MC et al (2023), American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
- In Lung function tests and race correction in spirometry: Official American Thoracic Society workshop (2021) and review of newer evidence (n=not applicable). Current ATS standards promoted race- and ethnicity-specific reference equations; concern grew that this gives a false view of fixed differences and may mask differential exposures and norm health disparities. The statement recommends replacing them with race-neutral average reference equations, alongside a broader re-evaluation of how lung function tests are used for clinical, employment and insurance decisions, a call to include missing stakeholders, and a caution about uncertain effects and potential harms.

## A Race-neutral Approach to the Interpretation of Lung Function Measurements
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bowerman-2023-36383197/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383197/
Citation: Bowerman C, Bhakta NR, Brazzale D, Cooper BR et al (2023), American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
- In Lung function tests and race correction in spirometry: NHANES III data (6,984 people) and the original GLI data (74,185 people) (n=74185). Adding sitting height and the Cormic index slightly improved precision but did not explain observed spirometry differences between NHANES III race and ethnic groups. The GLI-Global (2022) equations, which do not require choosing a race, fitted about as well as the GLI 2012 'other' equations but with wider limits of normal. The authors say the equations need careful use with symptoms and medical history when used for clinical, employment and insurance decisions.

## Race-neutral spirometry reclassification in self-identified Black and White patients
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/cai-2026-42741266/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42741266/
Citation: Cai X, Canaday F, Gao S, Merrell E et al (2026), ERJ Open Research
- In Lung function tests and race correction in spirometry: 6,107 spirometry tests in a 2010 to 2020 retrospective cohort, self-identified Black and White patients (n=6107). Switching to the race-neutral approach reclassified 530 results (9%) for FEV1 and 595 (10%) for FVC. Black patients reclassified as abnormal had higher healthcare use and worse outcomes, including hospitalisation, than those consistently normal; White patients reclassified as normal also had worse outcomes, including higher mortality. The authors say clinical judgment is needed for results near the cut-off.

## The Incidence and Prevalence of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in New York County (Manhattan), New York: The Manhattan Lupus Surveillance Program
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/izmirly-2017-28891252/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28891252/
Citation: Izmirly PM, Wan I, Sahl S, Buyon JP et al (2017), Arthritis and Rheumatology
- In Lupus: symptoms, risk and getting diagnosed early: Residents of New York County (Manhattan) with lupus, 2007 prevalence and 2007 to 2009 incidence, by race and ethnicity (n=not stated in the abstract). Age-standardised prevalence was 62.2 and incidence 4.6 per 100,000 person-years by ACR criteria, about 9 times higher in women than men. Prevalence in non-Hispanic Black women was 210.9 per 100,000 against 64.3 in non-Hispanic white women, 138.3 in Hispanic and 91.2 in non-Hispanic Asian women. Incidence was 15.7 in Black women against 6.5 in white and Hispanic women and 6.6 in Asian women.

## Epidemiology and prognosis of childhood lupus nephritis in the Afro-descendant population of the French Overseas Departments of America
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/michau-2026-42157049/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42157049/
Citation: Michau C, Osei L, Elenga N, Delion F et al (2026), BMC Nephrology
- In Lupus: symptoms, risk and getting diagnosed early: 27 children with lupus nephritis of Afro-descendant background, French Overseas Departments of America, 2000 to 2024 (n=27). Mean age at diagnosis 11.3 years; 55% had kidney involvement at diagnosis and 75% had class III or IV disease. Kidney flares were more frequent under age 12. Six (22%) had eGFR under 60 at last follow-up, two on dialysis and two transplanted. The authors say outcomes showed higher dialysis and kidney failure than Caucasian series.

## Severe Organ Involvement in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Retrospective Single-Center Study From Morocco
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lakdim-2026-43006003/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43006003/
Citation: Lakdim L, Naitlhou A, Carroll R (2026), Cureus
- In Lupus: symptoms, risk and getting diagnosed early: 61 people with lupus at one internal medicine department in Casablanca, Morocco, 2017 to 2022 (n=61). 90.2% were women, mean age at diagnosis 40.3 years. Fatigue (82.0%), joint pain (70.5%) and malar rash (59.0%) were most common; anaemia affected 47.5% and renal involvement 16.4%. The authors note restricted access to advanced targeted treatments.

## Magnesium for skeletal muscle cramps
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/garrison-2020-32956536/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32956536/
Citation: Garrison SR, Korownyk CS, Kolber MR, Allan GM et al (2020), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Magnesium supplements for sleep and cramps: People with skeletal muscle cramps in 11 randomised trials (five in pregnancy, five idiopathic, one cirrhosis) (n=735). For idiopathic cramps, largely in older adults (mean age about 62 to 69), cramp frequency differences between magnesium and placebo were small and statistically non-significant (moderate-certainty evidence). The pregnancy and cirrhosis trials were at high risk of bias.

## Oral magnesium supplementation for insomnia in older adults: a Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mah-2021-33865376/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33865376/
Citation: Mah J, Pitre T (2021), BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies
- In Magnesium supplements for sleep and cramps: Older adults with insomnia in three randomised trials, in three countries (n=151). Sleep onset latency was 17 minutes shorter with magnesium (95% CI 7 to 27 minutes). Total sleep time improved by 16 minutes, which was not significant. All trials were at moderate to high risk of bias and the evidence was rated low to very low quality.

## Magnesium deficiency in African-Americans: does it contribute to increased cardiovascular risk factors?
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/fox-2003-12749615/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12749615/
Citation: Fox CH, Mahoney MC, Ramsoomair D, Carter CA (2003), Journal of the National Medical Association
- In Magnesium supplements for sleep and cramps: African Americans (narrative review of observational evidence on magnesium status) (n=not applicable). The authors report that lower dietary and serum magnesium go with hypertension, insulin resistance and diabetes, and that occult magnesium deficiency may be more prevalent in African Americans than in other groups. They say trials that correct magnesium status in African Americans still need to be done.

## Stress reduction in the secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease: randomized, controlled trial of transcendental meditation and health education in Blacks
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/schneider-2012-23149426/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23149426/
Citation: Schneider RH, Grim CE, Rainforth MV, Kotchen T et al (2012), Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes
- In Meditation: 201 Black men and women with coronary heart disease, US (n=201). The primary outcome (death, heart attack or stroke) was 48% lower in the TM group (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.29-0.92, P=0.025). The wider secondary composite fell 24% (HR 0.76, 0.51-1.13, not significant). Systolic blood pressure was 4.9 mmHg lower, and anger scores improved. Adherence was linked to survival.

## Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/goyal-2014-24395196/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24395196/
Citation: Goyal M, Singh S, Sibinga EM, Gould NF et al (2014), JAMA Internal Medicine
- In Meditation: 47 trials, 3,515 participants in diverse adult clinical populations (n=3515). Mindfulness meditation programmes had moderate evidence of improved anxiety (effect size 0.38 at 8 weeks), depression (0.30) and pain (0.33), and low evidence of improved stress and mental-health quality of life. Low or insufficient evidence for positive mood, attention, substance use, eating habits, sleep and weight. No evidence that meditation programmes were better than any active treatment (drugs, exercise, other behavioural therapies).

## Evaluation of a mindfulness-based intervention program to decrease blood pressure in low-income African-American older adults
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/palta-2012-22302233/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22302233/
Citation: Palta P, Page G, Piferi RL, Gill JM et al (2012), Journal of Urban Health
- In Meditation: 20 low-income African American older adults in a residence (pilot) (n=20). Feasible and acceptable with high attendance. Average systolic pressure fell in both groups; the intervention group had a 21.92 mmHg lower systolic pressure than the social support group afterwards (p=0.020) and a 16.70 mmHg lower diastolic (p=0.003). The authors call the results preliminary and call for larger trials.

## Stress Reduction to Decrease Hypertension for Black Women: A Scoping Review of Trials and Interventions
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/collins-2022-34606073/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34606073/
Citation: Collins SV, Hines AL (2022), Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
- In Meditation: Black women with hypertension (6 studies) (n=6 studies). The authors report stronger evidence from one randomised trial of transcendental meditation, with reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure up to 7 mmHg, and describe non-randomised pilots with reductions up to 9 mmHg systolic.
- In Stress, burnout and blood pressure: Black women with hypertension (6 studies) (n=6 studies). The authors report stronger evidence from one randomised trial of transcendental meditation, with reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure up to 7 mmHg, and describe non-randomised pilots with reductions up to 9 mmHg systolic.

## Meditation and Cardiovascular Risk Reduction: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/levine-2017-28963100/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28963100/
Citation: Levine GN, Lange RA, Bairey-Merz CN, Davidson RJ et al (2017), Journal of the American Heart Association
- In Meditation: Scientific statement (n=not applicable). Studies suggest a possible benefit on cardiovascular risk, although the overall quality and in some cases quantity of data are modest. Given low cost and low risk, meditation may be considered as an adjunct to guideline-directed risk reduction.
- In Stress, burnout and blood pressure: Scientific statement (n=not applicable). Studies suggest a possible benefit on cardiovascular risk, although the overall quality and in some cases quantity of data are modest. Given low cost and low risk, meditation may be considered as an adjunct to guideline-directed risk reduction.

## Melasma Treatment: An Evidence-Based Review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mckesey-2020-31802394/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31802394/
Citation: McKesey J, Tovar-Garza A, Pandya AG (2020), American Journal of Clinical Dermatology
- In Melasma: Participants in 113 controlled studies of melasma (6,897 people); groups not broken down in the abstract (n=6897). Triple combination cream (hydroquinone, tretinoin, steroid) and hydroquinone alone were the most effective and best studied. Peels and lasers were equal or inferior to topical creams with more adverse effects. Oral tranexamic acid is promising. The authors cite small samples, mixed designs and lack of long-term follow-up.

## Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study of oral tranexamic acid in the treatment of moderate-to-severe melasma
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/del-2018-28987494/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28987494/
Citation: Del Rosario E, Florez-Pollack S, Zapata L et al (2018), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Melasma: 44 people with moderate-to-severe melasma, mostly Hispanic women, single centre (n=44). Melasma severity score fell 49% on tranexamic acid and 18% on placebo at 3 months; 3 months after stopping the gap had narrowed (26% against 19% from baseline). No serious adverse events.

## Efficacy of melatonin for chronic insomnia: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/choi-2022-36179487/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36179487/
Citation: Choi K, Lee YJ, Park S, Je NK et al (2022), Sleep Medicine Reviews
- In Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country: People with chronic insomnia in 24 randomised placebo-controlled trials, analysed by age group (n=not stated in the abstract). In adults with chronic insomnia melatonin did not significantly improve sleep onset, total sleep time or sleep efficiency. In children and adolescents it did, for sleep onset and total sleep time. The authors say further studies by age are needed.

## Effect of melatonin supplementation on sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/fatemeh-2022-33417003/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33417003/
Citation: Fatemeh G, Sajjad M, Niloufar R, Neda S (2022), Journal of Neurology
- In Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country: Adults with various conditions in 23 randomised trials (n=not stated in the abstract). Melatonin improved Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores by 1.24 points (95% CI 0.71 to 1.77), with large differences between studies (I2 80.7 per cent). Gains were larger in people with respiratory diseases and metabolic disorders than in people with sleep disorders (0.67 points).

## Nighttime administration of high-dose, sustained-release melatonin does not decrease nocturnal blood pressure in African-American patients: Results from a preliminary randomized, crossover trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rahbari-oskoui-2019-30935524/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30935524/
Citation: Rahbari-Oskoui FF, Abramson JL, Bruckman AM, Chapman AB et al (2019), Complementary Therapies in Medicine
- In Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country: Self-defined African American patients with essential hypertension, urban academic medical centre, United States (n=40). Night-time and daytime blood pressure on 24-hour monitoring did not differ between melatonin and placebo. The authors note this contrasts with studies in other populations.

## Ethnic Differences in Nighttime Melatonin and Nighttime Blood Pressure: A Study in European Americans and African Americans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/jeong-2019-31112592/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31112592/
Citation: Jeong J, Zhu H, Harris RA, Dong Y et al (2019), American Journal of Hypertension
- In Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country: Young adults in the Georgia Stress and Heart study: 71 African American and 79 European American (n=150). After adjustment, African American participants had lower night-time melatonin excretion and higher night-time systolic blood pressure. Lower melatonin went with higher night-time blood pressure in both groups, and melatonin partly explained the group difference in pressure.

## Melatonin Natural Health Products and Supplements: Presence of Serotonin and Significant Variability of Melatonin Content
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/erland-2017-27855744/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27855744/
Citation: Erland LA, Saxena PK (2017), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine
- In Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country: 31 commercial melatonin supplements (different brands and forms) (n=31). Melatonin content ranged from 83 per cent below to 478 per cent above the label. Lot-to-lot variation reached 465 per cent. More than 71 per cent of products missed the label by more than 10 per cent, and serotonin was found in eight (about a quarter).

## Acne keloidalis nuchae: prevalence, impact, and management challenges
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ogunbiyi-2016-28008278/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28008278/
Citation: Ogunbiyi A (2016), Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology
- In Men's afro hair: waves, fades, durags and the nape: Review of acne keloidalis nuchae (folliculitis keloidalis nuchae) (n=not stated). AKN is a chronic scarring folliculitis seen mostly in men of African descent after puberty and is classed as a primary scarring alopecia. The cause is unknown; suggested inciting factors include androgens, inflammation, infection, trauma, genetics and ingrowing hairs.

## Health risks of the clean-shave chiskop haircut
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khumalo-2013-23802217/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23802217/
Citation: Khumalo NP, Gantsho N (2013), South African Medical Journal
- In Men's afro hair: waves, fades, durags and the nape: 390 HIV-positive South African men, clinic (n=390). Haircut-associated bleeding and FKN were studied in men who wear the very close "chiskop" haircut; FKN prevalence was similar to published population data. The abstract is truncated beyond that in the record read.

## Reduction of "Ashiness" in Skin of Color with a Lipid-rich Moisturizing Body Wash
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/feng-2011-21464886/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21464886/
Citation: Feng L, Hawkins S (2011), Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
- In Moisturising and 'ashy' skin: 55 healthy women with skin types IV-VI and visible ashiness, Dallas (n=55). The body wash improved transepidermal water loss and expert- and self-assessed dryness; participants reported reduced ashiness at all sites. Similar results were seen with the syndet bar. The authors concluded that regular use of mild cleansers that support the barrier was associated with reduced ashiness.

## Skin type, but neither race nor gender, influence epidermal permeability barrier function
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/reed-1995-7574829/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7574829/
Citation: Reed JT, Ghadially R, Elias PM (1995), Archives of Dermatology
- In Moisturising and 'ashy' skin: 22-38 year-old White (8), Asian (6) adults; skin type II/III (14) against skin type V/VI (7) (n=21). Barrier function did not differ by race or sex. Skin type II/III needed 29.6 tape strips to disrupt the barrier against 66.7 for skin type V/VI, and V/VI recovered faster (43% against about 20% at 6 hours). The authors conclude skin type, not race, influences barrier function.

## Structural and functional differences in barrier properties of African American, Caucasian and East Asian skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/muizzuddin-2010-20654785/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20654785/
