Citation: Muizzuddin N, Hellemans L, Van Overloop L, Corstjens H et al (2010), Journal of Dermatological Science
- In Moisturising and 'ashy' skin: African American, Caucasian and East Asian volunteers (n=not stated). African American skin showed low ceramide levels and high protein cohesion in the upper layers. The authors interpret this as consistent with the high prevalence of xerosis in black skin.

## Transepidermal water loss, stratum corneum hydration, and skin surface pH of female African and Caucasian nursing students
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/young-2019-30028039/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30028039/
Citation: Young MM, Franken A, du Plessis JL (2019), Skin Research and Technology
- In Moisturising and 'ashy' skin: 19 African and 31 Caucasian female South African nursing students (n=50). No difference in water loss between groups. Stratum corneum hydration was lower (P<=0.05) and surface pH higher (P<=0.0001) in the African students. The authors suggest a higher risk of occupational skin disease.

## Ethnic skin types: are there differences in skin structure and function?
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rawlings-2006-18492142/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18492142/
Citation: Rawlings AV (2006), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Moisturising and 'ashy' skin: Narrative review (n=not stated). Studies have mostly been small, and in some interindividual differences in skin quality overwhelm racial differences. The authors call for studies that address genetic as well as phenotypic differences.

## Effects of Moringa oleifera Lam. Supplementation on Cardiometabolic Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials with GRADE Assessment
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/crisan-2025-41305552/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41305552/
Citation: Crisan D, Gavrilas L, Paltinean R, Frumuzachi O et al (2025), Nutrients
- In Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health: Adults in 9 randomised trials of Moringa oleifera (12 arms); countries not listed in the abstract (n=9 trials (341 intervention, 308 control)). Moringa showed no significant effects on most outcomes (weight, lipids, glycaemic indices). A modest fall in diastolic blood pressure was not robust in sensitivity analyses. The authors rated the certainty of evidence very low for all outcomes and say current evidence does not support consistent cardiometabolic benefits.

## Effects of Moringa oleifera leaves on the blood glucose, blood pressure, and lipid profile of type 2 diabetic subjects: A parallel group randomized clinical trial of efficacy
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/afiaenyi-2025-37229639/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37229639/
Citation: Afiaenyi IC, Ngwu EK, Okafor AM, Ayogu RN (2025), Nutrition and Health
- In Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health: 40 adults with type 2 diabetes in a rural Nigerian community (n=40). Fasting blood glucose did not differ between groups. The 40 g group had lower systolic pressure and higher triglycerides after the intervention, but after adjusting for baseline values there was no significant difference in any measure. The authors call the improvements marginal and not dose-dependent.

## Effect of Moringa oleifera Leaf Powder on Postprandial Blood Glucose Response: In Vivo Study on Saharawi People Living in Refugee Camps
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/leone-2018-30322091/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30322091/
Citation: Leone A, Bertoli S, Di Lello S, Bassoli A et al (2018), Nutrients
- In Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health: Saharawi people living in refugee camps (diabetic and healthy volunteers; numbers not in my copy of the abstract) (n=not shown in the abstract copy read). In the diabetic volunteers the glucose rise peaked earlier and was lower at 90, 120 and 150 minutes with moringa, and the mean meal response was lower. Healthy volunteers showed no difference. The authors say the 20 g dose tasted poor and lower doses should be tested, and that trials of longer-term effects are needed.

## Moringa oleifera Lam. in Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/watanabe-2021-34207664/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34207664/
Citation: Watanabe S, Okoshi H, Yamabe S, Shimada M (2021), Molecules
- In Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health: Diabetic rodent models (349 treated, 350 controls) (n=44 animal studies). Extracts of Moringa oleifera lowered blood glucose in diabetic rodents (pooled effect size -3.92) with substantial heterogeneity, and improved triglycerides and cholesterol.

## Review of the Safety and Efficacy of Moringa oleifera
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/stohs-2015-25808883/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25808883/
Citation: Stohs SJ, Hartman MJ (2015), Phytotherapy Research
- In Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health: Humans and animals (narrative safety and efficacy review) (n=five human studies of leaf powder). Animal safety studies of aqueous leaf extract indicate a high degree of safety, and the authors say no adverse effects were reported in human studies. They describe the five human studies as showing anti-hyperglycaemic and anti-dyslipidaemic activity, and call for human studies with standardised extracts.

## Racial and ethnic differences in the polycystic ovary syndrome metabolic phenotype
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/engmann-2017-28104402/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28104402/
Citation: Engmann L, Jin S, Sun F, Legro RS et al (2017), American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
- In PCOS, endometriosis and heavy periods: 702 women with PCOS aged 18-40 wanting to conceive, in a US multicentre trial (non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic black, Hispanic) (n=702). Non-Hispanic black women had a lower prevalence of metabolic syndrome than Hispanic women (24.5% against 42.2%) and lower triglycerides than Hispanic and white women. BMI and waist did not differ. The authors conclude non-Hispanic black women have an overall milder PCOS phenotype than Hispanics and in some respects than white women.

## Race and ethnicity reporting in endometriosis literature: a systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/raffone-2025-41030014/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41030014/
Citation: Raffone A, Doglioli M, Aguzzi A, Girardi L et al (2025), Facts, Views and Vision in ObGyn
- In PCOS, endometriosis and heavy periods: 648 endometriosis studies published in 2022 (n=648). Only 65 studies (10.0%) reported participants' race or ethnicity, and the quality of that reporting was poor. The authors call for improved documentation.

## Glycaemic index and load values tested in normoglycemic adults for five staple foodstuffs: pounded yam, pounded cassava-plantain, placali, attieke and maize meal stiff porridge
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kouame-2015-25690417/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690417/
Citation: Kouame AC, Kouassi KN, N'dri YD, Amani NG (2015), Nutrients
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Healthy adults in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire (numbers not in the abstract) (n=not stated in the abstract). Most of the five staples tested had a high glycaemic index above 70; attieke was lower at 63. Attieke had a high glycaemic load (29), placali and maize stiff porridge a medium one (17 and 16), and pounded cassava-plantain and pounded yam 26 and 22.

## Glycaemic index of selected staples commonly eaten in the Caribbean and the effects of boiling v. crushing
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ramdath-2004-15182400/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15182400/
Citation: Ramdath DD, Isaacs RL, Teelucksingh S, Wolever TM (2004), British Journal of Nutrition
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Healthy volunteers in Trinidad and Tobago, groups of 8 to 10 across three studies (n=about 8 to 10 per study). Cassava (glycaemic index 94) and dasheen (about 76) were high. Breadfruit (60), green banana (65), sadha roti (65), white yam (62), eddoes (61) and tannia (55 to 60) were intermediate, and Irish potato about 70. Crushing did not change the index. The authors say replacing high-glycaemic staples with intermediate ones may bring health benefits.

## Impact of resistant starch in three plantain (Musa AAB) products on glycaemic response of healthy volunteers
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/oladele-2016-25542206/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25542206/
Citation: Oladele EO, Williamson G (2016), European Journal of Nutrition
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Ten healthy volunteers (UK study with Nigerian plantain products) (n=10). Mean glycaemic index was 44.9 for boiled unripe plantain, 55.0 for the crisps and 38 for ripe raw plantain, lower than the Nigerian review's reported plantain values. The authors say the link with resistant starch is confounded by other constituents.

## Dietary approach for management of Type-2 diabetes: An overview of glycemic indices of commonly consumed foods in Nigeria
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/okoduwa-2023-36584553/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36584553/
Citation: Okoduwa SIR, Abdulwaliyu I (2023), Diabetes and Metabolic Syndrome
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Nigerian staples (literature overview) (n=not applicable). Many staples (tuwo, amala, fufu, garri, pounded yam, rice, beans and plantain) were reported as high glycaemic index (75 to 97). Less common foods such as maize pudding, moi-moi, fonio and dambu showed lower values (14 to 53). The authors say the lower-index foods may need certification before people with diabetes rely on them.

## Glycemic index, glycemic load, and cereal fiber intake and risk of type 2 diabetes in US black women
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/krishnan-2007-18039988/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039988/
Citation: Krishnan S, Rosenberg L, Singer M, Hu FB et al (2007), Archives of Internal Medicine
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: About 59,000 US Black women in the Black Women's Health Study, 8 years' follow-up, 1,938 new cases of diabetes (n=about 59,000). Women in the highest fifth for dietary glycaemic index had 23% higher diabetes rates than the lowest fifth (IRR 1.23, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.44), and women in the highest fifth for cereal fibre had 18% lower (IRR 0.82). Associations were stronger in women with a BMI under 25.

## Konzo and continuing cyanide intoxication from cassava in Mozambique
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/cliff-2011-20654676/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20654676/
Citation: Cliff J, Muquingue H, Nhassico D, Nzwalo H et al (2011), Food and Chemical Toxicology
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Communities in Mozambique with epidemics of konzo, a paralysis linked to cassava (n=over 1,800 cases across epidemics). Konzo epidemics came at times of drought, war or crisis when people depended on insufficiently processed bitter cassava; mostly women of child-bearing age and children were affected, with high thiocyanate in blood or urine. Prevention focused on less toxic cassava varieties and processing methods such as grating and flour wetting.

## Cyanide Content of Cassava Food Products Available in Australia
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/quinn-2022-35626954/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35626954/
Citation: Quinn AA, Myrans H, Gleadow RM (2022), Foods
- In Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety: Cassava products sold in Melbourne, Australia (n=not stated). Cyanide was highest in ready-to-eat cassava chips (mean 48.4 ppm), higher in imported products (95.9 ppm) than Australian-made (1.0 ppm), against Australia's limit of 10 ppm. Frozen products were significantly reduced by processing as directed on the packet.

## A national cohort study and confidential enquiry to investigate ethnic disparities in maternal mortality
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/knight-2022-34977514/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34977514/
Citation: Knight M, Bunch K, Vousden N, Banerjee A et al (2022), EClinicalMedicine
- In Pregnancy risk and safe maternity care for Black women: 1,894 women who died during or up to a year after pregnancy in the UK, 2009-18; care of 54 re-examined (18 Black, 19 Asian, 17 White) (n=1,894 deaths; 54 re-examined). Causes of death did not differ greatly by ethnic group; cardiovascular disease was the leading cause in all. Multiple areas of bias were found in care, including lack of nuanced care (notable among Black women who died) and microaggressions (most prominent among Asian women). The authors conclude that multiple structural and other biases exist in UK maternity care.

## Probiotics for the Prevention of Antibiotic-associated Diarrhea in Adults: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trials
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/liao-2021-33234881/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33234881/
Citation: Liao W, Chen C, Wen T, Zhao Q (2021), Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology
- In Probiotics and gut health: Adults taking antibiotics in 36 randomised, placebo-controlled trials (n=9312). Probiotics reduced antibiotic-associated diarrhoea by 38 per cent (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.74), more when started early. Adverse events were no more common than with placebo (relative risk 1.00).

## Feasibility, safety and tolerability of estrogen and/or probiotics for improving vaginal health in Canadian African, Caribbean, and Black women: A pilot phase 1 clinical trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gill-2025-39836666/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39836666/
Citation: Gill B, Wessels JM, Hayes CL, Ratcliffe J et al (2025), PLoS One
- In Probiotics and gut health: African, Caribbean and Black women aged 18 to 49 in the Greater Toronto Area (50 enrolled, 41 finished) (n=50). The trial was feasible (80 per cent enrolment, 82 per cent retention, 93 per cent adherence) and safe. There were 88 adverse events in 29 participants, 75 per cent mild, no serious events, and no clinically significant blood changes. It was not designed to show whether vaginal health improved.

## Risk and safety of probiotics
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/doron-2015-25922398/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25922398/
Citation: Doron S, Snydman DR (2015), Clinical Infectious Diseases
- In Probiotics and gut health: General population (review of probiotic safety) (n=not applicable). Probiotics have been used safely for years, but safety outcomes are inconsistently reported. Theoretical risks include systemic infections, harmful metabolic activity and excess immune stimulation in susceptible people. The authors say more research is needed on how often and how severe adverse events are.

## Lifetime risk of being diagnosed with, or dying from, prostate cancer by major ethnic group in England 2008-2010
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lloyd-2015-26224061/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26224061/
Citation: Lloyd T, Hounsome L, Mehay A, Mee S et al (2015), BMC Medicine
- In Prostate cancer risk and PSA testing: Prostate cancer registrations and deaths in England 2008-2010 by ethnic group, from Public Health England (n=not stated). Lifetime risk of diagnosis was about 1 in 8 (13.3%) for White men, 1 in 4 (29.3%, range 23.5-37.2%) for Black men and 1 in 13 (7.9%) for Asian men. Lifetime risk of death was about 1 in 24 (4.2%) for White, 1 in 12 (8.7%) for Black and 1 in 44 (2.3%) for Asian men. The authors say Black men are at twice the risk of being diagnosed with and dying from the disease.

## Marginal traction alopecia severity score: development and test of reliability
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/khumalo-2007-18047612/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18047612/
Citation: Khumalo NP, Ngwanya RM (2007), Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology
- In Protecting your edges and hairline: Women with marginal traction alopecia (n=not stated). The Marginal Traction Alopecia Severity score divides the scalp margins into regions so that hairline loss can be measured. The authors state that traction alopecia is common in African females.

## Incidence of schizophrenia and other psychoses in England, 1950-2009: a systematic review and meta-analyses
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kirkbride-2012-22457710/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22457710/
Citation: Kirkbride JB, Errazuriz A, Croudace TJ et al (2012), PLoS One
- In Psychosis, sectioning and misdiagnosis in the UK: 83 citations, people aged 16 to 64 with first-onset psychosis, England 1950 to 2009 (n=83 studies). Rates of psychosis were higher in several ethnic minority groups than in white British people. For schizophrenia the pooled rate ratio was 5.6 for Black Caribbean people (95% CI 3.4 to 9.2) and 4.7 for Black African people (3.3 to 6.8). The studies were mostly cross-sectional, which limits conclusions about cause.

## Ethnic variations in compulsory detention under the Mental Health Act: a systematic review and meta-analysis of international data
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/barnett-2019-30846354/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30846354/
Citation: Barnett P, Mackay E, Matthews H et al (2019), Lancet Psychiatry
- In Psychosis, sectioning and misdiagnosis in the UK: 71 studies, about 1.95 million participants, UK and international (n=71 studies). Black Caribbean patients were more likely to be compulsorily admitted than white patients (odds ratio 2.53, 95% CI 2.03 to 3.16), as were Black African patients (2.27, 1.62 to 3.19). Black Caribbean patients were also more likely to be readmitted (2.30). Explanations offered included higher prevalence of psychosis, perceived risk of violence, police contact, mistrust of GPs and ethnic disadvantage; the authors say these need culturally specific study.

## Racial bias and reproducibility in pulse oximetry among medical and surgical inpatients in general care in the Veterans Health Administration 2013-19: multicenter, retrospective cohort study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/valbuena-2022-35793817/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35793817/
Citation: Valbuena VSM, Seelye S, Sjoding MW, Valley TS et al (2022), BMJ
- In Pulse oximeters and dark skin: 30,039 paired readings in general-care inpatients, Veterans Health Administration, 2013-2019 (21.6% from non-Hispanic Black patients) (n=30039). Among SpO2 readings of 92% or more, the unadjusted probability of occult hypoxaemia (SaO2 below 88%) was 15.6% in white patients and 19.6% in black patients (P<0.001, similar in adjusted models). The authors say this could limit access to oxygen and other treatment for black patients.

## Uncovering the genetic architecture and evolutionary roots of androgenetic alopecia in African men
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/janivara-2025-40134218/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40134218/
Citation: Janivara R, Hazra et al (2025), HGG Advances
- In Receding hairline and hair transplants in Black men: 2,136 men from Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa (n=2136). Polygenic scores from European studies predicted baldness poorly in these men (AUC 0.513 to 0.546); 51 independent associations were found.

## Biohistory of slavery and blood pressure differences in blacks today. A hypothesis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/wilson-1991-1986989/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1986989/
Citation: Wilson TW, Grim CE (1991), Hypertension
- In Salt and blood pressure: Historical argument about the slave trade and blood pressure in Black Americans (n=not applicable). The authors argue that salt-depleting diseases such as diarrhoea during the slave trade and slavery favoured people who could conserve salt, so that Black Americans carry more salt-conserving genes than African Black people. It is a prediction, not a measurement.

## The slavery hypothesis for hypertension among African Americans: the historical evidence
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/curtin-1992-1456349/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1456349/
Citation: Curtin PD (1992), American Journal of Public Health
- In Salt and blood pressure: Historical evidence on salt, the slave trade and conditions of slavery (n=not applicable). The review finds there was no salt deficiency in the parts of Africa that supplied slaves, present-day West Africans do not have a high incidence of hypertension, deaths aboard slave ships were not shown to have been mainly salt-depleting, and the West Indies evidence was not relevant to the US.

## Exploring gender and ethnic disparities in sarcoidosis: insights from the British Thoracic Society UK Interstitial Lung Disease Registry
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/b-czek-2025-41253405/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41253405/
Citation: Bączek KK, Leng Cheng S, Amanda G, Achaiah A et al (2025), BMJ Open Respiratory Research
- In Sarcoidosis: symptoms, risk and follow-up: 1,071 adults with confirmed pulmonary sarcoidosis in the British Thoracic Society ILD Registry, 2013 to 2024 (ethnicity recorded for 918: 55.4% white, 14.2% non-white including Black, South Asian and mixed) (n=1071). Non-white patients presented younger (52 against 54 years) with more breathlessness (46% against 33%) and cough (44% against 27%), more CT nodularity (54% against 36%) and abnormal liver tests (16% against 9%), and more comorbidity. Lung physiology was comparable. Immunosuppression was more likely with non-white ethnicity (odds ratio 3.20) and male sex (2.34). The authors say treatment decisions were more influenced by sex and ethnicity than by lung function or imaging.

## Race Comparisons in Patients With Cardiac Sarcoidosis: Insights From the Cardiac Sarcoidosis Consortium
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/trongtorsak-2025-40557494/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40557494/
Citation: Trongtorsak A, De La Rosa Martinez J, Crawford TC, Bogun FM et al (2025), Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology
- In Sarcoidosis: symptoms, risk and follow-up: 619 patients with cardiac sarcoidosis (362 White, 193 Black, 64 other) in an international registry of over 25 centres (n=619). Black patients were diagnosed younger (50.5 against 53.7 years) with lower left ventricular ejection fraction (44.6 against 48.3) and more lung (80.3% against 72.7%), skin (22.8% against 12.4%) and eye (13.5% against 5.5%) involvement, and more hypertension, diabetes and kidney disease. Treatment patterns were similar and the combined outcome (death, assist device, transplant or defibrillator therapy) did not differ (29.5% against 28.5%).

## Diversity and disparity in the treatment and care of sarcoidosis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/obi-2023-37431305/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37431305/
Citation: Obi ON (2023), Current Opinion in Pulmonary Medicine
- In Sarcoidosis: symptoms, risk and follow-up: Published literature on sarcoidosis by race, sex and place (n=not applicable). African Americans and women have the highest incidence, more advanced presentations and higher death rates, and African American women have the highest mortality. The author says the differences may reflect healthcare disparities and income more than genetics or biology alone: patients in the lowest income strata present with the most severe disease and report more barriers to care.

## Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/laukkanen-2015-25705824/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25705824/
Citation: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, Laukkanen JA (2015), JAMA Internal Medicine
- In Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks: Middle-aged men (42 to 60) in eastern Finland, Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease cohort (n=2315). Compared with one session a week, men using a sauna 4 to 7 times a week had about two-thirds lower risk of sudden cardiac death (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.75), and lower fatal heart and all-cause mortality. Sessions over 19 minutes were linked to lower risk than sessions under 11 minutes.

## Acute and short-term efficacy of sauna treatment on cardiovascular function: A meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/li-2020-32814462/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32814462/
Citation: Li Z, Jiang W, Chen Y, Wang G (2020), European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing
- In Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks: People in 16 studies of sauna treatment (healthy people and people with heart problems) (n=not stated in the abstract). Straight after a sauna, body temperature rose 0.94 degrees C and heart rate 18 beats a minute, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure fell by about 5.6 and 6.5 mmHg. Over 2 to 4 weeks, flow-mediated dilation, ejection fraction and walking distance rose and blood pressure fell. The authors describe the trials as limited.

## The acute effect of whole-body heat therapy on peripheral and cerebral vascular reactivity in Black and White females
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/martin-2023-37024072/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37024072/
Citation: Martin ZT, Akins JD, Merlau ER, Kolade JO et al (2023), Microvascular Research
- In Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks: Eighteen healthy young females: nine Black (average 21) and nine White (average 27), United States (n=18). Before heating there was no difference in vascular function between the groups. Heat improved forearm blood flow response and brachial artery flow-mediated dilation in both groups (6.2 to 8.8 per cent), with no effect on cerebral vascular reactivity.

## Severe rhabdomyolysis and renal failure triggered by a sauna visit in sickle cell trait: a case report
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/eisenbach-2005-15786826/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15786826/
Citation: Eisenbach C, Pohl J, Dikow R, Stremmel W (2005), Clinical Nephrology
- In Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks: One 29-year-old African American with sickle cell trait (n=1). A sauna visit triggered severe rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) and acute kidney failure.

## Effect of mineral oil, sunflower oil, and coconut oil on prevention of hair damage
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rele-2003-12715094/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12715094/
Citation: Rele AS, Mohile RB (2003), Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Scalp oiling and greasing: Hair fibres of several types (an industry combing study) (n=not stated). Coconut oil was the only one of the three oils found to reduce protein loss in undamaged and damaged hair when used before or after washing. Sunflower and mineral oils did not reduce protein loss.

## Benefit of coconut-based hair oil via hair porosity quantification
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kaushik-2022-35377477/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35377477/
Citation: Kaushik V, Kumar A, Gosvami NN, Gode V et al (2022), International Journal of Cosmetic Science
- In Scalp oiling and greasing: Hair fibres (laboratory) (n=not stated). Coconut-based oil prevented the rise in hair porosity caused by surfactant washing and reversed the fall in break stress in lab testing.

## Sea Moss
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/drugs-2006-41730053/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41730053/
Citation: Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed) (2006), LactMed, National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
- In Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals: Breastfeeding mothers and infants (database summary) (n=not applicable). Sea moss (Irish moss, Chondrus crispus) is used as food and medicine, although no medicinal value has been proven. It contains carrageenan and minerals including iodine, and some toxic heavy metals such as arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury from the water. Excess iodine from seaweed in a mother's diet has caused thyroid suppression in breastfed infants, so it should be avoided while breastfeeding unless iodine and heavy metal levels are shown to be low enough.

## Metals in edible seaweed
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rubio-2017-28152409/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28152409/
Citation: Rubio C, Napoleone G, Luis-Gonzalez G et al (2017), Chemosphere
- In Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals: Edible seaweed samples (Chondrus, Eisenia, Gelidium, Himanthalia, Laminaria, Palmaria, Porphyra, Undaria) from Asia and the EU (n=not stated in the abstract). Red seaweed showed higher concentrations of trace and toxic elements. At 4 g a day of seaweed the intake of aluminium, cadmium and lead was low and the authors saw no serious concern, but they say other toxic metals should be monitored.

## Excess iodine intake: sources, assessment, and effects on thyroid function
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/farebrother-2019-30891786/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30891786/
Citation: Farebrother J, Zimmermann MB, Andersson M (2019), Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
- In Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals: General population (review of excess iodine intake) (n=not applicable). High iodine intakes are well tolerated by most healthy people, but in some people excess iodine may trigger hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, goitre or thyroid autoimmunity. People with existing thyroid disease or past iodine deficiency may be more susceptible, in some cases at intakes only slightly above need. Certain seaweeds are named as sources of excess iodine.

## Evidence and hypotheses on adverse effects of the food additives carrageenan (E 407)/processed Eucheuma seaweed (E 407a) and carboxymethylcellulose (E 466) on the intestines: a scoping review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/tahiri-2023-38032203/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38032203/
Citation: Tahiri M, Johnsrud C, Steffensen IL (2023), Critical Reviews in Toxicology
- In Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals: Humans, experimental mammals and cells (scoping review of the additives carrageenan E407 and processed Eucheuma seaweed E407a) (n=262 publications (5 in humans for carrageenan)). The most studied adverse effects of carrageenan on the intestines were inflammation, the gut microbiome, intestinal permeability, and cancer, metabolic and immune effects. Only five publications on carrageenan were in humans. The authors call for randomised trials of realistic dietary exposures.

## Shave frequency and regimen variation effects on the management of pseudofolliculitis barbae
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/daniel-2013-23652888/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23652888/
Citation: Daniel A, Gustafson CJ, Zupkosky PJ, Candido A et al (2013), Journal of Drugs in Dermatology
- In Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): 90 African American men with pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB) (n=90). Papule and pustule counts did not differ between groups at 12 weeks, and investigator-graded severity did not differ (P=.43). Ingrown hairs were significantly fewer in the 2-3 times a week group than in either daily group (P=.005 against daily standard, P=.04 against daily advanced). Participants in the daily advanced products group reported more perceived improvement (P=.007) and less itching (P=.002) than the 2-3 times a week group.

## Comparative evaluation of men's depilatory composition versus razor in black men
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/kindred-2011-21916277/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21916277/
Citation: Kindred C, Oresajo CO, Yatskayer M, Halder RM (2011), Cutis
- In Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): Black men (single centre, 1 week) (n=not stated). The depilatory creams produced fewer papules and more irritation than the razor; the irritation was transient. One composition was withdrawn because of a high rate of adverse events. Skin looked and felt smoother with the creams. The authors recommend depilatories for people who develop PFB or are unsatisfied with razors.

## Topical eflornithine hydrochloride improves the effectiveness of standard laser hair removal for treating pseudofolliculitis barbae: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/xia-2012-22226431/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22226431/
Citation: Xia Y, Cho S, Howard RS, Maggio KL (2012), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): 27 men with PFB in a military population (n=27). The eflornithine side had a median hair reduction of 99.5% against 85.0% on the placebo side, with fewer inflammatory papules. Follow-up ended at 16 weeks.

## Defining pseudofolliculitis barbae in 2001: a review of the literature and current trends
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/perry-2002-11807473/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11807473/
Citation: Perry PK, Cook-Bolden FE, Rahman Z, Jones E et al (2002), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): Literature (n=not stated). PFB is most often seen in men and women of African American and Hispanic origin who have tightly curled hair and who shave or tweeze frequently. The authors state follicle shape, hair cuticle and direction of hair growth each play a role, and that prevention and early intervention are the mainstays; no treatment is completely curative.

## Review of treatments for pseudofolliculitis barbae
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dalia-2023-36840647/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36840647/
Citation: Dalia Y, Khatib J, Odens H, Patel T (2023), Clinical and Experimental Dermatology
- In Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): Review 1987-2023 (n=not stated). Treatment needs a multifaceted approach: preventive measures, antibiotics, corticosteroids, keratolytics, depilatories or laser. Topical therapies are the mainstay; laser hair removal is a potential long-term option needing more study of efficacy and permanence.

## Patient acceptability, efficacy, and skin biophysiology of a cream and cleanser containing lipid complex with shea butter extract versus a ceramide product for eczema
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hon-2015-26314567/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26314567/
Citation: Hon KL, Tsang YC, Pong NH, Lee VW et al (2015), Hong Kong Medical Journal
- In Shea butter: 34 children with atopic dermatitis, Hong Kong (not people of African descent) (n=34). After 4 weeks, itch score fell from 6.7 to 6.0 and the children's dermatology quality-of-life score improved from 10.0 to 8.0, in the group who rated the product good or very good. No control group, so this cannot show the shea did anything.

## Ethnopharmacological evaluation of Vitellaria paradoxa triterpenes for wound healing: In vivo evidence of lupeol and α/β-amyrin in promoting dermal regeneration
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/anyanwu-2026-41619863/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41619863/
Citation: Anyanwu EG, Onuchukwu CL, Ojukwu CP, Anyanwu CN (2026), Journal of Ethnopharmacology
- In Shea butter: 34 adults in a Nigerian hospital with wounds that had not healed in over 4 weeks (n=34). The triterpene ointments were associated with wound contraction and better wound scores. These are isolated compounds in an ointment, not shea butter as sold or used.

## African oils in dermatology
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ayanlowo-2022-33928725/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33928725/
Citation: Ayanlowo O, Cole-Adeife O, Ilomuanya M, Ebie C et al (2022), Dermatologic Therapy
- In Shea butter: Literature review plus interviews with traditional healers in Nigeria (n=not stated). The oils contain fatty acids, ceramides, phospholipids and antioxidants that have been shown in laboratory and some other work to support barrier function and wound healing. Adverse effects were mainly attributed to how the product was processed and stored. The authors say further studies are required.

## Evidence-based treatment of atopic dermatitis with topical moisturizers
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/micali-2018-29368843/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29368843/
Citation: Micali G et al (2018), Giornale Italiano di Dermatologia e Venereologia
- In Shea butter: No human trial of plain shea butter on skin found (n=0). My search found no controlled trial of plain shea butter applied to skin in any population. A 2018 review of eczema moisturisers (Micali, in the 12 Nov research file) reached the same position: shea cannot be isolated as the active.

## Contact allergy to Butyrospermum parkii butter in a patient with cheilitis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/castelain-2024-38123238/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38123238/
Citation: Castelain F et al (2024), Contact Dermatitis
- In Shea butter: Case reports (n=1). Contact allergy to shea butter is documented but appears rare in the literature I found (3 hits in my search).

## Maternal and perinatal outcomes amongst haemoglobinopathy carriers: a systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/jans-2010-20946275/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20946275/
Citation: Jans SM, de Jonge A, Lagro-Janssen AL (2010), International Journal of Clinical Practice
- In Sickle cell disease, trait and pregnancy: Pregnant women carrying haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell trait or thalassaemia minor); the abstract says 780 subjects were identified, of which nine (studies) were included (n=9 studies included (780 subjects identified)). A protective effect of sickle cell trait was found for premature birth, low Apgar score and perinatal mortality. No significant effect was found for low birth weight, growth retardation, urinary tract infection or high blood pressure. The risk of anaemia and bacteriuria was increased (urinary tract infection itself was not significant, though the authors still advise awareness of it). The authors conclude risks among pregnant carriers are low and midwives need to be aware of anaemia and urine infection.

## Haemoglobinopathies and the clinical epidemiology of malaria: a systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/taylor-2012-22445352/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22445352/
Citation: Taylor SM, Parobek CM, Fairhurst RM (2012), Lancet Infectious Diseases
- In Sickle cell disease, trait and pregnancy: 62 studies of children and pregnant women in malaria regions (n=62 studies). Haemoglobin AS (the trait) cut the risk of severe falciparum malaria (odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.06-0.12) and was the only genotype consistently protective against uncomplicated malaria (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.61-0.79).

## Sickle Cell Trait, Rhabdomyolysis, and Mortality among U.S. Army Soldiers
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/nelson-2016-27518662/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27518662/
Citation: Nelson DA, Deuster PA, Carter R, Hill OT et al (2016), New England Journal of Medicine
- In Sickle cell trait and hard exercise: 47,944 Black US Army soldiers tested for sickle cell trait (HbAS), 2011-2014 (n=47944). No significant difference in death risk between soldiers with and without the trait (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.46-2.13). Exertional rhabdomyolysis risk was higher with the trait (adjusted HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.12-2.12), similar in size to the effect of tobacco use (HR 1.54) and of a BMI of 30 or more (HR 1.39).

## Sickle cell trait associated with a RR of death of 37 times in National Collegiate Athletic Association football athletes: a database with 2 million athlete-years as the denominator
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/harmon-2012-22442191/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22442191/
Citation: Harmon KG, Drezner JA, Klossner D, Asif IM (2012), British Journal of Sports Medicine
- In Sickle cell trait and hard exercise: 273 NCAA athlete deaths over 1,969,663 athlete-years, 2004-2008 (n=273). Five deaths (2%) were associated with sickle cell trait, all in Black Division I football players. The risk of exertional death in Division I football players with the trait was 1 in 827, which was 37 times higher than in players without it.

## Sudden Death Associated With Sickle Cell Trait Before and After Mandatory Screening
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/buchanan-2020-32271134/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32271134/
Citation: Buchanan BK, Siebert DM, Zigman Suchsland ML, Drezner JA et al (2020), Sports Health
- In Sickle cell trait and hard exercise: 8,309,050 NCAA athlete-years, 2000-2019 (n=8309050). In Division I football the incidence of death associated with the trait fell from 1 in 28,145 athlete-years before legislation (9 deaths) to 1 in 250,468 after (1 death), a relative risk of 0.112 (95% CI 0.003-0.811). Cases outside football were rare. The authors' stated hypothesis was that legislation would reduce incidence.

## Clinical Outcomes Associated With Sickle Cell Trait: A Systematic Review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/naik-2018-30383109/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30383109/
Citation: Naik RP, Smith-Whitley K, Hassell KL, Umeh NI et al (2018), Annals of Internal Medicine
- In Sickle cell trait and hard exercise: 41 observational studies in children and adults (n=41 studies). High-strength evidence for a positive association between trait and pulmonary embolism, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease. Moderate-strength evidence for exertional rhabdomyolysis, and for no association with deep vein thrombosis, heart failure or stroke. Absolute risks of thromboembolism and rhabdomyolysis were small. The authors state that sickle cell trait is largely a benign carrier state that is a risk factor for a few outcomes.

## Aging Differences in Ethnic Skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/vashi-2016-26962390/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26962390/
Citation: Vashi NA, de Castro Maymone MB, Kundu RV (2016), Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
- In Skin ageing in dark skin: Literature on ageing across groups, including African American, Asian and Hispanic descent (n=not stated). Differences in epidermal melanin make darkly pigmented people more vulnerable to dyspigmentation, while a thicker and more compact dermis makes facial lines less noticeable. Most common signs of ageing in every skin type are dark spots, loss of elasticity and volume, and wrinkles.

## Ethnicity and Aging Skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/alexis-2017-29028856/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29028856/
Citation: Alexis AF, Obioha JO (2017), Journal of Drugs in Dermatology
- In Skin ageing in dark skin: Literature on ageing across groups (n=not stated). Skin of colour is less susceptible to photodamage, so signs of ageing are less pronounced and occur later than in Caucasians.

## Ethnic differences among patients with cutaneous melanoma
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/cormier-2006-17000949/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17000949/
Citation: Cormier JN, Xing Y, Ding M, Lee JE et al (2006), Archives of Internal Medicine
- In Skin cancer and moles on dark skin: 251 African Americans and 48,143 White patients with melanoma, SEER registry, 1992-2002 (n=251). Melanoma incidence was 0.8 per 100,000 in African Americans against 18.4 in White people. African Americans were 4.2 times as likely to present at stage IV. Overall 5-year survival was 72.2% to 81.1% for minorities against 89.6% for White patients.
- In Sunscreen on dark skin: 251 African Americans and 48,143 White patients with melanoma in the US cancer registry (SEER), 1992-2002 (n=251). Melanoma incidence was 0.8 per 100,000 in African Americans against 18.4 in White people. African Americans were 4.2 times as likely to present at stage IV, and had a 1.48-fold higher risk-adjusted, stage-specific mortality. Overall 5-year survival was 72.2% to 81.1% for minorities against 89.6% for White patients.

## Acral lentiginous melanoma: incidence and survival patterns in the United States, 1986-2005
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bradford-2009-19380664/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19380664/
Citation: Bradford PT, Goldstein AM, McMaster ML, Tucker MA (2009), Archives of Dermatology
- In Skin cancer and moles on dark skin: 1,413 acral lentiginous melanoma cases, SEER 1986-2005 (n=1413). Acral lentiginous melanoma was 36% of melanoma in Black patients, the largest share of any group.

## Acral Lentiginous Melanoma: Incidence and Survival in the United States, 2006-2015, an Analysis of the SEER Registry
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/huang-2020-32208196/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32208196/
Citation: Huang et al (2020), Journal of Surgical Research
- In Skin cancer and moles on dark skin: Black and non-Hispanic White patients with melanoma, SEER 2006-2015 (n=not stated here). Five-year melanoma-specific survival was 66.9% in Black patients against 84.3% in non-Hispanic White patients; Black patients had thicker, more ulcerated tumours and acral melanoma was 32.6% of Black cases.

## Disparities in acral lentiginous melanoma: Factors beyond delayed diagnosis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/grant-2025-40562077/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40562077/
Citation: Grant S, Revan D, Tang L et al (2025), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Skin cancer and moles on dark skin: Cutaneous melanoma cases in SEER compared by race (n=not stated). No significant difference in disease severity at diagnosis between Black and White patients with acral lentiginous melanoma, yet Black patients had double the risk of dying from it (hazard ratio 2.04). The authors say delay in diagnosis does not fully explain the gap.

## Skin cancer in skin of color
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gloster-2006-17052479/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17052479/
Citation: Gloster HM Jr, Neal K (2006), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Skin cancer and moles on dark skin: Literature on skin cancer in skin of colour (n=not stated). In dark-skinned groups squamous cell carcinoma is most common, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma usually occur on non-sun-exposed sites, and UV is not an important cause except for basal cell carcinoma. Skin cancer is less common but often has greater morbidity and mortality.

## The global prevalence and correlates of skin bleaching: a meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/sagoe-2019-29888464/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29888464/
Citation: Sagoe D et al (2019), International Journal of Dermatology
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 68 studies, 67,665 people worldwide (n=67665). Pooled lifetime prevalence of skin bleaching was 27.7%, and 27.1% in Africa, with very high heterogeneity, so the figure is a rough average of unlike samples. The highest prevalence in a subgroup analysis was 51.8%, associated with topical corticosteroid use (the abstract does not say whether this is the share of users who applied steroids); the pooled sample is global, not Black-specific.

## Skin diseases associated with the cosmetic use of bleaching products in women from Dakar, Senegal
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mahe-2003-12653741/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12653741/
Citation: Mahe A, Ly F, Aymard G, Dangou JM (2003), British Journal of Dermatology
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 425 women who used bleaching products, plus 368 women screened, in Dakar, Senegal (n=425). 52.7% of 368 women questioned were current users. Users reported hydroquinone (89%), glucocorticoids (70%), mercury iodide (10%) and caustic agents (17%). Hydroquinone in analysed samples was 4% to 8.7%. The main skin problems in users included dermatophyte infections (105 women) and scabies (69).

## Spectrometric analysis of mercury content in 549 skin-lightening products: is mercury toxicity a hidden global health hazard?
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/hamann-2014-24321702/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24321702/
Citation: Hamann CR, Boonchai W, Wen L, Sakanashi EN et al (2014), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 549 skin-lightening products from 32 countries bought in the US, Taiwan, Japan, China, Thailand and Sri Lanka (n=549). 33 products (6.0%) contained mercury above 1,000 ppm, and 45% of the mercury-containing samples contained more than 10,000 ppm. Of products bought in the US, 3.3% had mercury over 1,000 ppm. The US legal limit is 1 ppm.

## A Systematic Review of Mercury Exposures from Skin-Lightening Products
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/bastiansz-2022-36367779/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36367779/
Citation: Bastiansz A, Ewald J, Rodriguez Saldana V, Santa-Rios A et al (2022), Environmental Health Perspectives
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 41 papers from 22 countries; 787 product samples and 1,042 human biomarker measurements (n=863). Mercury is widely present as an active ingredient. The Minamata Convention bans manufacture, import or export of lightening products above 1 ppm mercury.

## Inorganic mercury poisoning associated with skin-lightening cosmetic products
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/chan-2011-22070559/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22070559/
Citation: Chan TY (2011), Clinical Toxicology (Philadelphia)
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 31 relevant reports of mercury poisoning from lightening cosmetics (to March 2011) (n=31). Mercury and its salts are prohibited as skin-lightening agents because of high toxicity. The kidneys are the major site of deposition; renal damage includes reversible proteinuria, acute tubular necrosis and nephrotic syndrome. Gastrointestinal effects include a metallic taste, gingivostomatitis, nausea and hypersalivation. A single case report (Tang 2006, PMID 16912361) documented a woman with nephrotic syndrome whose proteinuria remitted 9 months after stopping the cream.

## Exogenous ochronosis associated with hydroquinone: a systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/ishack-2022-34486734/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34486734/
Citation: Ishack S, Lipner SR (2022), International Journal of Dermatology
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: 126 patients with hydroquinone-associated ochronosis in 56 case reports (n=126). Of cases, 55.5% were reported as Black and 52.4% were Fitzpatrick V-VI. Median use was 5 years; four cases came after 3 months or less and eight after a year or less. Concentrations above 4% were most often implicated. All had blue-black or grey-blue lace-like marks on the face; treatment is often unsatisfactory.

## Minimal change disease following exposure to mercury-containing skin lightening cream
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/tang-2006-16912361/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16912361/
Citation: Tang HL et al (2006), Hong Kong Med J
- In Skin lightening and bleaching creams: listed as a source, no finding recorded.

## Racial/Ethnic Differences in Sleep Disturbances: The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA)
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/chen-2015-25409106/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25409106/
Citation: Chen X, Wang R, Zee P et al (2015), Sleep
- In Sleep, short sleep and sleep apnoea: 2,230 US adults aged 54 to 93 (MESA Sleep cohort), including Black participants (n=2,230). Compared with white adults, Black adults had higher odds of sleep apnoea syndrome (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.63), short sleep under 6 hours (OR 4.95, 3.56 to 6.90), poor sleep quality (OR 1.57) and daytime sleepiness (OR 1.89). Only 7.4% to 16.2% of people with moderate or worse sleep-disordered breathing reported a prior diagnosis.

## Everyday and major experiences of racial/ethnic discrimination and sleep health in a multiethnic population of U.S. women: findings from the Sister Study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/gaston-2020-32505024/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32505024/
Citation: Gaston SA, Feinstein L, Slopen N et al (2020), Sleep Medicine
- In Sleep, short sleep and sleep apnoea: 40,038 US women in the Sister Study (8% non-Hispanic Black) (n=40,038). Non-Hispanic Black participants most often reported everyday (76%) and major (52%) racial discrimination. Reporting both types was linked to short sleep (prevalence ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.25) and insomnia symptoms (1.10, 1.01 to 1.20).

## Atypical parkinsonism in the Caribbean island of Guadeloupe: etiological role of the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor annonacin
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lannuzel-2008-18816693/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18816693/
Citation: Lannuzel A, Ruberg M, Michel PP (2008), Movement Disorders
- In Soursop (graviola): cancer cure, blood sugar and safety: Patients with atypical parkinsonism on Guadeloupe; midbrain cell cultures; rats (n=not stated in the abstract). On Guadeloupe atypical parkinsonian patients were two-thirds of all parkinsonism cases, against about 5% in European data. Epidemiological data suggested a close association with regular consumption of soursop. Annonacin, a mitochondrial complex I inhibitor in the fruit and leaves, was identified in cell cultures as a probable cause, and giving it to rats reproduced the brain lesions.

## Creatine kinase in the U.S. population: Impact of demographics, comorbidities, and body composition on the normal range
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/george-2016-27537560/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27537560/
Citation: George MD, McGill NK, Baker JF (2016), Medicine (Baltimore)
- In Starting training, rest days and recovery: 10,096 non-pregnant US adults aged 20 and over, NHANES 2011-2014 (n=10096). Black race was strongly associated with creatine kinase: the odds of an abnormal result were 5.08 times higher (95% CI 3.65-7.08) for Black women and 8.39 times higher (6.11-11.52) for Black men. Body size and composition mattered but did not explain the racial difference. The 97.5th percentile was 382 in white men and 1001 in black men; 295 in white women and 487 in black women.

## Exploring the relationship between stigma and help-seeking for mental illness in African-descended faith communities in the UK
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/mantovani-2017-27124178/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27124178/
Citation: Mantovani N, Pizzolati M, Edge D (2017), Health Expectations
- In Stigma, talking to family and starting therapy: 26 men and women in Christian faith communities, south London (n=26). Help-seeking was shaped by beliefs about the causes of mental illness, silencing driven by stigma, and stigma kept up at community level. People with a diagnosis could face triple jeopardy in stigma. The authors say one-size-fits-all approaches will not meet diverse needs.

## Perceived racial discrimination and hypertension: a comprehensive systematic review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dolezsar-2014-24417692/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24417692/
Citation: Dolezsar CM, McGrath JJ, Herzig AJM et al (2014), Health Psychology
- In Stress, burnout and blood pressure: 44 articles, 32,651 people, mainly US (n=44 articles, 32,651). Perceived racial discrimination was associated with hypertension (small effect, Z 0.048, 95% CI 0.013 to 0.087) but not with resting blood pressure. The link was stronger among men, Black participants and older people, and strongest for night-time ambulatory blood pressure in Black participants.

## Racial/Ethnic Differences in Burnout: a Systematic Review
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/lawrence-2022-33428158/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33428158/
Citation: Lawrence JA, Davis BA, Corbette T, Hill EV et al (2022), Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
- In Stress, burnout and blood pressure: Burnout in racial and ethnic minority groups (n=16 studies). Differences in burnout between underrepresented minority and other groups were inconclusive, though several studies had nuanced findings. The authors call for better measurement and mitigation among underrepresented groups.

## Cocoa butter lotion for prevention of striae gravidarum: a double-blind, randomised and placebo-controlled trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/osman-2008-18715434/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18715434/
Citation: Osman H, Usta IM, Rubeiz N et al (2008), BJOG
- In Stretch marks and fading scars: 210 first-time pregnant women in Lebanon, 175 completed (n=210). Stretch marks developed in 45.1% with cocoa butter and 48.8% with placebo (P=0.730), with no difference in severity.

## Topical preparations for preventing stretch marks in pregnancy
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/brennan-2012-23152199/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23152199/
Citation: Brennan M, Young G, Devane D (2012), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
- In Stretch marks and fading scars: 800 pregnant women in six trials (n=800). No statistically significant difference in developing stretch marks with topical preparations against placebo or no treatment (risk ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.03).

## Dominant modifiable risk factors for stroke in Ghana and Nigeria (SIREN): a case-control study
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/owolabi-2018-29496511/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29496511/
Citation: Owolabi MO, Sarfo F, Akinyemi R, Gebregziabher M et al (2018), Lancet Global Health
- In Stroke: signs to act on and what raises the risk: 2,118 adults with stroke confirmed by CT or MRI and 2,118 age- and gender-matched stroke-free controls at 15 sites in Nigeria and Ghana, 2014 to 2017 (n=4236). Eleven modifiable risk factors accounted for 98.2% of stroke risk. Hypertension had odds ratio 19.36 (95% CI 12.11 to 30.93) and a population-attributable risk of 90.8%. Dyslipidaemia (1.85), regular meat consumption (1.59), a raised waist-to-hip ratio (1.48), diabetes (2.58), low green leafy vegetable intake (2.43), stress (1.89), added salt at the table (2.14), cardiac disease (1.65), physical inactivity (2.13) and current smoking (4.42) followed. Of the cases, 68% had ischaemic and 32% haemorrhagic stroke.

## Ethnic and socioeconomic inequalities in stroke risk factors and primary prevention: the South London Stroke Register cohort study 1995-2024
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/emmett-2026-42472283/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42472283/
Citation: Emmett ES, Pantoja-Ruiz C, Lim E, Khanolkar AR et al (2026), EClinicalMedicine
- In Stroke: signs to act on and what raises the risk: 8,515 participants with first stroke in the South London Stroke Register, 1995 to 2024 (62.4% White, 15.5% Black Caribbean, 13.3% Black African) (n=8515). 12.0% of strokes in Black African participants (median age 59.0) occurred without any pre-stroke risk factor diagnosis, against 6.3% in White participants (median age 74.1). Black participants had more hypertension (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.29 for Black Caribbean, 1.47 for Black African) and diabetes (2.23 and 1.92) but less atrial fibrillation. Inequalities widened for hypertension and diabetes over time. 36% of strokes occurred in people with diagnosed but untreated risk factors; Black participants had higher treatment rates for hypertension and diabetes.

## Long-term trends in incidence and risk factors for ischaemic stroke subtypes: Prospective population study of the South London Stroke Register
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/wafa-2018-30289919/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30289919/
Citation: Wafa HA, Wolfe CDA, Rudd A, Wang Y (2018), PLoS Medicine
- In Stroke: signs to act on and what raises the risk: 3,088 first ischaemic stroke patients in the South London Stroke Register, 2000 to 2015 (n=3088). Age-adjusted ischaemic stroke incidence fell 43% (137.3 to 78.4 per 100,000 per year) across the period, in both White and Black groups, though the fall in the Black group was not significant (144.6 to 116.2; P=0.31). Statin use before stroke rose four-fold while preventive blood pressure and antiplatelet use fell, despite more hypertension.

## Clinical Features and Outcomes of Black Patients With Melanoma
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/wix-2024-38265787/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38265787/
Citation: Wix SN, Brown AB, Heberton M, Adamson AS et al (2024), JAMA Dermatology
- In Sunscreen on dark skin: 48 Black patients with melanoma at two Dallas centres, 2006-2022 (n=48). Of 40 primary cutaneous melanomas, 30 (75%) were on acral skin. 13 patients (27%) developed stage IV disease. Melanoma in Black individuals is about 1 in 100,000 a year.

## Photoprotection for skin of all color: Consensus and clinical guidance from an expert panel
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rigel-2022-34942296/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34942296/
Citation: Rigel DS, Taylor SC, Lim HW, Alexis AF et al (2022), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Sunscreen on dark skin: Dermatologists and photobiologists (expert panel) (n=panel). The panel states that visible light can induce hyperpigmentation in people with dark skin types (Fitzpatrick IV-VI) and exacerbate melasma. The specific product recommendations are in the full text, which I did not open.

## Misconceptions of photoprotection in skin of color
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/taylor-2022-34942293/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34942293/
Citation: Taylor SC, Alexis AF, Armstrong AW, Chiesa Fuxench ZC et al (2022), Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
- In Sunscreen on dark skin: Review (n=not stated). The authors report that misconceptions about the benefits of photoprotection, particularly among people with Fitzpatrick V-VI skin, are still common among clinicians and patients, and that use of photoprotection in skin of colour is low.

## Clinical studies of sweat rate reduction by an over-the-counter soft-solid antiperspirant and comparison with a prescription antiperspirant product in male panelists
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/swaile-2012-22385032/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22385032/
Citation: Swaile DF, Elstun LT, Benzing KW (2012), British Journal of Dermatology
- In Sweat, body odour and deodorant: Male panellists in hot-room sweat tests; ethnicity not stated in the abstract (n=not stated). The over-the-counter "clinical strength" antiperspirant reduced sweat rate on average 34% more than the prescription product and caused significantly less skin irritation; the authors say it can be an alternative for heavy sweating.

## Traction alopecia: the root of the problem
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/billero-2018-29670386/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29670386/
Citation: Billero V, Miteva M (2018), Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology
- In Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles: Women of African descent (clinical review) (n=not stated). Traction alopecia is described as affecting one in three women of African descent who wear traumatic styles for long periods. Risk rises with the extent of pulling, the duration, and chemical relaxation. Tight buns and ponytails, attached weaves or extensions and tight braids are believed to be highest risk. In late stages it can become permanent scarring. The authors state there is currently no cure.
- In Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles: Treatment trials (n=0). My search found no randomised trial of a treatment for traction alopecia. A 2018 review says there is no cure.

## Efficacy and Safety of Curcumin and Curcuma longa Extract in the Treatment of Arthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/zeng-2022-35935936/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35935936/
Citation: Zeng L, Yang T, Yang K, Yu G et al (2022), Frontiers in Immunology
- In Turmeric and curcumin supplements: People with arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile arthritis, gout) in 29 randomised trials (n=2396). Curcumin and turmeric extract improved pain and inflammation markers in arthritis in the pooled trials and appeared safe. The authors warn the trials are low quality and few, and that the conclusions need careful interpretation.

## Liver Injury Associated with Turmeric-A Growing Problem: Ten Cases from the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network [DILIN]
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/halegoua-demarzio-2023-36252717/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36252717/
Citation: Halegoua-DeMarzio D, Navarro V, Ahmad J, Avula B et al (2023), American Journal of Medicine
- In Turmeric and curcumin supplements: Ten people in the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network with turmeric-associated liver injury (eight women; nine White; median age 56) (n=10). Five were hospitalised and one died of acute liver failure. Injury began 1 to 4 months after starting, mostly hepatocellular, and turmeric was confirmed in all seven products tested (three also contained black pepper extract). Seven carried HLA-B*35:01 (allele frequency 0.45 against 0.06 to 0.07 in controls). The authors say turmeric liver injury appears to be increasing.

## Evidence of turmeric adulteration with lead chromate across South Asia
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/forsyth-2024-39053552/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39053552/
Citation: Forsyth JE, Mistree D, Nash E, Angrish M et al (2024), Science of the Total Environment
- In Turmeric and curcumin supplements: Turmeric root and powder samples from bazaars in 23 cities in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Nepal (2020 to 2021) (n=356). Fourteen per cent (51 samples) had lead above 2 micrograms per gram, and samples at 18 or more had lead-to-chromium ratios pointing to lead chromate added as a colouring. Lead levels exceeded 1,000 micrograms per gram in Patna (India), Karachi and Peshawar (Pakistan).

## Inequalities in type 2 diabetes incidence in a multiethnic population: a cohort study investigating the impact of ethnicity, migration and mental health comorbidities
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/shamsutdinova-2026-42018145/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42018145/
Citation: Shamsutdinova D, Stahl D, Das-Munshi J (2026), Diabetologia
- In Type 2 diabetes risk and blood sugar: About 340,000 adults without diabetes in South London primary care, followed 2012-2019 (n=340000). South Asian, Black African and Black Caribbean groups had 2 to 3 times the type 2 diabetes risk of White British people, which was only partly explained by socioeconomic and clinical factors. Being born outside the UK raised risk by 29% across all groups. Depression, anxiety and severe mental illness were also linked to higher risk.

## Vitamin D-binding protein and vitamin D status of black Americans and white Americans
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/powe-2013-24256378/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24256378/
Citation: Powe CE, Evans MK, Wenger J, Zonderman AB et al (2013), New England Journal of Medicine
- In Vitamin D and dark skin: 2,085 Black and White adults in Baltimore (Healthy Aging in Neighborhoods of Diversity across the Life Span) (n=2085). Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 15.6 ng/ml in Black participants against 25.8 in White. Vitamin D-binding protein was also lower (168 against 337 ug/ml). In people homozygous for the same genotype, bioavailable 25(OH)D was similar (2.9 against 3.1 ng/ml). Bone mineral density was higher in Black participants (1.05 against 0.94 g/cm2).
- In Vitamins and supplements: what the NHS says: 2,085 Black and white US adults (n=2085). Mean total 25(OH)D was 15.6 against 25.8 ng/mL in Black against white participants, and vitamin D-binding protein was 168 against 337 micrograms/mL; Black participants had higher bone mineral density. Genetic variants explained about 79% of variation in the binding protein.

## A randomized controlled trial of vitamin D3 supplementation in African American women
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/aloia-2005-16043680/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16043680/
Citation: Aloia JF, Talwar SA, Pollack S, Yeh J (2005), Archives of Internal Medicine
- In Vitamin D and dark skin: 208 healthy Black postmenopausal American women aged 50-75 (n=208). No significant difference in bone mineral density between vitamin D and placebo groups at any point; no relationship between blood level reached and bone loss. No significant adverse events were attributed to vitamin D.

## Vitamin D Supplementation in Elderly Black Women Does Not Prevent Bone Loss: A Randomized Controlled Trial
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/aloia-2018-29905969/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29905969/
Citation: Aloia J, Fazzari M, Islam S, Mikhail M et al (2018), Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
- In Vitamin D and dark skin: 260 healthy Black American women aged 60 or over (n=260). No bone-loss benefit of vitamin D over placebo; the groups were equivalent. Baseline 25(OH)D was 54.8 nmol/L. The authors concluded that Black Americans should have the same vitamin D exposure as White Americans.

## Effect of vitamin D supplementation on bone health in Black, Asian and other non-White ethnic adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/dong-2026-42815577/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42815577/
Citation: Dong H, Shardow JY, Mulligan K, Oyibo P et al (2026), American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
- In Vitamin D and dark skin: 12 trials, 8,023 non-White adults (Black African, South Asian, South Korean, Chinese) (n=8023). Of 8 trials measuring bone density, one in South Asians found a benefit. A meta-analysis showed a higher bone-specific alkaline phosphatase marker (SMD 0.96, 95% CI 0.09-1.83), which lost significance after excluding one clinically distinct study. One fracture study (n=5,106) found no difference. The authors conclude evidence supporting supplementation for bone health in non-White adults remains limited.

## Two Phase 3, Randomized, Controlled Trials of Ruxolitinib Cream for Vitiligo
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/rosmarin-2022-36260792/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36260792/
Citation: Rosmarin D, Passeron T, Pandya AG et al (2022), New England Journal of Medicine
- In Vitiligo: 674 people aged 12 or over with nonsegmental vitiligo in North America and Europe (two trials); how many were Black is not in the abstract (n=674). At week 24, 29.8% (trial 1) and 30.9% (trial 2) on ruxolitinib cream reached a 75% improvement in facial vitiligo score, against 7.4% and 11.4% on vehicle.

## Efficacy and Safety of Ruxolitinib Cream in Vitiligo by Patient Characteristic Subgroups: Descriptive Pooled Analysis From Two Phase 3 Studies
URL: https://vilivity.com/studies/seneschal-2025-40156697/
PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40156697/
Citation: Seneschal J, Wolkerstorfer A, Desai SR et al (2025), Dermatology and Therapy
- In Vitiligo: The same 674 patients, pooled post hoc (n=674). At week 52, 50.3% of those applying ruxolitinib cream throughout reached the facial score target; responses were seen across subgroups including Fitzpatrick skin type. The abstract gives no numbers for dark skin types.

# Comparisons

## Relaxer, silk press or natural hair
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/relaxer-vs-silk-press-vs-natural/
Verdict: Relaxers have the most data, and it is mixed on cancer and clear that relaxed hair under tight styles carries the highest hair-loss risk. Heat styling and going natural have not been tested in people, so the entries cannot rank the three on outcomes.

## Shea butter, cocoa butter or coconut oil
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/shea-vs-cocoa-vs-coconut/
Verdict: None of the three has been shown to beat another: plain shea is untested on skin, cocoa butter made no difference to stretch marks in one trial, and coconut oil's evidence is lab work on hair strands. The linked entries report no comparison between them.

## Braids, locs or wigs and your edges
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/braids-vs-locs-vs-wigs-for-edges/
Verdict: In each entry the risk to the hairline is pull, whatever the style is called: tight braids, tight twisting at the roots, and glue or tight sew-ins. Braids carry the firmest harm evidence, from observational data, while locs and wigs have not been tested for protecting hair.

## Mineral, chemical or tinted sunscreen on dark skin
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/mineral-vs-chemical-vs-tinted-sunscreen/
Verdict: The bank has no head-to-head of mineral, chemical and tinted sunscreens on dark skin, so it cannot rank them. What the entry supports is a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher daily, with an iron-oxide tint as one way to blend in and guard against visible light.

## Razor, clippers, hair-removal cream or laser for razor bumps
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/razor-vs-clippers-vs-cream-vs-laser-for-razor-bumps/
Verdict: The only comparisons in the bank are shaving frequency in one trial and small trials of creams against a razor, which gave fewer bumps but more irritation; clippers have not been tested against razors. Laser can work in medium to dark skin but carries a higher risk of burns and dark or pale marks, so the entry advises an experienced clinician.

## Meditation, breathwork or cold exposure for stress
URL: https://vilivity.com/compare/meditation-vs-breathwork-vs-cold-exposure-for-stress/
Verdict: Meditation has the best-tested evidence of the three, including a trial in Black adults, though that result is about heart events and the stress benefit comes from a large review in which it was no better than other treatments. Breathwork lowers stress a little in adults generally with mixed results in African American studies, while the cold exposure entry rests on muscle soreness, warns against believing it treats depression or anxiety, and carries a harm signal.
